papers.title: Biodiversity science’s missing species
papers.abstract: This week in the United States, a Trump administration rule took effect that narrows the meaning of “harm” under the Endangered Species Act by abandoning a long-standing interpretation that recognized substantial habitat destruction as a way of injuring or killing protected wildlife. Actions that directly harm or destroy animals remain prohibited, but altering the places where they feed, shelter, or reproduce may no longer qualify as harm in the same way. This distinction makes little ecological sense. A species cannot be separated from the living system that sustains it. Destroy nesting trees, pollute a stream, or remove essential food plants, and the line between harming an animal and harming its habitat quickly collapses. This change is also not happening in isolation: The public comment period closes next week for the administration’s proposal to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule, which has limited road construction and timber harvesting across vast areas of national forest.

papers.title: Germline EGFR T790M mutation and lung cancer risk
papers.abstract: Most lung cancers are tobacco related, with genetic factors influencing smoking behavior identified through genome-wide association studies. However, inherited risk in familial and non-smoking-related lung cancers, including risk in carriers of EGFR T790M, remains poorly understood. Here, in more than 3.3 million individuals, the EGFR T790M germline variant is significantly associated with lung cancer risk, with no increased risk for 17 other cancers and no interaction with polygenic risk. This risk exceeds that conferred by smoking and is several-fold higher in never-smokers. Global geographic and ancestry analyses show higher T790M prevalence in the US than in British- and Irish-descendant populations, reflecting a Southern Appalachian founder event about 200 to 225 years ago, increasing regional prevalence and affecting those of British, Irish, and African descent. Recognition of high-risk carriers may inform targeted genetic testing and screening strategies.

papers.title: Multi-organelle signatures map cell-state diversity and metabolic adaptation in tissues
papers.abstract: Cell-state diversity drives tissue adaptability, repair, and disease resilience, but capturing this complexity is a challenge. Current approaches rely on transcriptional profiling and overlook organelle structure, a key indicator of metabolism and stress. We developed spatial Organellomics (sOrganellomics), an imaging workflow that integrates automated segmentation with machine learning to classify and spatially map cell states from multi-organelle signatures. In liver and pancreas, these signatures distinguished broad cellular classes. In liver, sOrganellomics revealed that zonal position did not fully explain organelle-defined hepatocyte categories. Instead, hepatocytes formed intermixed communities within canonical zones, supporting a refined subzonal diversity model. Nutritional stress reshaped this organization. Intravital imaging linked fasting-induced organelle remodeling with altered mitochondrial membrane potential in vivo, supporting multi-organelle architecture as a structural readout of tissue adaptation.

papers.title: Transcriptome-based classification in mice with ASD-risk mutations
papers.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition with a strong genetic component. Large-scale human genetic studies have identified >1200 ASD-risk genes. We report a sex-balanced atlas of 1008 prefrontal RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) profiles from 17 mouse lines carrying ASD-risk mutations. Our analysis identified two opposing transcriptomic states. The two groups differed in sex bias, regional specificity, developmental stability, cell type remodeling, and responses to fluoxetine and lithium. Single-nucleus RNA-seq revealed broader cell type remodeling in group 1 than in group 2, and cell type–specific modules showed reciprocal associations that mirrored bulk transcriptomic signatures. The framework classifies independent mouse lines and identifies subgroups with conserved synaptic directionality, supporting molecular stratification.

papers.title: Quantum jumps of sound
papers.abstract: Quantum mechanics predicts that a vibrating object’s energy comes in discrete packets, yet no measurement of its position reveals this discreteness. Resolving individual energy levels requires a qualitatively different measurement, one coupling to the resonator’s energy rather than its displacement. We use a superconducting qubit dispersively coupled to a nanomechanical resonator to perform repeated quantum nondemolition measurements of the phonon number. An aligned transfer-print technique integrating the qubit and resonator yields a mechanical lifetime of T 1 = 2.1 milliseconds and a dispersive shift of 2 χ / 2 π = 328 kilohertz per phonon. We heralded single-phonon states with 85% fidelity and observed quantum jumps between the resonator’s first excited state and ground state. These discontinuous transitions are a striking manifestation of quantum mechanics in a massive, vibrating object.

papers.title: Atmospheric methane lifetime during the Last Glacial Maximum was reduced owing to dust-mediated chlorine chemistry
papers.abstract: Atmospheric methane (CH 4 ) plays a central role in Earth’s climate, yet the drivers of its decline during the high-dust conditions of glacial periods, such as the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM), remain uncertain. Previous explanations imply source-driven changes, assuming an atmospheric lifetime comparable to that of present day. Recent work shows that interactions between mineral dust and sea salt aerosols produce CH 4 -removing chlorine radicals. In this work, we show that during the LGM, CH 4 lifetime shortened to 7.8 years, 20% lower than that of present day. Chlorine contributed ~15% of global CH 4 loss, fourfold that of present day. Our results reproduce ice core CH 4 isotopic evidence, demonstrating that stronger-than-assumed atmospheric sinks can explain CH 4 variability without invoking substantial source changes, highlighting the overlooked role of chlorine chemistry in the glacial CH 4 budget.

papers.title: Fast, continuous, and coherent atom reloading in a neutral-atom qubit array
papers.abstract: Neutral-atom quantum processors are a promising platform for scalable quantum computing. An obstacle to implementing deep quantum circuits is managing atom loss. Current approaches require at least an order of magnitude longer time than gate and measurement operations to replace lost atoms. In this work, we demonstrate fast, continuous atom reloading that leverages the metastable 171 Yb qubit. A continuously loaded reservoir near the computation zone enables on-demand atom extraction with tweezers up to 500 times per second. New, stochastically filled qubit arrays can be initialized 30 times per second when including single-atom preparation, nondestructive imaging, and initialization. Existing qubits in the metastable state are undisturbed by the reloading process. This work establishes a complete foundation for the implementation of fast, fully fault-tolerant quantum circuits with unlimited depth.

papers.title: Nuclear tests at Mt. Mantap have reactivated intraplate faults
papers.abstract: Underground nuclear explosions typically produce short-lived seismic sequences that decay rapidly after testing ceases. By contrast, seismicity near the Punggye-ri nuclear test site at Mt. Mantap in the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea has persisted and intensified for years after the final large-yield explosion in 2017, evolving from diffuse activity to spatially organized distribution along fault-controlled structures. Analysis of 17 years of continuous waveform data reveals a progressive increase in seismicity and delayed reactivation of shallow faults. Earthquakes cluster beneath asymmetric topography, indicating progressive stress redistribution within a critically stressed crustal volume. These observations challenge conventional expectations, showing that under specific geological conditions, underground nuclear testing can drive multiyear fault reactivation and extend posttest seismicity well beyond the immediate aftermath of an explosion.

papers.title: Free inquiry depends on freedom of movement
OpenAI leap triggers ‘existential crisis’ in math
papers.abstract: Solution to Navier-Stokes problem has mathematicians at odds over AI’s implications for field

papers.abstract: Stratifying genetic mutations points to different pathophysiological pathways to a neurodevelopmental disorder

papers.title: Ancient DNA unveils distinctive ancestries in the Bronze and Iron Ages of East Tianshan
papers.abstract: The East Tianshan Mountains occupy a key corridor between Central and East Asia, but their population history remains poorly understood. Here we report genome-wide data from 135 ancient individuals from 11 archaeological sites. We identify a previously unrecognized Bronze Age admixture between populations related to Yellow River millet farmers and steppe pastoralists associated with the Chemurchek culture. In contrast, we find little genetic contribution from contemporaneous middle-to-late Bronze Age steppe pastoralists, despite their eastward expansion across the Eurasian Steppe. By the Iron Age, regional populations had become more heterogeneous, incorporating additional eastern and steppe-related sources while retaining variable contributions from Early Bronze Age groups. These results reveal sustained demographic interactions in eastern Central Asia nearly 1800 years preceding the establishment of the historic Silk Road.

papers.title: Alberta’s ill-advised black bear hunting
The Virtual Biotech: A multi-agent AI framework for therapeutic discovery and development
papers.abstract: Drug development requires evidence integration across biological scales and modalities, but relevant tools are fragmented. We introduce the Virtual Biotech, an organization of artificial intelligence (AI) agents modeled on a drug-development company, with agentic divisions spanning target discovery, safety assessment, modality selection, and clinical development. We demonstrate its utility at three drug-development decision points. First, over 37,000 agents annotated outcomes from 55,984 trials and found that drugs targeting cell-type-specific genes were 48% more likely to reach market with 32% fewer adverse events. Second, it integrated multimodal evidence to propose a therapeutic strategy in lung cancer. Third, it analyzed a terminated ulcerative colitis trial and inferred potential mechanisms of failure. These results demonstrate that human-guided multi-agent systems can conduct transparent, multiscale analyses to inform therapeutic-development decisions.

Top income taxation: Efficiency, social welfare and the Laffer curve
papers.abstract: This paper develops a structural framework for analyzing top income taxation and applies it to six decades of U.S. tax history and to eight other advanced economies. The paper derives explicit expressions for top-bracket tax revenue and total excess burden across the full range of tax rates, while preserving local consistency with the sufficient-statistics approach of Saez (2001) . Applied to the United States, the analysis implies that the current excess burden of the top federal tax bracket is $101 billion and that raising the top marginal tax rate to its revenue-maximizing level of 72 percent would increase annual revenue by $111 billion, given a taxable income elasticity of 0.25. The current tax rate is lower than what is consistent with a purely utility-based notion of social welfare. By contrast, Nordic countries and the United States in earlier decades appear to have operated at tax rates exceeding revenue-maximizing levels.

papers.title: Prosecutor politics: The impact of election cycles on criminal sentencing in the era of rising incarceration
papers.abstract: I investigate how political incentives affect the behavior of district attorneys (DAs). I develop a theoretical model that predicts DAs will increase sentencing intensity in an election period compared to the period prior. To empirically test this prediction, I compile one of the most comprehensive datasets to date on the political careers of all district attorneys in office during the steepest rise in incarceration in U.S. history (roughly 1986-2006). Using quasi-experimental methods, I find causal evidence that being in a DA election year increases total admissions per capita and total months sentenced per capita. I estimate that the election year effects on admissions are akin to moving 0.85 standard deviations along the distribution of DA behavior within state (e.g., going from the 50th to 80th percentile in sentencing intensity). I find evidence that election effects are larger (1) when DA elections are contested, (2) in Republican counties, and (3) in the southern United States--all these factors are consistent with the perspective that election effects arise from political incentives influencing DAs. Further, I find that district attorney election effects decline over the period 1986-2006, in tandem with U.S. public opinion softening regarding criminal punishment. These findings suggest DA behavior may respond to voter preferences--in particular to public sentiment regarding the harshness of the court system.

papers.title: Flood Protection and Adaptation Labor in Jakarta, Indonesia
papers.abstract: Jakarta is undergoing an infrastructural transformation in response to increasing flood risks, constructing new dams, flood canals, reservoirs and retention ponds, and ongoing normalization of the city’s rivers. However, one crucial element of responding to severe flood risks that has so far been overlooked in Jakarta and other vulnerable cities is the work of building and maintaining this flood protection infrastructure. In this article, we respond to this research gap by analyzing the work of the Blue Troops, a new provincial workforce who construct and maintain Jakarta’s flood protection infrastructure. Drawing from extensive fieldwork interviewing and observing the Blue Troops in Jakarta, we catalog their adaptation labor practices, showing the accumulated health and safety risks of their work. At the same time, we demonstrate that the workers find this to be reliable and meaningful collective work, essential for reproducing cities in a time of climate catastrophe. In short, we show that workers trade precarious labor practices and bodily risks against secure public-sector employment and a sense of contributing to their city. This article, therefore, contributes to a growing scholarly concern with the labor implications of climate change, suggesting that the organization, conditions, and value of this work will be crucial political and analytical terrain.

papers.title: The Role of Regional Recombination Capacity in Shaping the Technological Space
papers.abstract: This article investigates the role of regions’ recombinatorial technological capacity in shaping the technological space. To do so, we identify novel combinations of technologies and track their evolution by tracing all subsequent inventions that incorporate the same combination. Building on the concepts of relatedness and geographic proximity, we focus on the relevance of the technological antecedents of a pair of technologies combined for the first time in determining their success. This is due through the estimation of the likelihood of a new technological combination eventually becoming embedded within the broader knowledge space. Using patent data from 1976 to 2022 in the case of the European regions, we find strong evidence that a higher degree of relatedness between the technological antecedents of the two combined technologies significantly increases the likelihood that the combination will be reused in future inventions. Additionally, we find that the success of a new combination also benefits from the presence of dissimilar knowledge—not directly involved in the combination’s antecedents but accessible within the surrounding technological environment. In these cases, the greater the relatedness between the new invention’s antecedents and the broader regional knowledge base, the more likely it is to generate a high number of follow-on inventions and contribute meaningfully to the formation of the technological space.

papers.title: Private Equity and Gas Emissions: Evidence from Electric Power Plants
papers.abstract: Abstract We examine the effect of private equity buyouts on the environmental performance of U.S. fossil fuel power plants. Output-scaled CO 2 emissions are, on average, 4.2% lower after buyouts, predominantly because of fuel-saving improvements in production efficiency. Emission intensities decline more significantly following buyouts backed by pro-ESG private equity because of not only greater efficiency gains but also enhanced emission control. Our results suggest that while private equity firms are effective at implementing environmentally beneficial operational changes that also increase profitability, they do not have strong incentives to undertake environmentally beneficial changes that are privately costly, except for those with pro-ESG preferences.

papers.title: Cultural transmission, property rights, and treatment of the elderly
Frontier technology adopters and the aggregate decline of routine jobs
papers.abstract: We provide micro-founded evidence on how establishment-level adoption of frontier technologies shapes the economy-wide occupational employment structure. Linking survey data on technology adoption between 2011 and 2016 by 1660 German incumbent establishments to administrative worker records, we find that establishments adopting frontier technologies such as AI or smart factories contributed disproportionately to the overall decline in routine jobs. Crucially, these overall effects do not stem from average within-establishment adjustments but from a subset of large and less routine-intensive adopters. Our findings highlight that frontier technology adoption is not routine-replacing per se: establishment size and an initially non-routine-intensive workforce are key conditions for de-routinization to occur.

papers.title: Global inequality in vaccine access, mortality and economy: An agent-based exploration
papers.abstract: We develop an agent-based model to study the economic and public health impact of global vaccine inequality. Our model contains two world regions (higher-income vs. lower-income) and captures the co-evolution between economic activity, the spread and evolution of a hypothetical novel pandemic virus, and public health responses. We calibrate and estimate the model parameters empirically with data from the COVID-19 pandemic to capture the economic and social response to pandemic viruses in both regions. Our simulations suggest that vaccine inequality can drastically exacerbate inequality in mortality in the two regions. This is because the lower-income region suffers from drastically increased mortality, while the higher-income region generally only experiences a small (if any) decrease in mortality in most simulations. However, vaccine inequality harms both regions economically. This is driven by the fact that severe vaccine inequality eliminates the prospect of eradicating a mutating virus. Any trade-off between mortality in higher- and lower-income regions can be mitigated by increasing the production of vaccine doses. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the higher-income region benefits economically from paying for increased vaccine production.

papers.title: The petrochemical pivot: geostrategic globalization and the future of oil and gas
papers.abstract: While demand for oil as an energy source is projected to decline, petrochemical demand is expected to grow significantly. Toward securing future profitability, oil and gas (O&G) firms are pivoting toward petrochemicals. We contend that this ‘petrochemical pivot’ demands an explicitly geopolitical account of firm strategy; it is unfolding within a conjuncture shaped by intensifying geopolitical rivalry and the global resurgence of state capitalist practices. By foregrounding these tensions, alongside changes in the geography of petrochemical production, we analyze how transnational private and state-owned O&G firms navigate these shifts. We argue that divergent firm-level strategies constitute forms of ‘geostrategic’ globalization as firms seek to hedge against or align with major energy powers. Through four vignettes of leading International and National Oil Companies (IOCs and NOCs), we show how geopolitical imperatives and variegated strategies are reconfiguring fossil capital within a fragmenting global energy order.

papers.title: Ergodic robust maximisation of asymptotic growth with stochastic factor processes
papers.abstract: Abstract We consider a robust asymptotic growth problem under model uncertainty in the presence of stochastic factors. We fix two inputs representing the instantaneous covariance for the asset price process $X$ X , which depends on an additional stochastic factor process $Y$ Y , as well as the invariant joint density of $X$ X and $Y$ Y . The factor process $Y$ Y has continuous trajectories, but is not required to be a semimartingale. Our setup allows drift uncertainty in $X$ X and model uncertainty for the local dynamics of $Y$ Y . This work builds on a recent paper of Kardaras and Robertson [20], where the authors consider an analogous problem but without the additional factor process. Under suitable, quite weak assumptions, we are able to characterise the robust optimal trading strategy and the robust optimal growth rate. The optimal strategy is shown to be functionally generated and, remarkably, does not depend on the factor process $Y$ Y . Our result provides a comprehensive answer to a question proposed by Fernholz in 2002. We also show that the optimal strategy remains optimal even in the more restricted case where $Y$ Y is a semimartingale and the joint covariation structure of $X$ X and $Y$ Y is prescribed as a function of $X$ X and $Y$ Y . Our results are obtained using a combination of techniques from partial differential equations, calculus of variations and generalised Dirichlet forms.

papers.title: Analysis of Markov chain approximation for regime-switching jump-diffusions with nonsmooth coefficients: deformed contour integration approach
Care without value: institutional valuation and social reproduction
papers.abstract: Reproductive labour is essential to social reproduction and capitalist economies, yet it remains persistently undervalued despite increasing institutional recognition. This article argues that reproductive devaluation cannot be explained solely by invisibility, unpaid labour, or exclusion from economic measurement. Drawing on feminist political economy, the article develops the Reproductive Value Axis (RVA) to analyse how institutions differentially integrate reproductive labour through wage relations, welfare systems, measurement practices, and knowledge infrastructures. The RVA shows that recognition does not necessarily produce transformation: reproductive activities may become visible, compensated, or regulated while remaining shaped by unequal distributions of responsibility and institutional support. By shifting attention from whether reproductive labour possesses value to how value is institutionally produced and allocated, this article advances a framework for understanding the governance and politics of reproductive valuation.

papers.title: The historical evolution of international business: growth trajectory of an academic field of study
The impact of migration and institutions on new business creation: integrating social capital theory and institutional theory
papers.abstract: Abstract Migration and remittances now shape entrepreneurial ecosystems across the developing world, yet their effects remain contradictory: financial remittances sometimes spur new ventures and sometimes suppress them, and emigrant stocks produce inconsistent outcomes across contexts. We help to resolve this puzzle by theorizing nonlinear relationships and institutional contingencies. Drawing on transnational social capital theory and institutional theory, we introduce Social Connectivity Capacity (SCC), the structural capacity of transnational networks to transmit entrepreneurially relevant knowledge, operationalized as the product of emigrant stocks and internet penetration. Panel analyses of 85 migrant-sending countries (2006–2020) show that financial remittances exhibit a convex, accelerating relationship with new business creation, while SCC follows an inverted U-shape. Formal institutional quality moderates both relationships: stronger governance amplifies remittance-driven entrepreneurship and shifts SCC's optimum rightward. Results are robust across GLS and panel-corrected-SE estimators and to log-transformation. These findings account for prior mixed evidence and show that migration's entrepreneurial effects depend jointly on remittance intensity, digital connectivity, and institutional context. Policymakers in migrant-sending countries can therefore strengthen entrepreneurial outcomes by calibrating diaspora engagement strategies to their specific combination of remittance intensity, digital infrastructure, and governance quality.

papers.title: What Future for Genetics in Management Research?
papers.abstract: Abstract The author teams on this Point‐Counterpoint debate agree that the search for genetic explanations of organizational behaviours has been underwhelming – yet they have very different visions for the future of genetics in management research. The Point argues for a deeper dive into the field of genetics to ensure more precise measurement and make better causal inferences. In contrast, the Counterpoint cautions against reducing complex human behaviour to molecular causes and sees genetics as better suited to explain distal evolutionary conditions from which behaviours emerge. The introduction to this collection summarizes the core ideas in each article and their recommendations. The introduction then positions the Point‐Counterpoint debate against the broader challenge of seeking to advance management research with knowledge from a different discipline. It concludes with a call for researchers to carefully consider when and under what conditions it is warranted to search for genetic explanations, rather than uncritically embracing genetic explanations or dismissing them outright.

papers.title: Beyond Value: On the Role of Symmetry in Demand for Information
papers.abstract: We study demand for symmetric and asymmetric information sources in the laboratory. Although participants respond to incentives and instrumental considerations, they exhibit a systematic bias towards symmetric sources. These patterns persist among individuals with higher cognitive abilities and better task comprehension, and they are not accounted for by their elicited subjective beliefs. This paper was accepted by Dorothea Kübler, behavioural economics and decision analysis. Funding: This project was supported by a British Academy/Leverhulme Small Research [Grant SG171679]. R. Z. acknowledges support from the Israel Science Foundation [Grant 524/24]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08449 .

papers.title: Strategic Reporting Through Counterpoised Disclosure: Evidence From the Biopharma Industry
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines managers' strategic use of counterpoised disclosure, defined as the concurrent dissemination of product information to mitigate the expected impact of a material negative disclosure about another product. We focus on the biopharmaceutical industry, where individual drug outcomes have significant valuation implications. As such, investors rely heavily on product‐level disclosures in this industry, which is characterized by high uncertainty, information asymmetry, and limited traditional financial metrics. Using 8‐K filings and press releases (8‐Ks/PRs) reporting drug development milestones, we empirically support three predictions. First, managers are more likely to provide counterpoised disclosures in 8‐Ks/PRs revealing negative news (e.g., Food and Drug Administration [FDA] rejections) than those revealing positive news (e.g., FDA approvals). Second, we confirm that such disclosures attenuate negative market reactions. Last, we document that counterpoised drugs are more likely to progress through subsequent FDA approvals as compared with those that do not receive counterpoised disclosure. Combined, our findings suggest counterpoised disclosure reflects a strategic managerial disclosure mechanism used to assist investors in assessing the valuation implications of a negative product signal within the firm's broader drug development portfolio.

papers.title: Managing the Emotional Dynamics of Open Strategy
papers.abstract: Open strategy (OS) increases transparency and actor involvement in strategy making, promising benefits such as wider expertise and heightened commitment. Yet, its adoption and enactment can trigger emotions among the different actors involved that prevent these benefits from materializing. Drawing on action research across eleven OS processes in large and medium-sized European firms, this article identifies emotional challenges spanning adoption, formulation, and implementation. This article introduces the concept of “emotional architecture”—the deliberate design of processes through which top managers anticipate and manage emotional dynamics—and distills five design principles to help top managers successfully implement OS processes.

papers.title: Beyond a Technocentric Transition: A Diverse Economies Perspective for Social Justice in Circular Economy Business Models
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The circular economy, dominated by capitalocentric, technocentric, and eco‐modernist discourses, risks perpetuating systemic injustice because of its limited consideration of the social and of what is possible. In this article, we examine how social justice can be embedded into circular business models (CBMs)—key drivers of the circular economy transition—within and beyond capitalist enterprises, traditionally the focus of CBM literature. Building on a systematic literature review of 55 articles and informed by a diverse economies framework, we constructed an inventory of interventions that can help firms uphold recognition, procedural, and distributive justice. Our analysis of these interventions, based on the extent to which they are embedded into business models (justice as an add‐on vs. justice as a design principle) and deviate from the dominant capitalist paradigm, reveals a typology of strategies that firms implicitly adopt to push just outcomes at the system level. This article also describes structural conditions that debunk the assumption that firm‐level justice interventions automatically translate to desirable system‐level outcomes (i.e., addressing systemic injustice). Analyzing CBMs through a combined diverse economies and social justice framework encourages us to recognize a greater diversity of economic and enterprise activity as legitimate, question the extent to which enterprises can achieve systemic change under a capitalist system, and (re)ignite a connection between micro and macrolevels of analysis called for in the strategic management literature.

papers.title: How Organizations Evaluate Eco‐Innovation Investability: A Managerial Cognition Perspective
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Eco‐innovation is widely recognized as a key mechanism through which firms pursue sustainability objectives. However, little is known about the microfoundations through which specific eco‐innovation initiatives secure internal investment support within organizations. Drawing on managerial cognition theory, this study examines how organizations evaluate the investability of eco‐innovation initiatives. Based on 20 semi‐structured interviews conducted within a large multinational energy company and analyzed using the Gioia methodology, the study identifies three complementary managerial cognitive maps that inform organizational evaluations of eco‐innovation initiatives: a strategic inevitability map, which frames sustainability as a strategic priority; a dual‐value causal map, which links environmental and economic value; and a feasibility map, which assesses technological maturity, scalability, and implementation risk. We further identify governance mechanisms, including innovation committees and stage‐gate systems, as organizational arenas where these complementary managerial perspectives are articulated and considered during investment deliberations. Findings show that organizational investment decisions draw upon complementary managerial perspectives concerning strategic legitimacy, value creation, and implementation feasibility. By conceptualizing eco‐innovation investability as the organizational evaluation through which eco‐innovation initiatives become eligible for organizational resource commitment, this study develops a microfoundational explanation of eco‐innovation investment decisions and extends both eco‐innovation research and managerial cognition theory.

papers.title: Climate Policy Uncertainty and Entrepreneurship: Lubricant or Retardant?
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT In the context of global climate crisis, climate policy uncertainty has become an increasingly prominent factor influencing economic development and technological advancement. This research aims to examine the relationship between Chinese climate policy uncertainty (CCPU) and entrepreneurship and further explore its underlying mechanisms. The findings reveal that CCPU is positively associated with entrepreneurship. Mechanism analysis suggests that financing conditions and green innovation may serve as important channels through which CCPU is associated with entrepreneurship. Further analysis shows that CCPU is linked to higher levels of entrepreneurship in coastal regions and cities with advanced financial development and a favorable business environment. It also shows a stronger positive relationship with medium‐sized enterprises and productive service industries. Notably, only when the level of regional resource misallocation is below the threshold value of 1.3207 (the 59th percentile) and the level of digital development is above the threshold value of 0.1570 (the top 14%) can this effect be realized. This study not only contributes to the existing literature on the consequences of CCPU but also provides policy recommendations aimed at fostering high‐quality entrepreneurship under conditions of uncertainty.

papers.title: From Cosmetic Standards to Circular Value: A Systematic Review of Business Strategies for Suboptimal Foods
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Suboptimal foods, that is, safe and nutritious products that deviate from market standards because of cosmetic defects, packaging damage, or proximity to date labels, constitute a major source of avoidable food waste. Evidence on how firms can reduce this waste and capture value still remains fragmented across disciplines and supply‐chain stages. We conduct a PRISMA‐guided systematic literature review of empirical research on interventions addressing suboptimal foods, drawing on business strategy, marketing, operations, and sustainability studies. Using thematic synthesis, we classify interventions along the food waste hierarchy and map them across upstream and downstream supply‐chain stages. The literature concentrates on prevention‐oriented approaches (pricing, packaging and labeling, assortment and placement, communication, nudging, inventory and logistics, and coordination), while reuse strategies (reprocessing and redistribution) receive less attention and are rarely evaluated at scale. Across contexts, isolated interventions often underperform, and stronger outcomes emerge when marketing levers are aligned with operational practices and governance choices (e.g., procurement standards, forecasting, and channel design). Retailers act as pivotal gatekeepers by setting quality norms that shape both upstream production and downstream consumer expectations. We synthesize the main mechanisms, trade‐offs, and boundary conditions and outline an agenda for more field‐based, cost‐sensitive, and cross‐country research. Overall, managing suboptimal foods should be treated as a strategic capability to embed waste prevention into business models that jointly advance environmental performance and competitive advantage.

papers.title: Digital Product Passport as a Transparency Tool for Sustainable Fashion Retailing: Benefits, Barriers, and Strategic Implications
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Transparency is increasingly recognized as a critical factor in advancing the sustainability of production processes and products, particularly in fashion retailing. In response, the European Union is developing standardized transparency mechanisms, most notably the Digital Product Passport (DPP). Despite its imminent adoption in the fashion industry, research on the DPP remains scarce, especially from the perspectives of its direct stakeholders: retailers and consumers. This study examines how retailers and consumers perceive transparency tools like the DPP, focusing on the key drivers and barriers to its adoption. Using signaling theory and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT/UTAUT2) framework, the research involved a qualitative analysis of retailers' perceptions followed by a mixed‐method exploration of consumer views. The findings reveal that although retailers as signal strategists can enhance product oversight and discourage unethical practices through the DPP, benefiting from signal observability and credibility, they face challenges due to signal cost (implementation costs) and signal observability (standardization issues). Consumers, on the other hand, recognize that the DPP can improve their decision‐making and increase awareness of sustainability in a pleasant way, thereby enhancing their purchasing experience. The benefits of the DPP may help mitigate cultural barriers and skepticism about green initiatives by providing comparable information. This paper advances theory by using signaling theory to interpret stakeholders' qualitative perceptions of the DPP as a transparency signal, while applying UTAUT/UTAUT2 to examine consumers' intention to use DPP. It offers guidance for retailers and policymakers on overcoming adoption barriers and maximizing transparency benefits.

papers.title: Internal Drivers and Financial Outcomes of Global Hospitality Chains' Green Strategies: An Application of the Natural Resource–Based View
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Despite growing concerns for protecting the natural environment, research on how eco‐friendly practices of firms in the hospitality industry impact their performance is relatively limited. Using the natural resource–based view of the firm as a theoretical platform, we propose a conceptual model focusing on the internal drivers and performance outcomes of environmental strategies, which was tested with secondary data collected from 116 global hospitality chains. The results indicate a strong association between the hospitality chain's green human resource management, strategic proactivity, and environmental targeting with each of the four environmental strategies examined, namely, product/service eco‐friendliness, resource efficiency, waste/emissions management, and green procurement. However, although the first two strategies were found to positively affect the firm's operating ROA, the last two strategies had a negative effect on it.

papers.title: From Message Framing to Purchase Intention: The Mediating Role of Attitude Towards the Message in Pro‐Environmental Food Communication
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Developing effective communication for pro‐environmental foods requires understanding the persuasive link between message stimuli and consumer response. This study integrates message framing theory with the dual mediation hypothesis to examine attitude towards the message as a key mediator between induced emotions and purchase intention. A between‐subjects experiment ( N = 1483) employing multigroup SEM in Spain and Denmark shows that attitude towards the message constitutes the primary mechanism through which emotions—particularly positive ones—exert their influence. Crucially, cross‐national variation in the estimated structural pattern was observed. While Denmark exhibits a model of total mediation through attitude towards the message, Spain displays a dual pathway in which mediated and direct emotional effects coexist. These findings advance research on pro‐environmental food communication by indicating that framing‐induced emotions are associated with more favourable purchase intentions primarily through positive evaluations of the message, with differences in the strength of these estimated pathways being consistent with broader contextual variation in pro‐environmental market maturity and product involvement.

papers.title: Green Intellectual Capital, Sustainability Control Systems, and Environmental Performance: Bridging Natural Resource Orchestration and Levers of Control Perspectives
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Understanding how organizations translate sustainability‐oriented intangible assets into tangible environmental outcomes remains an important challenge in sustainability accounting and management control research. Drawing on the natural resource orchestration perspective, this study examines how sustainability control systems, grounded in Simons' levers of control framework, help translate green intellectual capital (GIC) components into improved environmental performance. Using survey data from 175 listed Indian firms and applying partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS‐SEM), the results show that GIC is positively associated with environmental performance, and the sustainability control systems variable mediates this relationship. The study contributes to the sustainability management control literature by integrating natural resource orchestration theory with the levers of control framework. The findings offer firm‐level implications by showing that merely possessing green knowledge assets does not necessarily lead to improved environmental performance. Instead, firms need to orchestrate these assets through sustainability control systems by effectively structuring, bundling, and leveraging them to translate GIC into stronger environmental outcomes. The findings also provide practical insights for managers and regulators seeking to strengthen environmental performance through the strategic integration of GIC and sustainability control systems.

papers.title: Adult-only: When excluding children reveals a flaw in hospitality management approach
papers.abstract: This research note explores social servicescape in hospitality settings, considering recent regulatory debates questioning the exclusion of children. Although children are often positioned as either sovereign consumers or a marginalised group, their impact on guest satisfaction remains largely unexplored. Drawing on 90,045 TripAdvisor reviews from 72 international resorts, we applied advanced natural language processing techniques, including BERT-based sentiment analysis and child-reference classification using a local Large Language Model to examine whether references to children influence customer evaluations. By comparing satisfaction scores across reviews that mention or omit children, we explore whether these differences reflect broader managerial, academic, and policy-related challenges. This study contributes to ongoing debates on adult-only vs inclusive hospitality by highlighting how children’s presence is addressed in guest feedback, and by raising questions about the potential limitations in current hospitality management practices.

papers.title: Why and when customer-related social stressors impair service performance: A conservation of resources perspective
papers.abstract: Building on the conservation of resources theory, we investigate how customer-related social stressors impact service performance among hospitality employees. To explore this, we gathered data from 350 supervisor-employee pairs across twelve hotels in China through a three-wave survey. The results show that customer-related social stressors detrimentally affect work engagement, which in turn reduces service performance. Furthermore, job social support and employees’ social skills emerge as two key moderators, buffering both the direct impact of customer-related social stressors on work engagement and the indirect effect on service performance via work engagement. These findings provide a nuanced understanding of the interactions among customer-related social stressors, work engagement, and service performance, offering significant implications for both theory and practice.

papers.title: Leveraging big data analytics for sustainable competitive advantage: A model of operational performance
papers.abstract: Big Data Analytics (BDA) has become an important organizational capability for strengthening firm performance and sustaining competitive advantage. This study examines how Big Data Acceptance, Big Data Assimilation, and Big Data Routinization contribute to Organizational Performance with Big Data Analysis (OPBDA), and how the resulting organizational benefits, such as smarter management decisions, increased innovation and agility, and improved organizational efficiency, relate to sustainable competitive advantage. Survey data collected from 414 respondents in China were analyzed using IBM SPSS 23.0 and partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 4. The findings show that acceptance, assimilation, and routinization of big data positively and significantly influence OPBDA. OPBDA, in turn, significantly improves management's decision-making and organizational efficiency, while its relationship with Increased Innovation and Agility is not statistically significant. The study highlights the importance of effectively assimilating and routinizing BDA within organizational processes to strengthen managerial decision-making, operational efficiency, and sustained competitive positioning.

papers.title: Conceptualising a scale to measure customers’ off-premise dining experience (OPDineX) with third-party food delivery services
Caught in the line of fire: tariffs and the global hospitality workforce
papers.abstract: Purpose This critical reflection article critically examines how contemporary tariff regimes, particularly reciprocal and retaliatory trade measures, are reshaping the global hospitality workforce. Moving beyond traditional economic analyses of tariffs, by developing three propositions, it foregrounds labour dynamics to explore how trade policy functions as an indirect but powerful determinant of employment stability, mobility, equity and workforce development in hospitality. Design/methodology/approach This critical reflection paper synthesises interdisciplinary literature from international trade, tourism economics, labour studies, hospitality management and shock/crisis literature. The macro-meso-micro analytical framework is used to conceptualise how tariff policies cascade from geopolitical and institutional contexts to firm-level responses and individual worker outcomes. Findings The analysis reveals that tariffs generate second- and third-order labour effects that are largely absent from trade and tourism policy debates. These include heightened labour-market volatility, suppressed wages, growth in informal and precarious employment, constrained international labour mobility, weakened global talent pipelines and underinvestment in workforce training. These impacts disproportionately affect migrant workers, women and early-career professionals, while intensifying regional and demographic inequalities, particularly in tourism-dependent and developing economies. Practical implications The paper outlines forward-looking interventions for firms, industry bodies and policymakers, including regionalised supply-chain strategies, investment in workforce multiskilling, inclusive adoption of technology, strengthened policy-industry coalitions and scenario-based workforce planning. It argues for embedding labour mobility, skills recognition and workforce protection into future trade frameworks to enhance sectoral resilience. Originality/value This study reframes tariffs as labour-shaping mechanisms rather than purely macroeconomic tools, offering one of the first workforce-centred conceptualisations of trade policy impacts in hospitality. By repositioning the hospitality workforce at the centre of tariff discourse, the paper advances theory, informs policy and provides a foundation for future empirical research on trade-labour-tourism interdependencies.
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

papers.title: How accessibility barriers accumulate across the guest journey: a dual-perspective inquiry
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how hotel accessibility barriers accumulate across customer journey touchpoints, creating exclusion for people with disabilities (PWDs). Design/methodology/approach Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 13 PWDs and 10 hotel managers in Singapore. PWDs’ accounts were analyzed phenomenologically; managers’ accounts were analyzed through applied thematic analysis. Customer journey mapping was informed by the social relational model, embodiment theory and the capability approach. Findings Barriers accumulated across journey stages. Inadequate pre-arrival information carried forward into the entrance, room, bathroom and staff-mediated barriers during the stay. PWDs prioritized functional transparency, bathroom usability and proactive service recognition. Managers framed accessibility in terms of retrofit constraints, perceived low demand and ableist assumptions, resulting in implementation gaps despite goodwill. Research limitations/implications The study is based on qualitative interviews conducted in Singapore and does not capture all types of disability or stakeholder perspectives. Future research could examine these mechanisms across hotel segments, national contexts and longitudinal accessibility interventions. Originality/value This research explains failures in hotel accessibility by integrating embodied guest experiences with managerial decision-making. It extends accessible hospitality research by showing how barriers cascade across journey stages and by distinguishing the provision of accessible features from capability enablement in use.
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

papers.title: On and off the podium: long-term impact evaluation of European R&D Grants on patenting performance
papers.abstract: Abstract This study evaluates the impact of the European SME Instrument (SMEi) on patent performance and technological specialization in small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). More specifically, using data from Phase 2 of the European program (2014–2018), we compare SMEs that received funding with those that were evaluated as eligible but remained unfunded due to budget constraints. This comparison enables a robust causal analysis of the policy’s long-term effects. By applying entropy balancing and interaction-weighted estimators for dynamic treatment effects, we examine how R&D funding affects not only the scale of patenting but also the quality, novelty, and the technological direction of firms’ innovation activities. First, funded firms statistically decreased their overall patent output, while facing a short-term increase. Second, we observe an increase in technological specialization among funded firms, suggesting that SMEi funding promotes focused R&D efforts. The performance gap between funded and eligible firms narrows down over time, which suggests that eligible firms have a high potential, since they are also capable of advancing their innovation trajectories, albeit at a slower pace in comparison to funded ones. Overall, the results confirm a short-term effectiveness of SMEi grants in stimulating innovation while revealing the latent potential of high-quality, non-funded applicants. These findings contribute to the literature on innovation policy and offer actionable insights for designing complementary innovation support mechanisms that combine financial assistance with broader capability-building interventions capable of sustaining long-term innovation trajectories in SMEs.

papers.title: Opposing effects of authentic pride and hubristic pride on funding outcomes in new venture pitches: The mediating role of competence and warmth
papers.abstract: We investigate how entrepreneurs’ pride expressions influence funding outcomes in new venture pitches. Drawing on Social Functional Theory of emotions, we argue that authentic and hubristic pride have opposing effects on investors’ decisions through perceptions of competence and warmth. Across three experimental studies with crowdfunders (N1 = 196, N2 = 593, N3 = 159), we examined verbal and bodily pride expressions. Verbal expressions of authentic pride indirectly increased funding intentions via perceived competence, whereas hubristic pride indirectly decreased funding through reduced perceptions of both competence and warmth. These effects did not vary across variations in campaign size and technological innovation. Bodily expressions replicated the negative indirect effect of hubristic pride compared to authentic pride. Our findings suggest entrepreneurs should convey authentic pride during pitches, as hubristic pride may undermine success by signaling arrogance and diminishing perceived competence and warmth.

papers.title: The typology of learning from successive failures—the overconfidence effect on judgment errors
papers.abstract: While entrepreneurial failure has been widely studied, it remains unclear why repeated failures do not always lead to learning, particularly when decision-making is shaped by cognitive biases. This study examines how interacting biases distort learning from successive failures, drawing on a longitudinal case of an entrepreneur who experienced repeated venture failures. Overconfidence, reinforced by optimism, motivational reasoning, and confirmation bias, produced persistent judgment errors in opportunity identification and venture evaluation. Applying attribution theory, we show that initial internal attributions at the organizational level enabled only superficial learning, while deeper learning emerged when the entrepreneur critically reassessed beliefs through hybrid attributions across individual, organizational, and environmental levels. The study’s key contribution lies in demonstrating that overconfidence operates through interactions with other biases, delaying reflective learning and allowing errors to persist. By theorizing these dynamics, the research clarifies when and why failure leads to transformative rather than repeated misjudgment.

papers.title: The interplay of social capital, digital transformation and sustainability for designing international marketing strategies: a systematic literature review
papers.abstract: Purpose This study systematically reviews the current literature on the role of social capital in adopting digital technologies and achieving sustainability. The current investigation identifies key insights across social capital, digital transformation and sustainability paradigms, and highlights how these findings guide business organisations in designing international marketing strategies. Design/methodology/approach A systematic literature review (SLR) was conducted using the PRISMA protocol. In total, 92 peer-reviewed articles out of 403 manuscripts, based on Scopus and Web of Science (WoS) database searches from 1980 to 2025, were identified and selected for conducting a thematic analysis and proposing a theoretical framework. Findings The analysis of this SLR revealed three main themes: (1) social capital for digital transformation, (2) social capital for achieving sustainability and (3) social capital for both digital transformation and achieving sustainability. Several sub-themes were also synthesised under each theme. Key findings include how social capital permits sustained customer-oriented culture, inter-organisational trust and artificial intelligence-based social networks – critical aspects for designing international market strategies. A potential theoretical framework is also proposed to explain how social capital influences the adoption of digital technologies and the achievement of sustainability goals, and how firms can entrench these identified attributes into sustained knowledge management, improved strategic positioning and market-oriented innovation. Originality/value This is the first study to propose a theoretical framework that connects social capital to digital transformation and sustainability in the context of international marketing. It offers practical insights for firms seeking to integrate social capital, digital technologies and sustainability initiatives into global strategy development.

papers.title: Cultural echoes in e-WOM: the role of self-presentation in brand agility perception
papers.abstract: Purpose This study seeks to expand the current understanding of perceived social media agility (PSMA) within the dynamic capabilities perspective by exploring its influence on positive electronic word-of-mouth (e-WOM) across culturally diverse settings. Specifically, it examines how cultural orientation (collectivist versus individualistic) and self-presentation behaviors moderate the relationship between PSMA and positive e-WOM. Design/methodology/approach Three experimental studies were conducted using online adult samples to test the research hypotheses. Studies 1 and 2 utilized a cross-national design with participants drawn from Türkiye (representing a collectivist culture) and the United Kingdom (representing an individualistic culture). In these studies, standard linear regression was used to evaluate the primary baseline relationship, while the PROCESS macro in SPSS (Models 1 and 3) was employed to test moderation and moderated moderation structures, exploring the conditional effects and interaction patterns among PSMA, self-presentation, and cultural context. Additionally, a post hoc analysis was performed to validate the use of nationality as a proxy for cultural orientation. Finally, Study 3 was conducted within a single-country framework (the United Kingdom) to rigorously evaluate and replicate the model at the individual psychographic level, utilizing a refined experimental design, an alternative operationalization of PSMA, and an individual-level measure of collectivism. Findings The findings across all three studies demonstrate that PSMA consistently and significantly enhances consumers' intentions to engage in positive e-WOM. In the cross-national framework (Studies 1 and 2), this main effect is heavily conditioned by cultural context and self-presentation tendencies. Specifically, the positive impact of PSMA on e-WOM is greater for Turkish participants than for UK participants, and a significant three-way interaction reveals that self-presentation behaviors play a more pronounced moderating role for UK consumers. Crucially, the single-country framework of Study 3 successfully replicates this cultural boundary condition at the micro-psychological level within an individualistic market, revealing a statistically significant interaction between brand agility and individual-level collectivism. Johnson-Neyman threshold analysis further demonstrates that even within an individualistic society, the positive returns of brand agility are significantly unlocked and amplified once a consumer's individual collectivism score crosses a critical activation baseline. Originality/value This research advances the literature on social media agility by positioning PSMA within the dynamic capabilities perspective, incorporating a psychological perspective through the lens of self-presentation, and addressing the scarcity of cross-cultural comparative studies through an explicit integration of cultural analysis. It offers a multilayered, cross-level framework that highlights culture not merely as contextual background, but as a central interpretive lens through which consumers understand and evaluate agile brand behavior on social media. In this way, the study provides robust multi-method validation demonstrating how both macro-level national culture and micro-level individual cultural traits systematically shape consumers' engagement with agile brands.

papers.title: Impact of artificial intelligence in international business – a comprehensive review
papers.abstract: Purpose The aim of this research article is to review the existing literature on the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on the international business (IB) phenomena. In particular, a comprehensive bibliometric method as well as a literature review is conducted, followed by focused future research directions for scholars. Design/methodology/approach This study adopts a systematic literature review approach, in which we conducted a thorough bibliometric analysis as well as a systematic literature review by analyzing each of the papers. Bibliometric analysis is performed using the Biblioshiny software, which merges data from the Scopus and Web of Science databases. In some cases, where the merged data do not show significant results, we used the VOSviewer software for analysis. Furthermore, we read the selected papers and created a detailed spreadsheet of the papers and then crafted themes to present our literature review. We then analyzed the gaps in existing literature to provide future research directions. Findings We could identify trends and patterns of AI's influence on IB scholarship, where there is a sudden jump in the articles post-COVID, i.e., 2020 onward. Furthermore, there is a diverse range of streams currently publishing on this topic indicates the infancy of an evolving research domain. In addition, there is a wide range of countries that are publishing on this topic, which suggests growing awareness and adoption of AI; however, several African, Asian and South American countries require significant catch-up. Next, our themes derived from the findings of the literature reveal that AI is driving innovation and efficiency, amplifying cultural and behavioral dynamics, facilitating critical knowledge and improving governance for MNEs to impact IB. Finally, we suggest five future research directions, i.e., geopolitical environment, regulatory frameworks, dark side of AI, ESG and culture, which are critical to any MNE's success in a foreign country. We encourage scholars to study IB through the lens of AI's impact on these research agendas. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this is one of the first systematic and bibliometric analyses of AI's influence on the IB. Furthermore, ours is one of the few attempts to merge the two databases, i.e., Scopus and the Web of Science, to provide a comprehensive set of articles for the bibliometric analysis. We also provide the R-code on how to merge the two databases. Finally, we review the existing literature by providing four novel themes and present five unique future research directions.

papers.title: Microfoundations of Adaptive Decision‐Making Capability: How Chief Supply Chain Officers Convert Technology‐Enabled Visibility Into Coordinated Action
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Supply chain leaders increasingly operate with extensive technology‐enabled visibility, yet many firms still struggle to convert shared signals into timely, coordinated action. We frame this tension as the visibility‐to‐action problem in supply chain management (SCM): executives observe more than they can process and often fail to route, prioritize, and execute quickly enough for information to translate into coordinated outcomes. We examine how Chief Supply Chain Officers (CSCOs) close this gap. Drawing on dynamic capabilities and microfoundations research, we adopt a theory‐elaborating qualitative design that pairs a theories‐in‐use approach with the Gioia methodology, analyzing 25 CSCO interviews spanning manufacturing, retail, logistics, and technology sectors. Informants theorize that technology‐enabled advantage depends less on tool acquisition than on the intentional design of interoperable data architectures, conversion routines that filter and route exceptions to accountable owners, and learning stabilizers that preserve reliable adjustment over time. We conceptualize these as the microfoundations of adaptive decision‐making capability (ADMC), a higher‐order managerial capability linking information, judgment, and action into self‐reinforcing learning cycles. As a theorized downstream implication, participants further suggest that ADMC supports the development of adaptive supply chain capability (ASCC), reflected in agility, resilience, alignment, and learning velocity. The study extends microfoundations and dynamic capabilities research by specifying the cognitive, governance, and exception‐management mechanisms through which technology‐enabled visibility becomes coordinated action in data‐intensive SCM settings.

papers.title: Shaping sustainable investment through digital technologies: Strategic perspectives for the transformation era
papers.abstract: This paper examines the importance of technological infrastructure in influencing sustainable investment, with particular reference to gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) and foreign direct investment (FDI). We use principal component analysis (PCA) and data envelopment analysis (DEA) to uncover the structural interdependences among digital readiness, innovation capacity and macroeconomic stability. Countries that are identified as DEA-efficient, with high internet penetration, extensive mobile uptake and strong high-tech exports, are consistently receiving greater investment. Inflation impacts economies in different ways, it prevents capital accumulation in less efficient economies and it helps promote investment in more efficient economies. This highlights the importance of context sensitive macroeconomic strategies. Unemployment is still a big hurdle to sustainable investment, limiting GFCF and FDI especially in economies with structural rigidities. The outlier analysis identifies Vietnam, China and Malta as examples of ICT-driven investment resilience, while Sudan illustrates how structural and labor-market constraints can impede capital accumulation despite moderate digital progress. A robust digital infrastructure, innovation capacity and a stable macroeconomic and labor-market are essential to sustain competitive investment strategies. This alignment of factors strategically promotes inclusive growth and long-term investment resilience in countries. It provides actionable guidance to policy makers and business leaders to advance sustainable economic development.

papers.title: From standards to patent pools: SEP-owner heterogeneity and the staged formation of collective licensing
papers.abstract: Patent pools enable owners of standard-essential patents (SEPs) to coordinate licensing for standards-based technologies, but doing so requires agreement among firms with divergent competitive positions, technological capabilities, and commercialization interests. We develop a staged governance framework in which SEP-owner composition is associated with patent pool formation through theorized stage-contingent mechanisms. The conditions that increase the governance necessity and coalition feasibility of collective licensing in Stage 1 need not be the same conditions that enable rapid agreement in Stage 2; in some cases, the same compositional feature can operate in opposite directions across the two stages. Using a new dataset covering nearly 1000 ICT standards, of which 57 became viable pool candidates, we estimate a two-stage survival-selection model that jointly examines whether a standard enters the pool-formation process and, conditional on entry, the time required to launch a pool. We find that greater heterogeneity in SEP owners' knowledge domains increases the likelihood of pool candidacy but slows formation, suggesting that fragmented technological ownership raises governance necessity while impeding execution. Business-domain heterogeneity is associated with slower formation but has no detectable association with candidacy, a pattern consistent with an execution-stage friction. SEP-quality dispersion is associated with lower candidacy and slower formation, a pattern consistent with asymmetric outside options weakening coalition feasibility and bargaining efficiency. The findings provide ex ante observable indicators of licensing-coordination delay risk and suggest that standard establishment alone is insufficient for timely commercialization when IP ownership is fragmented across heterogeneous SEP owners.

papers.title: Unveiling the dynamics of data driven innovation in human resource analytics: A grounded theory of strategic approach to HRM
papers.abstract: Data-driven innovation (DDI) in Human Resource Analytics (HR Analytics) presents a significant potential for strategic organizational change. A persistent gap exists between the theoretical promises of HR Analytics and its practical, value-generating implementation within organizations. This study aims to develop a conceptual model for the effective implementation of HR Analytics within private-sector organizations in a developing economy (Iran), framed through the lens of DDI. Employing a Grounded Theory (GT) approach, specifically the systematic coding methodology of Strauss and Corbin, this research gathered rich qualitative data through in-depth, semi-structured interviews with HR Analytics and Business Analytics experts operating within the Iranian organizational context. Data analysis, facilitated by MAXQDA, involved rigorous open, axial, and selective coding until theoretical saturation was achieved, with study rigor confirmed via Lincoln and Guba's criteria. The resulting conceptual model elucidates the complex interplay of causal conditions (e.g., transformation in human resource management, data-driven approach), context (e.g., technology adoption, cultural contexts), strategies (pre-adoption, decision-making, adoption phases), intervening obstacles, and possible outcomes. By highlighting the contextual features of the Iranian economic environment, this model offers a coherent framework to assist private enterprises in comparable settings to more effectively navigate their transition toward data-driven HR management, offering insights for organizations aiming to leverage HR Analytics as a driver for strategic innovation and business value enhancement.

papers.title: The Age‐Fit Hypothesis: Celebrity Age, Content Type, and Consumer Engagement on Social Media
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Although prior work has examined celebrity influence in digital contexts, how celebrity age shapes follower responses to sponsored versus non‐sponsored content remains underexplored. Integrating role congruity theory with the ageing stability hypothesis, we propose an age‐fit hypothesis. We test this proposition across three studies using a multimethod design. Study 1 analyzes 22,619 posts from 286 celebrities. Study 2 applies sentiment analysis to 67,778 follower comments. Study 3 employs a 2 × 2 between‐subjects experiment ( N = 290) to replicate the interaction effect and test the underlying mechanism. Results consistently reveal that older celebrities elicit lower engagement and less positive emotional responses for sponsored posts relative to non‐sponsored posts, whereas younger celebrities elicit higher sponsored posts, with followers expressing more positive emotional responses toward their sponsored content. Study 3 further demonstrates that this interaction effect is sequentially mediated by perceived interest fit and social identification: reduced congruence between older celebrities and sponsored content diminishes followers’ interest alignment and identification, ultimately undermining engagement. By theorizing age‐based role congruity as a boundary condition in celebrity endorsement effectiveness, this research advances understanding of how stereotype‐driven identity processes shape consumer digital engagement.

papers.title: Guidelines for Meta‐Analytic Structural Equation Modeling: Steps, Resources, and Illustrations
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The goal of science is to build incremental, structured, and reliable knowledge over time. Yet, many strands of marketing and related disciplines exhibit symptoms of cumulative stagnation, including lack of replicability and weak theoretical integration. Existing remedies such as replication studies, multistudy investigations, and open science practices offer safeguards for future research, but they are not designed to reconcile past evidence now under scrutiny. Meta‐analytic structural equation modeling (MASEM) offers a complementary route to improving the cumulative character of marketing research by aggregating past fragmented evidence into a multivariate test of an overarching theory. Given that such examination occurs at the cumulative level, MASEM offers higher‐level contributions by exposing structural inconsistencies, adjudicating contested mechanisms, and revealing obscured mediating mechanisms across entire literature streams. Uptake, however, remains limited as its implementation requires a long chain of technical decisions that are rarely reported in a reproducible form. Moreover, methodological recommendations remain fragmented across studies, leaving researchers to integrate the overall workflow on their own. This article develops an integrated set of guidelines for conducting MASEM that address these barriers in three important ways. First, the guidelines provide a six‐step methodological guide that integrates fragmented methodological knowledge into a coherent workflow. Second, the guide is operationalized through an empirical illustration, providing a practical application of the six steps. Third, the guidelines are accompanied by modular open resources to facilitate accessible MASEM implementation. In sum, the guidelines support a more rigorous and widespread application of MASEM.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Platform Complementors’ Diversification Strategies and the Role of Venture Capital
papers.abstract: Digital entrepreneurs play a critical role as complementors in platform ecosystems yet often face formidable power imbalances vis-à-vis platform owners and venture capitalists (VCs). To explore how entrepreneurs buffer against powerful platforms and enhance their own bargaining power, we conceptualize their diversification strategies as “escape routes”—across product categories (portfolio diversity) and across platforms (multihoming)—through the lens of native platform choice and VC funding. We propose three distinctive models of complementors’ diversification choices that arise when the VC’s interests align with those of the complementor, platform or neither, illustrating the triadic platform-complementor-VC dynamics. Using data on iOS and Android app developers, and their VC funding status, we find that originating on Apple’s iOS platform correlates with relatively narrow portfolio breadth but a stronger tendency to serve multiple platforms. Conversely, originating on Google’s Android platform is associated with greater portfolio diversity yet a lower propensity for cross-platform expansion. Interestingly, neither VC funding nor native platform choice alone fully predict all diversification choices; rather, the additive effects of these factors reveal the “escape routes” or “all-in” focused approaches. Notably, regardless of the native platform, developers securing VC funding appear to specialize, suggesting a ‘VC standalone’ model, whereby independent of the platform power dynamics, external capital may prefer strategic depth over breadth. Our conceptual model and findings highlight how powerful platforms and scarce venture capital shape entrepreneurial choices, offering new insights into how these stakeholders’ interests may converge or diverge in collective enterprises such as platform ecosystems.

papers.title: EXPRESS: A CONFIGURATIONAL THEORY OF BUSINESS COLLECTIVE ACTION
papers.abstract: Firms facing institutional pressures often respond collectively through established organizations such as trade associations. However, they may also create new organizations that supplement, redirect, or challenge these incumbent vehicles. Yet we know little about what shapes firms’ choice among these different forms of collective action. Adopting a configurational approach, we theorize how collective responses reorganize the set of organizational vehicles through which business interests are aggregated, represented, and coordinated in organizational fields – the BCA infrastructure. We identify critical contingencies related to institutional pressures, field structure, and existing BCA infrastructure, and we theorize how combinations of these contingencies generate four recurrent coordination problems––contribution problems, distributional conflict, capacity gaps, and representational authority problems––that give rise to distinct BCA infrastructure outcomes: consolidation around incumbent vehicles, complementation through new BCA vehicles offering functional differentiation, cooptation of existing vehicles, or competition via rival BCA vehicles. In doing so, we offer a conceptual lens for understanding the proliferation of business associations, coalitions, platforms, and initiatives across organizational fields.

papers.title: Recurrent and eroding challenges in creative tourism: A longitudinal study of entrepreneurial resilience among urban handicraft artisans
Renovating for Relevance: How to Rewrite a Traditional Manuscript for Academy of Management Perspectives
The innovation tug‐of‐war: Local grit versus global grit in emerging markets
papers.abstract: Abstract Research Summary Drawing on vicarious learning, competition‐driven innovation incentives, and the temporal dynamics of competitive activity, this study explores which type of competition, local versus foreign, most benefits advanced economy MNEs' (AEMNEs) emerging market (EM) innovation performance, when and in what temporal patterns. We predict that local competition contributes more to AEMNEs' EM innovation performance and that this positive impact is reinforced by foreign competition. We further predict that irregular local competition amplifies the innovation performance‐enhancing effect of local competition, whereas irregular foreign competition diminishes the benefits of foreign competition for innovation performance. Our multi‐level analysis of AEMNEs operating in China's high‐tech sector supports these predictions. The findings offer novel insights into how competition heterogeneity and its temporal dynamics shape the innovation performance of AEMNEs in EMs. Managerial Summary AEMNEs face competition from both local and foreign rivals, but not all competition equally drives innovation.
