Hindered From Making a Difference: How Increasing Organizational Constraints Undermine Public Servants' Perceptions of Prosocial Impact and Why It Matters
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Public servants often work under organizational constraints that hinder how they experience and carry out their work. Drawing on conservation of resources theory, this research examines how changes in these constraints affect public servants' perceptions that their work benefits others and, in turn, their well‐being and withdrawal behavior. Using data from two longitudinal studies conducted in the United States and France, the findings show that increases in organizational constraints are associated with declines in perceived prosocial impact, which in turn predict lower well‐being and greater withdrawal over time. These results identify perceived prosocial impact as a key psychological resource that links changing work conditions to employee functioning. By emphasizing the dynamic nature of organizational constraints, this study advances the understanding of how evolving administrative conditions can weaken the psychological foundations that sustain meaningful and effective public service.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence and Punctuated Equilibrium: Shaping Government Attention in the Digital Age
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT How do government attention and policy agendas shift when information constraints are relaxed through technological advancement? Punctuated equilibrium theory links agenda‐setting dynamics to governments' limited information‐processing capabilities, yet we know little about whether and how technology improvement such as artificial intelligence (AI) influences policy agendas. This article proposes a conditional digital punctuation framework to specify the conditions under which technological advancements drive agenda shifts. Using China's implementation of AI initiatives as a quasi‐natural experiment, we find that government attention exhibits a punctuated pattern. AI increases technology‐focused attention, signaling incremental changes, while having minimal impact on general government attention. This selective impact stems from AI's asymmetric effects on information processing. Specifically, AI significantly increases the procurement‐based indicator of information quantity, which is associated with greater attention to technology sectors; however, no significant change is observed in the corresponding indicator of information quality, consistent with its limited impact on general government attention.

papers.title: Interpretive leadership skill as the meaning-making leadership competency in public service organizations: content, construct, and criterion validity
papers.abstract: This research examines the conceptualization and measurement of interpretive leadership skill (ILS) in public service organizations. ILS is conceptualized as an individual leadership competency for meaning-making whose function is interactive: the leader’s capacity to read the working context, build shared understandings that promote coherent action for the organization, and revise those understandings as conditions change. This research reports three studies using two large-scale samples to validate the psychometric and predictive properties of ILS in the public service logic. Study 1 develops and validates a multidimensional measure of ILS and demonstrates its content validity. Study 2 establishes construct validity by situating ILS within a three-level model of leader development. Study 3 demonstrates criterion validity by showing ILS’s predictive property on organizational public service performance. Together, these studies validate ILS as the meaning-making competency of public service leaders and provide implications for leadership theory and practice across public and non-profit organizations.

papers.title: From reform to reality: governance mechanisms and social capital development in mandated healthcare networks
papers.abstract: Mandated healthcare networks are introduced to achieve reform objectives through collaboration, yet imposed arrangements may not generate the social capital needed for collective action. We examine how governance mechanisms activate key sources of social capital (opportunity, ability, motivation) and shape its subsequent development. Using a longitudinal case study of a mandated hospital network governed by a Network Administrative Organization (NAO), we analyse 55 interviews along with documentary data. We find that while the NAO expanded opportunities for social capital development through network governance mechanisms, these were pseudo-opportunities that failed to enhance the ability and motivation of network members to collaborate. We contribute to theory by explaining how imposed governance can simultaneously appear to provide a key condition for social capital (interaction opportunities) and nevertheless inhibit successful collective action and generate disenchantment. The study highlights the need to distinguish between technical integration and meaningful collaboration in the implementation of governance mechanisms.

papers.title: Two-dimensional dynamic analysis of vehicle sideway lane changing based on size-dependent driving risk potential field
Control-risk-informed spectrum-power allocation for virtual coupling of heavy-haul trains
papers.abstract: Heavy-haul train virtual coupling requires spectrum-power allocation that protects both packet-level quality of service (QoS) and the freshness of train-control commands. This paper proposes CRISP, a control-risk-informed spectrum-power allocation method implemented on a low-band OFDMA resource-grid abstraction. The method combines a double deep Q-network with TCS-prioritized replay, feasible-action filtering, and guard-band fallback. A timestamped command-age state is propagated across packet, resource-allocation, and train-control clocks, and a physics-calibrated communication-induced control-degradation index combines spacing error, velocity error, and command staleness. Under the reference tunnel stress condition (four trains, four schedulable RBs, adjacent-channel leakage coefficient 0.1), CRISP reduces the TCS QoS violation rate to 0.8085 (SD 0.0112), compared with 0.9912 (SD 0.0111) for Vanilla-DDQN and 0.8548 (SD 0.0170) for Guard-Band-Greedy. Mean TCS command age is reduced to 94.0 ms from 1566.4 ms and 377.8 ms, respectively; no degradation event is observed and the mean minimum braking margin remains 987.5 m. Ablation, learning-convergence, decision-latency, and emergency-outage experiments identify the contribution and boundary of each module. Because the reference condition is intentionally communication-stressed, the results demonstrate degradation mitigation rather than field reliability certification or a formal safety guarantee.

papers.title: Driver-personalized risk assessment in car-following: validation of an optical-flow-based model using SHRP 2 naturalistic driving
papers.abstract: Traffic crashes remain a major cause of injury and mortality worldwide, yet the effectiveness of crash-preventive safety systems is often limited by a "one-size-fits-all" approach that ignores substantial inter-individual differences in driving behavior. To address this, we tailored an existing risk feeling formula (RFF) to individual drivers' braking styles. Using a subset of the SHRP 2 Naturalistic Driving Study dataset, we extracted 2,911 car-following sequences (gas-off to brake-on). To rigorously prevent data leakage, sequences were split at the trip level into independent calibration and validation sets. For the 38 drivers meeting a minimum sample criterion, the driver-specific RFF model (RFFprsn) normalized inverse time headway (1/THW) and inverse time-to-collision (1/TTC) by each driver's median values, calculated exclusively from their calibration set. Across the 38 drivers who met the minimum calibration criterion, personalized brake-on medians spanned 0.437-0.974 s-1 for 1/THWprsn and 0.049-0.131 s-1 for 1/TTCprsn, indicating substantial between-driver differences in preferred following and closing kinematics. Applied to the unseen validation set, RFFprsn discriminated gas-off from brake-on substantially better than the fixed-weight RFF (area under the curve = 0.942 vs. 0.820). However, the operating-point sensitivity under naturalistic conditions was lower than that observed in our earlier controlled simulator study. Complementary comparisons showed that, in gas-off versus brake-on state discrimination in low- to no-crash-risk situations, a driver-normalized 1/TTC-only model achieved the highest pooled discrimination, indicating that looming (1/TTC) accounts for most of the discriminative information. These results support static personalized normalization as a practical mechanism for aligning an optical-flow-based risk-feeling score with driver-specific braking timing. Future advanced driver assistance system (ADAS)-oriented applications would likely need dynamic, context-aware recalibration to address environmental factors and intra-individual variability.

papers.title: An integrated NKDE–MGWR framework for smoothing-scale and network-coverage sensitivity in rural highway crash modeling
papers.abstract: Crash-model estimates can depend on how crash events are spatially smoothed, which roadway segments are retained, and whether global or spatially varying regression is used. This study evaluated these sensitivities on 1071 rural divided multilane highway segments (1064.098 km) in Hamadan Province, Iran, using 2017-2019 data. Network kernel density estimation (NKDE) produced continuous crash-density outcomes at 1000 and 4000 m. Ordinary least squares (OLS), geographically weighted regression (GWR), and multiscale geographically weighted regression (MGWR) were estimated under a full-network regime and a selected-segment regime formed by removing 365 zero-crash removable segments while preserving connectivity. Raw crash frequency was retained as an unsmoothed benchmark and evaluated separately with Poisson and negative-binomial regression. Spatial models achieved higher adjusted R2 than OLS in the NKDE-based cases. The full-network 4000-m MGWR specification yielded the highest within-sample explanatory performance (adjusted R2 = 0.801), although MGWR was not uniformly superior across all cases. Segment removal did not consistently improve model performance. The 1000-m and 4000-m surfaces emphasized localized and corridor-scale patterns, respectively, and should be treated as complementary analytical scales. For raw crash frequency, the negative-binomial model showed better distributional adequacy than Poisson (AICc 4309.51 vs. 6001.62; dispersion ratio 0.988 vs. 4.588), although residual spatial dependence remained. Within the focused nine-predictor diagnostic subset, global collinearity was unchanged across NKDE outcomes because the predictor matrix was fixed, whereas local conditioning was sensitive to the GWR calibration neighbourhood. The framework supports scale-aware network screening while requiring count-specific modeling and engineering validation.

papers.title: “Nothing but a pair of shorts and a lifetime of trauma”: Trauma-related concerns of US foster caregivers
Generative artificial intelligence and commercial sexual exploitation of children: Implications for healthcare providers
How cultural world views moderate policy framing on Universal Basic Income
papers.abstract: Universal Basic Income (UBI) has gained global attention as a potential policy response to the AI revolution, yet public support remains divided. While existing research highlights the role of political predisposition in shaping attitudes towards UBI, such explanations rely on the presence of partisan/ideological cues. In contexts where UBI is not yet politicized, ideological alignment may offer limited explanatory power. This article examines how individuals’ cultural predispositions, as conceptualized by Cultural Theory (CT), shape responses to different UBI framings in Taiwan, a non-Western democracy where partisan cues on UBI are less salient. Using an online survey experiment, the article tests how cultural world views interact with framing conditions to influence support for UBI. Findings demonstrate framing effects are conditioned by cultural orientations, supporting CT that individuals filter policy information through stable value lenses. This study advances a theoretical framework for understanding how public opinion forms in the absence of partisan cues.

papers.title: Power, politics, and policy agency: towards a Functional Theory of Agency
papers.abstract:
This article examines how political position shapes policy agency in local policy making. Specifically, it asks: what patterns of policy agency functions do municipal councillors (
 regidores
 ) exhibit in the local policy process? Drawing on the Functional Theory of Agency framework and a sequential mixed-methods design combining a national survey of Mexican municipal councillors with follow-up semi-structured interviews, we analyse how councillors exercise four modes of policy agency: steering, innovation, intermediation, and intelligence.
 
 Our findings reveal systematic differences between majoritarian and opposition councillors. Majoritarian councillors dominate commissions, align with mayoral priorities, and primarily act as steerers and brokers of executive policy. By contrast, opposition councillors, who are often excluded from formal decision-making arenas, engage in disruptive innovation, cultivate vertical alliances beyond the municipality, and invest more heavily in knowledge production as a counter-power strategy. These distinct patterns suggest that political position shapes the policy agency functions available to local legislators and influences how they seek to affect policy outcomes.
 The article contributes to the consolidation of a Functional Theory of Agency by demonstrating how unequal access to formal policy-making authority structures actors’ behavioural repertoires within policy-making processes. It also advances comparative research on legislative actors by showing how local representatives adapt their policy agency strategies under conditions of unequal access to formal policy-making authority.

papers.title: Explaining the policy advisory success of non-governmental organisations in unlikely settings: a complexity-oriented approach
Extending the Advocacy Coalition Framework: measuring within-coalition belief variation in offshore wind policy conflicts
papers.abstract: This study advances the Advocacy Coalition Framework (ACF) literature by introducing new approaches to capture variation in actors’ belief expression and to analyse how such expressions are constrained by actors’ organisational affiliations. Moving beyond existing accounts of constrained belief expression, it reconceptualises constraint as measurable differences in the breadth and intensity of beliefs articulated by actors within a coalition. Drawing on debates over US offshore wind energy, the study examines how organisational affiliation shapes patterns of constrained belief expression in public discourse. To do this, the article develops two quantitative metrics – the Belief Variety Score and the Belief Extreme Score – which capture the range and intensity of belief expression within coalitions. These are complemented by network-based measures of cohesion across actor types. The findings show that purposive (value-oriented) groups are more cohesively connected in their belief-sharing, draw on a narrower range of concepts, and express more extreme beliefs than material (profit-oriented) groups. This suggests that actors in purposive groups may be more constrained in their belief expressions. These results provide empirical support for, and refinement of, ACF expectations regarding constrained belief expression, while demonstrating how within-coalition variation can be systematically measured. The study contributes a more precise conceptualisation and a novel measurement strategy for analysing belief expression in policy conflicts.

papers.title: A systematic review of policy conflict and its (un)productive consequences
papers.abstract: Like most collective decision-making processes, the formulation, adaptation, and implementation of public policies are not immune to conflict. Recently, various authors have lamented the lack of explicit attention to conflict in the policy process and called for more research into how policy conflicts unfold and what consequences they produce. This article contributes to that scholarship in two ways: first, through a systematic discussion of empirical studies on the consequences of policy conflict since 2000; and second, by bringing into conversation insights that are currently dispersed across fragmented research traditions. The systematic literature review focuses on three aspects: how and where policy conflicts have been studied; whether and how they have been conceptualised; and what their consequences are. In doing so, the article highlights the often overlooked productive potential of policy conflicts. Policy conflicts are studied primarily in relation to issues of the (built) environment, where contestation has been shown to produce detrimental effects such as trust erosion, frustration, and disengagement. Supporting an agonistic understanding of conflict, however, they have also been shown to drive productive outcomes such as policy change, stakeholder engagement, policy learning, and innovation. This study contributes to bridging policy conflict scholarship across theoretical perspectives, advancing empirical understanding of policy-conflict consequences, and raising awareness of their productive character in both theory and practice.

papers.title: Not yet partisan: Cultural Theory explains attitudes about solar radiation management in the US
papers.abstract: This article investigates the role of cultural theory (CT) in explaining attitudes towards solar radiation management (SRM) in the US. Partisanship traditionally provides a clear lens through which to view favourability to climate change policies; however, the lack of partisan attention to geoengineering policies, such as SRM, suggests other belief systems may be better explainers of attitudes. Previously, scholars have found climate attitudes to vary based upon cultural types, which are a function of how individuals see the role of authority in policy making and the extent to which individuals see themselves as part of a social unit. We find that partisanship is a weak predictor of SRM attitudes, while cultural affinities provide strong influences over SRM attitudes. Specifically, we find strong group affinities (particularly egalitarians) to lead to more favourable impressions of SRM research and deployment in the case of climate emergencies. Attitudes towards hierarchy, specifically cultural affinities that disfavour hierarchy, explain SRM scepticism. We contrast these results with a separate analysis of more widely known mitigation policies: carbon taxes, regulations on carbon emissions, taxes on higher income earners for green investment, and carbon cap and trade. For these better-known policy positions, partisanship is far more important. Our work contributes to the application of CT to policy attitudes as well as to explaining the shifting landscape of attitudes towards geoengineering and a variety of climate mitigation policies.

papers.title: Repurposing gas power stations for modular nuclear and hydrogen systems: a techno-economic assessment
papers.abstract: In the UK, many fossil-fuel power stations are approaching retirement, yet these sites retain valuable brownfield assets, notably developed industrial land and high-capacity grid connections, and can be repurposed for low-carbon generation. Repurposing such sites for low-carbon generation could therefore offer three linked advantages: lower upfront capital requirements through reuse of grid connections and developed industrial land; shorter project delivery times by reducing permitting needs and avoiding lengthy grid-connection queues; and higher system value through the provision of dispatchable flexibility and improved asset utilisation. This study examines repurposing end-of-life gas power stations into modular nuclear plants and further enabling hydrogen integration via high-temperature electrolysis, where the electricity-heat split is governed by endogenous reactor choice. A repurposing-oriented optimisation framework is proposed to embed inherited brownfield constraints, particularly land availability and grid-export limits, while co-optimising technology selection with hourly unit commitment and economic dispatch. Under the selected representative-week simulations, results show that the repurposed modular nuclear can deliver system-level flexibility comparable to that of gas turbines while meeting brownfield constraints. Nuclear‑hydrogen integration further increases reactor utilisation by using co-located electrolysis as a flexible local demand for nuclear-derived electricity and heat, eliminating renewable curtailment and substantially reducing plant-level levelised cost of electricity (LCOE) relative to power-only repurposing under these simulations. Among the electrolyser options, high-temperature electrolysis coupling gives the lowest plant-level levelised cost of hydrogen (LCOH), while producing the largest hydrogen output with the lowest plant-level upfront investment. This advantage arises from the ability of high-temperature electrolysis to use both electricity and cost-effective nuclear heat, reducing reliance on electricity-priced input energy. Sensitivity analysis identifies nuclear and high-temperature electrolyser capital costs as the main upward cost drivers, while stack lifetime remains the key durability-related lever. Overall, the findings indicate that brownfield nuclear‑hydrogen integration can provide a valuable pathway for converting retiring thermal power station sites into flexible low-carbon power and hydrogen production assets.

A coupled production-removal approach for Spirulina-derived biochar: Life cycle assessment and implications for carbon accounting
papers.abstract: Value-chain emissions constitute the majority of environmental impacts across industrial systems, yet scalable, life-cycle-based strategies for reducing these impacts remain limited. Biochar has been widely studied as a functional material with climate benefits, but its contribution to supply-chain decarbonization is typically constrained by moderate inclusion rates and limited impact per unit mass. This study evaluates a coupled production-removal system in which Spirulina biomass is simultaneously valorized into biochar and a waste-derived biostimulant for soil organic carbon enhancement, thereby directly linking microalgal production with land-based carbon removal. A comprehensive life cycle assessment (LCA) with a focus on climate impact (GWP100) is conducted on a cradle-to-gate basis, with 1 kg of biochar at the factory gate as the functional unit, including Spirulina cultivation, downstream processing and drying, pyrolysis, and waste-stream valorization through field application as a biostimulant for soil carbon enhancement. Soil carbon removal is based on primary field measurements of soil organic carbon, assessed using a 100-year GWP horizon and incorporating a 20% non-permanence discount and ± 20% uncertainty for the sequestration estimate. The results show a strongly net-negative climate impact of −613,428.6 kg CO₂-eq per kg biochar (GWP100), driven primarily by biostimulant-induced soil carbon removal of −615,690.6 kg CO₂-eq per kg biochar, while the non-climate impacts are mainly linked to the upstream cultivation rather than to the biochar itself. These impacts should therefore be seen as a part of the overall system. At product level, the low inclusion rates required (<7 g·t −1 ) result in negligible contributions to other impact categories, suggesting limited risk of burden shifting under the conditions assessed. Application across four supply chains - cotton textiles, cement/construction, corrugated cardboard packaging, and virgin ABS plastics - illustrates how integrating functional ingredients into upstream materials could generate system-level mitigation potential relevant to value chain decarbonization, provided that emissions, removals, and carbon storage are transparently reported and not treated as interchangeable within corporate inventories. These findings highlight the potential of coupled production-removal systems to contribute to sustainable production, while emphasizing the importance of site-specific conditions and robust monitoring frameworks.

Acid Leaching for Carbon Sequestration with Prospects for Critical Metal Recovery
papers.abstract: Abstract Reducing carbon emissions and supplying critical metals for the green energy transition are essential to limiting global warming to below 1.5 °C. Here, we propose heap leaching ultramafic material with sulfuric acid followed by sequential precipitation for nickel recovery and carbon sequestration. Ultramafic materials were subjected to benchtop-scale acid leaches using 0.08–0.8 M H2SO4. The leachates were combined with NaOH to precipitate Ni (oxy)hydroxide minerals and then with NaOH + Na2CO3 to precipitate Mg carbonate minerals. The carbon sequestration potential of each sample and the efficiency of each experimental stage were calculated to estimate carbon sequestration using these techniques. The acid leaching released 2–57% of the Mg2+ along with 6–64% of the Ni2+ into the leachate, depending on acid strength and tailings mineralogy, while carbonation precipitated up to 95% of the dissolved Mg2+ and 90% of the CO32– + HCO3– in solution, depending on initial Mg2+ concentrations. Techno-economic analysis demonstrates that treatment cost and Ni production are the most important factors determining the profitability of the process, with CO2 removal being less important due to the relatively low value of carbon credits compared to Ni, but still contributing to the sustainability of this process.

papers.title: Biochar–Straw Interaction Drives Soil Carbon Accrual by Modulating Microbial Metabolic Pathways
papers.abstract: Abstract Straw and biochar additions can enhance long-term carbon storage, yet how their interactions regulate carbon mineralization and allocation remains unclear. We conducted a 360-day microcosm incubation employing a reciprocal 13C-labeling design that paired 13C-labeled straw with unlabeled biochar and unlabeled straw with 13C-labeled biochar and used single-cell Raman spectroscopy and 13C-labeled cell metagenomics. At day 360, biochar reduced cumulative straw-derived 13CO2 from 1391 to 1199 mg C kg–1 soil, while increasing straw-C allocation to fulvic acid (FA) and humic acid (HA) fractions. This shift was associated with enrichment of bacterial taxa such as Chitinophagales and increased abundance of genes involved in phospholipid metabolism, the phenylacetyl-CoA pathway, and potential polyphenol-related processing. Conversely, straw increased biochar-derived dissolved organic carbon from 1.5 to 5.5 mg C kg–1 soil and cumulative 13CO2 release from 17 to 23 mg C kg–1 soil, increasing FA and HA allocation. This shift was associated with the enrichment of genes involved in oxidative degradation, membrane transport (for substrate uptake), exopolysaccharide (EPS) formation, and quinone biosynthesis. Overall, the biochar–straw interaction redirected exogenous carbon from rapid mineralization toward humic substance associated soil organic matter fractions, thereby enhancing soil carbon accrual.

papers.title: Haloacetic Acid Disinfection Byproducts in Follicular Fluid and In Vitro Fertilization Outcomes: A Prospective Cohort Study in China
papers.abstract: Abstract Drinking water disinfection byproducts (DBPs), particularly haloacetic acids (HAAs), can exert adverse effects on oocyte quality and embryo development. However, there has been a paucity of human evidence. We included 1176 women who underwent 1306 in vitro fertilization (IVF) cycles from the Tongji Reproductive and Environmental cohort (2018–2021). Dichloroacetic acid (DCAA) and trichloroacetic acid (TCAA) concentrations in follicular fluid were assessed. Elevated quartiles of DCAA and TCAA concentrations in follicular fluid had significant inverse exposure-response associations with all IVF outcomes (e.g., 16.67% and 10.14% reductions in proportion of clinical pregnancy for the highest vs lowest quartiles of DCAA and TCAA concentrations, respectively; both P for trend <0.01). The effects were more pronounced in women undergoing non-long GnRH agonist regimens and IVF insemination technology. The serial mediation analyses identified that a sequential pathway (oocyte → mature oocyte → zygotes with two pronuclei → good-quality embryos) mediated 21.1%–33.9% of HAA exposure-related inferior clinical pregnancy outcomes (implantation, clinical pregnancy, and live birth). Our findings suggest that elevated levels of HAAs in follicular fluid are associated with decreased oocyte quality and subsequent inferior IVF outcomes, strengthening human evidence that exposure to drinking water DBPs has detrimental effects on early reproductive outcomes.

papers.title: Decentralized Solar-Driven Plant Factories Secure an Adequate Global Vegetable Supply beyond the Electricity Grid and Water Limitations
papers.abstract: Abstract Conventional open-field vegetable production is increasingly constrained by climate volatility and natural resource endowments, creating supply instabilities and shortages that threaten global food resilience and human health. Here, we integrate solar photovoltaics and atmospheric water harvesting with plant factories, creating a technically mature off-grid agricultural system using plant factories (OASIS). By decoupling production from local water and grid infrastructure, OASIS significantly expands the area suitable for cultivation. Globally, OASIS can meet the recommended upper vegetable intake (600 g capita–1 day–1) for at least 98.3% of the population, leveraging mostly non-arable land. Cropland substitution could spare approximately 578,000 km2 for staple food production and, under the idealized zero-operational-loss case, reduce agricultural nitrogen and phosphorus losses by up to 9.90 and 0.95 Tg yr–1, respectively. Estimated global, production-weighted levelized costs were 3.8–4.0 USD kg–1 across six scenarios. Under the 600 g capita–1 day–1 scenario with cropland substitution, OASIS offered cost advantages over existing production benchmarks in 115 of 166 comparable countries, including all 26 low-income countries, which could meet modeled supply targets with a 32.2% average cost advantage. These results highlight OASIS’s potential to advance resilient, clean vegetable production and the Sustainable Development Goals across food security, health, and land conservation.

papers.title: Integrating Supply Chain Life Cycle Decisions: Empirical model validation for a large-scale case
Valorization of spent coffee grounds into metal–phenolic coatings for producing spray-dried microbial biostimulants for sustainable agriculture
papers.abstract: Dry microbial biostimulants offer a convenient and sustainable approach to enhancing crop health and yield. However, their efficacy is limited by the challenge of stabilizing microbes into dry products because scalable dehydration methods such as spray drying impose substantial thermal and osmotic stresses that often result in substantial viability losses. In this work, metal-phenolic network (MPN) coatings were applied to Klebsiella michiganensis M5al, a Gram-negative, plant-beneficial bacteria, prior to spray drying to enable their survival during the rapid thermal dehydration process. Uncoated cells lost 5.0 ± 0.21 log viability during spray drying, whereas tannic-acid-iron coatings reduced this loss to 3.2 ± 0.34 log with a streamlined, single-coat process, and 2.1 ± 0.47 log with a two-coat process. Furthermore, phenolics present in water extracts of spent coffee grounds (SCG) were shown to form MPNs with protective performance comparable to those formed from purified tannic acid, reducing viability loss during spray drying to 3.5 ± 0.19 log. Nano-scale infrared spectroscopy confirmed the presence of metal-phenolic coatings on cell surfaces, while atomic force microscopy indicated improved structural preservation during spray-drying. These findings show that SCG-derived phenolics can serve as sustainable feedstocks for protective MPN coatings and demonstrate the feasibility of using waste-derived phenolics as functional substitutes for purified reagents in MPN coatings. This approach simultaneously enables scalable production of dry microbial biostimulants and valorization of abundant, phenolic-rich agro-industrial residues.

papers.title: Supply-side perceptions of demand for natural food products in regional sustainable food systems: evidence from Finland
papers.abstract: Natural food products, items foraged from the wild that have been only minimally processed, are becoming more closely associated with sustainability transitions in food systems. However, their integration remains limited, and demand's influence on adopting such products is not well understood. We examine how supply-side actors in Finland understand and interpret demand for natural food products and how these interpretations shape sourcing and coordination within the regional food system. Based on 22 semi-structured interviews with nine restaurants, ten producers, processors, and wholesalers, and three sector experts, we show how supply-side stakeholders develop an understanding of demand through indirect signals amid uncertainty and low market transparency, and how these constructed perceptions, in turn, affect sustainability-related practices. The findings indicate that supply-side actors rely on indirect signals, such as perceived customer preferences, direct customer interactions, and product differentiation, to interpret demand, and that price sensitivity, seasonal availability, and infrastructure limitations further shape these interpretations. Price and infrastructure came out as the most mentioned barriers to sourcing, while collaboration and shared infrastructure were strongly identified as development opportunities.The way stakeholders interpret demand was found to affect their sourcing strategies, collaboration practices, and the degree to which natural food products are included in supply chains. This study contributes to the field of Sustainable Supply Chain Management by explaining how perception-based demand signals influence supply-side responses, and by stressing the importance of coordination, information flow, and the empirical verification of proposed development paths in sustainability-focused regional food systems.

papers.title: Mitigating seed sedimentation for sustainable sulfur hexafluoride hydrate formation using cyclopentane hydrate seeds
papers.abstract: Sulfur hexafluoride (SF 6 ) is a highly potent greenhouse gas with a long atmospheric lifetime, necessitating efficient and low-energy capture strategies. Hydrate-based SF 6 capture has emerged as a promising alternative due to its low operating cost and high uptake capacity compared with conventional technologies. This study investigates a static hydrate-based SF 6 capture process employing cyclopentane (CP) hydrate seeds and evaluates the synergistic effects of CP seeds and sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) under varying driving force (DF) conditions. Visual observations revealed an unfavorable seed-drowning phenomenon under 5 K DF, where SF 6 hydrate accumulation on CP seeds induced early sedimentation. Increasing CP seed concentration suppressed sedimentation by reducing the overall density and increasing the seed stability. Higher DF promoted vertical growth and wall adhesion, mitigating sedimentation even at low seed loadings. The optimized condition (0.0556 mol% CP seed and 500 ppm SDS, 10 K DF) achieved high SF 6 uptake (51.009 mmol SF 6 /mol H 2 O) and rapid formation ( t 90 = 0.492 h) without retardation. Compared with agitated or porous media systems, the CP seed process achieved comparable uptake while exhibiting significantly lower energy demand and improved volumetric efficiency. These findings demonstrate the application of CP seeds to static SF 6 hydrate formation while providing mechanistic design criteria for clean and feasible SF 6 capture.

Pilot-scale investigation of a convective fixed-bed reactor for CaO/Ca(OH)2 thermochemical energy storage
papers.abstract: The CaO/Ca(OH) 2 system is considered as one of the most promising thermochemical energy storage systems due to its high energy storage density and low material cost. However, existing studies are mainly limited to numerical simulations or laboratory-scale reactors, while pilot-scale investigations remain scarce. In addition, the high decomposition temperature of Ca(OH) 2 aggravates material sintering and limits the utilization of low- and medium-temperature heat sources. In this study, a pilot-scale convective fixed-bed reactor capable of loading 334.14 kg of CaO is proposed. During the heat storage stage, high-temperature N 2 directly transfers heat by convection while simultaneously removing reaction steam to reduce the decomposition temperature, whereas during the heat release stage, heat is indirectly extracted by heat transfer oil flowing inside finned tubes. Total 4 cyclic performance tests have been conducted with the max and final conversion ratio of 98.18% and 91.75%, respectively. For a typical heat release stage, it lasts for 105 min with maximum/average heat release powers of 75.03/52.89 kW and 318.17 MJ of energy is released. The overall/particle-side heat transfer coefficients are 97/107 W/(m 2 ·K). During the heat storage stage, it lasts for 1135 min with maximum/average reaction heat storage powers of 7.97/4.68 kW and 321.03 MJ of energy is stored. In addition, the decomposition temperature decreases to 420 °C. Based on energy balance analysis, the heat release, heat storage, and cycle efficiencies are 95.85%, 79.11% and 76.65%, respectively. This work demonstrates significant advantages in storage scale, conversion performance, and decomposition temperature, promoting practical applications of thermochemical energy storage technology.

Long-term field monitoring reveals dual-state operation and probabilistic operating envelopes of air-source heat pumps under extreme cold
papers.abstract: Air-source heat pumps (ASHPs) are central to low-carbon heating, but their long-term field behavior under extreme cold remains insufficiently characterized. Using seven months of field monitoring from a multi-split ASHP in Mohe, China, with outdoor temperatures down to −37.32°C, we show that performance degradation did not follow a single monotonic decline: COP > 1 and COP ≤ 1 states coexisted, revealing a dual-state operating pattern and a risk of losing the energy-saving advantage over direct electric heating. We therefore developed a field-data-driven framework that converts long-term monitoring data into low-efficiency risk thresholds, dominant controllable variables, and probabilistic operating references. Defining low-efficiency operation as COP ≤ 1, logistic regression identified an evaporating-temperature risk threshold of −29.17 °C at P(COP ≤ 1) = 0.2. Combined sensitivity and uncertainty analyses demonstrated the robustness of this threshold, yielding an overall 95% confidence interval of −29.50°C to −28.42°C. Random forest and Shapley Additive exPlanations (RF-SHAP) analysis identified compressor frequency and main electronic expansion valve (EEV) opening as the dominant discriminative controllable variables. Under approximately balanced indoor-side EEV openings, a Gaussian process classifier (GPC) yielded a P(COP > 1) = 0.5 transition boundary spanning 37.80–60.86 Hz and EEV openings of 124–453 steps. These findings show how long-term monitoring data can be converted into early-warning thresholds and probabilistic operating references for ASHP operation under extreme cold. The workflow can be adapted to other heat-pump systems with representative field data.

papers.title: Modulation of thermal properties by Al2O3 nanoparticle in LiCl-KCl molten salt: Experimental and molecular dynamics simulation study
papers.abstract: Molten salt thermal energy storage is a key technical means to address the intermittency and volatility of clean energy. However, the limited specific heat capacity and low thermal conductivity of molten salt storage materials restrict the heat transfer and storage efficiency. In this study, Al 2 O 3 /LiCl-KCl molten salt composites were prepared, and the effects of different Al 2 O 3 mass fractions on the thermal properties of the composites within the temperature range of 673-973 K were systematically investigated by combining experimental tests and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. The results show that with a Al 2 O 3 nanoparticle content of 1.25 wt%, a balanced enhancement in heat transfer performance and thermal storage capacity was achieved, with increases of 14.66% and 24.51%, respectively. Al 2 O 3 nanoparticle modulate the thermal properties of molten salts through a synergistic process involving structure, energy, and transport. The increase in specific heat stems from the interfacial region between the Al 2 O 3 nanoparticle and the molten salt, as well as local structural changes caused by ion adsorption and rearrangement at this interface, which in turn enhances heat storage capacity. The addition of Al 2 O 3 nanoparticle increases the Coulomb interaction energy in the system, while the long-range interactions are partially weakened. The average distance between ions decreases, and the local ion density increases, thereby forming a distinct ionic compression layer on the Al 2 O 3 nanoparticle surface. This layer spatially connects dispersed high-energy pathways, acting as a macroscopic thermal bridge. It provides the theoretical basis for molten salt composite materials designed for high-temperature thermal storage and heat transfer applications.

papers.title: A time-series clustering framework for sector-coupled capacity expansion models
A compact solar heat-electricity cogeneration unit integrating looped thermal diode, phase change material, and thermoelectric generators
papers.abstract: In the context of the energy transition, compact solar heat-electricity cogeneration shows great potential for outdoor and off-grid applications. However, the development of such systems is constrained by solar intermittency, efficiency degradation due to miniaturization, and system complexity. In response to these challenges, this study experimentally investigates a compact long-term solar heat-electricity cogeneration system integrating a loop heat pipe (LHP), a eutectic salt phase change material (PCM) with a melting point of 170°C, and thermoelectric generators (TEGs). A numerical model was established and analyzed to provide a theoretical basis for evaluating system performance. Indoor experiments were conducted to analyze the effects of the number of TEGs and heat loads. The system's power generation performance was also evaluated under varying real-world solar irradiation conditions. The system effectively converts intermittent solar energy into continuous electrical output and thermal energy storage across different time periods through the PCM. The demonstration tests show that the system achieved peak output voltages of 5.40 V and 8.11 V with corresponding output powers of 2.62 W and 3.25 W under cloudy and sunny conditions using a 50 mm(L) × 50 mm(W) TEG, and the total solar-to-electric efficiencies were 0.550% and 0.470%, respectively. Meanwhile, this small unit can also provide sufficient useful thermal energy for cooking and baking. The system's overall thermal energy storage efficiency reaches 69.79%.

An expert-informed framework for participatory soundscape design: From Interviews to co-design application
papers.abstract: Participatory approaches are widely recognised in soundscape standards and policy, yet their application remains fragmented and underreported. This study developed an expert-informed conceptual framework for participatory soundscape design, with a co-design experiment demonstrating its application. Semi-structured interviews were analysed using a Straussian grounded theory analytical procedure, identifying six categories: Stakeholder roles, Soundscape design elements, Assessment and design brief, Design and demonstration, Discussion and optimisation, Documentation and validation. Stakeholder roles describe participatory soundscape design as a dynamic multi-actor process involving soundscape specialists, local experts, clients, and planning authorities. Soundscape design elements are described as multimodal, linking sound with visual-spatial context and supported by interactive audio-visual tools. The four process phases are Assessment and design brief, where stakeholders assess the soundscape and develop the design brief; Design and demonstration, where proposals are developed and compared; Discussion and optimisation, where stakeholders discuss and refine proposals; and Documentation and validation, where design process and outcomes are documented and evaluated. Overall, the framework provides insights for organising participatory soundscape design, and its applicability should be evaluated across project contexts in future studies.

Employee Activism, Then and Now
papers.abstract: We review research on employee activism, with particular attention to developments over the past decade, and identify avenues for future research that reflect the evolving nature of the phenomenon. We first define employee activism and distinguish it from related forms of employee behavior. We then identify three themes in the evolution of research on employee activism: an expansion from organizational-change goals to also include society-oriented goals, from persuasive tactics to also include disruptive tactics, and from in-person mobilization to also include activism through online digital platforms. We next synthesize research on five central features of employee activism—participants, goals, contexts, behaviors, and outcomes—drawing on scholarship across social movement sociology, organizational theory, organizational behavior, and strategic management. We conclude by identifying opportunities for research that better captures contemporary forms of employee activism and advances understanding of its consequences for employees, organizations, and society.

papers.title: A Response to Don Kettl's Debate Article on the Future of Public Administration and Democracy
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This commentary critically engages with Kettl's analysis of the crisis of public administration (PA) scholarship and its relationship with democratic decline. It argues that both phenomena should be understood within broader global developments rather than primarily as problems specific to the United States. While acknowledging the role of governance failures in facilitating autocratization, it questions the claim that autocratization results predominantly from the failures of PA scholarship and practice. Rather, it emphasizes that broader societal phenomena, such as the erosion of societal trust and the power‐consolidating objectives of authoritarian leaders play a key role. Drawing on Hungary's experience, the commentary illustrates how authoritarian governance may perpetuate administrative instability and institutional transformation long after the (perceived) failures of democratic governance have been addressed in the early phase of illiberal transformation. However, it also argues that poor governance and declining policy performance can eventually undermine authoritarian rule, as illustrated by Hungary's 2026 political transformation. The commentary thus highlights the complex and potentially self‐undermining relationship between authoritarianism and public governance.

A Data-Driven Approach for the Development of a Time-Informed Adverse Outcome Pathway Network for the Cardiotoxicity of Environmental Chemicals
papers.abstract: Abstract We developed a bottom-up, data-driven approach for constructing a time-informed adverse outcome pathway (AOP) network for environmental chemical-induced cardiotoxicity. Mechanistic end points were systematically extracted from 339 in vitro and in vivo studies, yielding 1759 Key Event (KE) entries and 4938 Key Event Relationship (KER) entries, together with study metadata and essentiality evidence from intervention experiments. After quality filtering and minimum support thresholding, 62 unique KEs and 256 unique KERs were retained for network construction. Network analysis highlighted oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction as prominent, highly connected KEs linking diverse upstream perturbations to downstream cardiomyocyte injury, inflammation, cardiac remodeling (fibrosis and hypertrophy), decreased myocardial contractility, and reduced left ventricular function. A central methodological finding was that temporal information was more informative at the level of KERs than at the level of KEs. The same KE could occur across multiple durations depending on the relationship in which it was embedded, whereas KER-level time-scale annotation resolved distinct acute, subacute, and chronic pathway patterns not apparent from KE timing alone. This framework provides an evidence-weighted synthesis of the most consistently supported cardiotoxicity mechanisms and introduces a temporal layer for the mechanistic interpretation of heterogeneous evidence.

Rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) as a model organism for assessing long-term impacts of municipal wastewater pollution on early fish development
papers.abstract: The increasing release of micropollutants from wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) effluents poses growing risks to aquatic ecosystems; however, linking environmental exposure to biological responses under environmentally realistic conditions remains challenging. This study aimed to evaluate biological responses associated with WWTP effluent exposure during the early life stages of rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) using an integrated field-based approach. Five floating incubations containing 1000 eggs each were deployed at each of an upstream reference site and a downstream WWTP-affected site. Mortality, metabolic rate, growth, and development traits, and the concentrations of selected pharmaceuticals and personal care products (PPCPs) in fish and water were analysed regularly throughout development, followed by multi-tissue transcriptomic analyses after five months of release. Fish at the downstream site exhibited higher mortality (56% vs 23%), lower temperature-corrected growth and developmental rates, and greater depletion of energy reserves than fish at the upstream site. Meanwhile, more PPCPs were detected in fish from the downstream site, with generally higher concentrations than at the upstream site. Transcriptomic analyses further revealed coordinated changes in genes and pathways related to energy metabolism, immune regulation, neurotransmission, and oxygen delivery, suggesting molecular responses consistent with the observed physiological alterations. By integrating contaminant occurrence, bioaccumulation, organism-level endpoints, and transcriptomic responses within a single field-based study, this work provides a comprehensive assessment of biological responses associated with environmental conditions at a WWTP-affected site. Our findings suggest that rainbow trout can serve as a useful model species for evaluating biological responses associated with wastewater exposure under environmentally realistic conditions.

papers.title: Transfer kinetics, tissue distribution, and maternal transfer of short- and medium-chain chlorinated paraffins in laying hens: A laboratory-to-field validation and dietary exposure assessment
Legacy effects of invasive plants on subsequent plant growth under nitrogen deposition independent of management measures
papers.abstract: The ecological impacts of biological invasions are persistent and complex. Even after invasive plants are removed, their legacy effects can continue to influence subsequent plant growth. However, few studies have integrated invasion legacy effects, nitrogen deposition, and management measures into a unified framework to evaluate the risk of secondary invasion. In this study, a two-year controlled pot experiment was conducted to simulate soil legacy effects generated by single-species and mixed invasions, and to examine their influences on subsequent plant productivity under nitrogen deposition and management treatments. The results showed that both invasion legacy and nitrogen deposition significantly increased the biomass of subsequent plants, while no significant difference was found between single-species and mixed-species invasion legacies. However, this facilitative effect was mainly driven by invasive plants, and the legacy effect was stronger for heterospecific invasive plants. In contrast, the promotive effects of invasion legacy and nitrogen deposition on native plants were limited, and no significant differences were observed between native monocultures and native communities. In addition, no significant differences were detected among the three conventional management treatments. Interaction analyses further indicated that nitrogen deposition weakened the promotive effect of invasion legacy on the height of subsequent plants. This study revealed that nitrogen deposition can partially attenuate the strength of invasion legacy effects, but cannot eliminate the secondary invasion risk associated with these legacy effects. These findings provide new insights into the ecological consequences of invasion legacy effects in the context of global change.

papers.title: Enhancing post-wildfire soil recovery in northern Arizona using biochar from waste forest biomass
papers.abstract: Increasing wildfire severity in the southwestern United States degrades the soil and hinders forest recovery in these ecosystems. The current study evaluates the efficacy of biochar produced from local ponderosa pine ( Pinus ponderosa Lawson & C. Lawson: var. arizonica (Engelm.) Shaw) slash using a mobile CharBoss® system for post-wildfire soil restoration. We installed 3 replicates of 3 treatments: (1) Biochar applied and mixed in the soil at 10 t ha −1 (BC10), (2) biochar applied at 20 t ha −1 (BC20), and (3) a wildfire-burned control (negative control (NC)) to soils burned in the 2022 Pipeline Fire, near Flagstaff, Arizona, USA. In addition, we installed plots in an unburned positive control (PC). Ponderosa pine seedlings were planted across all treatments, and soil physico-chemical properties, water retention, and seedling survival were monitored for one year. The CharBoss® biochar from pine slash exhibited favorable characteristics for soil amendment, including high fixed carbon (66.17%), low volatile matter (5.48%), and a well-developed porous structure (surface area 185.1 m 2 g −1 ). The application of biochar, especially at 20 t ha −1 , significantly increased soil moisture retention (p < 0.05 at 12 months), with BC20 having the highest gravimetric soil moisture content at the end of the study, exceeding both NC and PC. Biochar also provided some pH buffering, improved the retention of available phosphorus and base cations, and added more stable soil organic carbon. Overall, seedling survival after one year was low due to harsh post-fire conditions, but it was highest in the BC20 treatment (17.8%) compared to the burned control (6.7%) (p = 0.011). These results show that producing and applying biochar from slash and other woody biomass on-site can enhance important soil water and chemical properties and help establish young trees in wildfire-affected semi-arid soils of northern Arizona. Biochar offers a promising, climate-friendly alternative to burning slash piles that helps soil recovery, carbon storage, and reforestation efforts. However, we need longer-term studies to evaluate lasting ecological benefits.

papers.title: Residual‐Risk Concentration and the Reliability of Value‐Weighted Portfolio Returns
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Value‐weighted factor portfolios can hold more than a thousand stocks yet remain exposed to firm‐specific risk through only a few. I measure this concentration with residual‐risk breadth , the effective number of firms contributing to return variation unexplained by standard equity factors. Across 70 anomaly portfolios from 1980 to 2024, median breadth falls from 12.7 to 4.0 while the stock count remains above 1000. Weight concentration explains about 41% of the decline; much of the remainder reflects erosion of a historical diversification advantage associated with lower residual variance among larger firms. Recent factor returns are consequently more sensitive to a few companies. A 10% constituent cap raises recent breadth by 81%, reduces the upper tail of residual returns by 14%, and lowers the median within‐predictor alpha standard error by 13% without increasing drift‐adjusted rebalancing turnover. The evidence points to declining reliability of realized value‐weighted factor returns.

papers.title: Communication failure: The hidden face of the tragedy of the commons
Foreign aid and power play: Political cycles in world bank’s procurement allocation
papers.abstract: This paper examines the existence of political cycles in the awarding of World Bank procurement contracts around elections. We analyze elections in the home country of firms winning these contracts, distinguishing between firms based in the aid recipient country (i.e., domestic firms) and those from other supplier countries (i.e., foreign firms). Our findings indicate that domestic firms are more likely to secure larger contracts around elections in their home country, especially when corporate donations to candidates are allowed. Additionally, our results reveal an increase in contract sizes awarded to foreign firms before elections in their home country. This cross-border political cycle appears to be driven by strong aid partnerships and historical colonial ties between the supplier and recipient countries. These findings reveal a political dimension in procurement dynamics with potential implications for development resource allocation. Understanding these patterns can help enhance the transparency and effectiveness of aid-funded contracting.

The Effects of Political Misalignment With the Government on Individual Well‐Being and Mental Health
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT While psychological well‐being and life satisfaction have been widely studied, the mental health effects of political events remain understudied. This paper examines how the ideological distance between individuals and their government affects well‐being and mental health. We use 11 years of panel data from the SHARE survey across 21 European countries, merged with cabinet ideology data from ParlGov. A two‐way fixed‐effects model reveals that greater ideological distance negatively impacts life satisfaction and mental health, and, to a lesser extent, overall well‐being, especially in polarized countries, among left‐leaning individuals after a right‐wing shift in the government, among younger adults in our sample (50–66 years) and when government identity is least predictable ex ante.

papers.title: Paid‐free differentiation in freemium: Understanding the balance between discovery and cannibalization and its implications for paid product sales
papers.abstract: Abstract Research Summary Entrepreneurs in digital markets often introduce free versions of their paid products to boost their visibility. This freemium strategy involves a trade‐off between discovery and cannibalization. We study how feature‐based differentiation between the paid product and its free version shapes this trade‐off and its consequences for paid product sales. We theorize that the relationship between paid‐free differentiation and paid product sales is inverted U‐shaped, because moderate levels of paid‐differentiation significantly reduce cannibalization costs while discovery benefits remain largely intact. We further argue that paid‐free differentiation is more salient when the value of the free version is enhanced through network effects, but less so if the free version contains value‐eroding, third‐party advertising. We analyze paid apps from the iOS App Store utilizing the freemium strategy. Managerial Summary Freemium strategies by which entrepreneurs introduce a free product version to boost the discoverability of their paid product have become enormously popular in digital markets. But aside from providing discovery benefits, the free version also cannibalizes the paid product's sales. We investigate whether this trade‐off can be resolved through value‐adding, feature‐based differentiation between the paid product and the free version. Analyzing paid apps from the iOS App Store utilizing the freemium strategy, we find that there is a point of optimal paid‐free differentiation that favors substantial, though not maximal, differentiation. Paid‐free differentiation is especially important when the free version provides more value to consumers by means of network effects. Paid‐free differentiation is less important when the free version contains third‐party advertisements that erode its value.

papers.title: Specialists' Evidence Evaluation and Judgments in Audits
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Audits of complex fair value estimates involve evaluating and challenging key client assumptions. Auditors generally lack the necessary expertise to perform this work, and thus, they often engage valuation specialists to perform this audit work. However, valuation specialists primarily perform advisory work and may not put enough care into their audit work. We examine whether valuation specialists' psychological ownership of audit work and auditors' infringement on that work affect specialists' judgment quality. Using a survey and an experiment with practicing valuation specialists, we find that higher psychological ownership improves specialists' evidence evaluation and judgments, but only when auditors do not behave intrusively by infringing on their work. When auditors behave intrusively, the benefits of specialists' higher psychological ownership disappear. Our findings show that audit quality depends not only on specialist behavior but also on auditor interactions with specialists. Our study offers practical guidance to audit firms on how to organize audit work and manage internal working relationships between auditors and valuation specialists.

papers.title: Do relationship disruptions increase spending on product categories high in eudaimonic value?
Leveraging HR Analytics Capability for Sustainable Supply Chains: The Roles of Green HRM, AI‐Driven Capabilities and Resource Commitment
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Among many firms in emerging economies, investments in HR analytics promise strategic insight yet often fail to translate into measurable sustainability gains. This study theorises and tests how HR analytics capability drives supply chain sustainability through the strategic enactment of Green HRM (GHRM). Drawing on dynamic capability theory and socio‐technical systems theory, we propose that HR analytics capability indirectly enhances supply chain sustainability by enabling firms to design and implement data‐informed GHRM strategies that align workforce practices with environmental objectives. We further argue that this indirect effect is contingent on two distinct enabling conditions: AI‐driven capability, which strengthens the translation of HR analytics capability into GHRM strategy, and organisational resource commitment, which strengthens the translation of GHRM strategy into sustainable supply chain outcomes. Using two‐wave survey data from 248 owner‐managers and managers of manufacturing SMEs in Ghana, we find support for the mediated relationship between HR analytics capability and supply chain sustainability through GHRM strategy, together with significant first‐stage moderation by AI‐driven capability and second‐stage moderation by organisational resource commitment. The findings advance theory by clarifying the micro foundations through which analytical capabilities shape sustainability performance and by identifying the boundary conditions under which such capabilities yield strategic environmental returns in resource‐constrained contexts.

papers.title: Co-alignment of adaptive resilience and environmental sustainability for firm performance: a configurational perspective in the transportation logistics context
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines whether adaptive resilience and environmental sustainability complement or substitute for one another in transportation logistics, and how their configurations relate to firm performance. Insights into this relationship can help firms allocate resources to adaptive resilience and environmental sustainability in ways that suit their context and enhance economic performance. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on configuration theory, the study explains why adaptive resilience and environmental sustainability may occur at different levels and in different combinations across firms. Survey data from 199 firms in Ghana are analyzed using cluster analysis and analysis of variance to identify configurations and compare their performance outcomes. Findings Four configurations of adaptive resilience and environmental sustainability are identified: high sustainability leaning (Cluster 1), high resilience-sustainability complementarity (Cluster 2), high resilience leaning (Cluster 3), and moderate sustainability leaning (Cluster 4). Cluster 1 outperforms Cluster 4 on market performance and Cluster 2 outperforms Cluster 4 on both financial and market performance. Performance outcomes do not differ significantly across the remaining configurations, suggesting equifinality. Originality/value The study advances existing debates on whether resilience and sustainability can coexist, or whether they complement or substitute for one another in improving economic performance outcomes. It reveals four distinct configurations of adaptive resilience and environmental sustainability and shows which configurations produce equifinal performance effects and which vary in their performance effects.
