papers.title: Dual pathways from adversity: CEO childhood famine experience, motivational orientations, and organizational resilience
papers.abstract: Organizational resilience is critical for sustained development in turbulent contexts; however, the mechanisms linking chief executive officers’ (CEOs) early-life adversity to organizational resilience and their boundary conditions remain underexplored. Drawing on imprinting and upper echelons theories, we argue that childhood famine experiences shape CEOs’ motivational orientations and thereby influence organizational resilience. Two pathways were identified: achievement and differentiation orientations. The empirical results show that childhood famine experiences increased achievement orientation but decreased differentiation orientation. However, only differentiation orientation served as a robust mediating mechanism, whereas the indirect effect of achievement orientation was not significant in the full sample. Further analyses showed that the achievement pathway became significant only under low organizational slack and was not significantly moderated by ownership, whereas the differentiation pathway was stronger under high slack and nonstate ownership. Taken together, these findings suggest that the two motivational mechanisms rely on distinct organizational conditions.

papers.title: Harvesting trade partners online with AI: A joint learning method for predicting the business role of massive web pages
papers.abstract: In small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), users often perform tedious and complex human–computer interactions between search engine data ( S D ) and webpage data ( W D ) when seeking potential business partners online via search engines (SEs). While artificial intelligence (AI) has been shown to improve search efficiency, conventional machine learning methods still face challenges in retrieval accuracy and efficiency, particularly in complex big-data environments. To address these limitations, this study proposes an AI module termed the Multi-source Data Joint Learning (MDJL) model, designed to assist SME users in efficiently retrieving online business partners. The MDJL model employs a multimodal information fusion approach to separately represent unstructured data elements in S D and W D as vectors. An encoder-decoder architecture then jointly learns the associations between S D and W D . Based on these learned joint representations, MDJL incorporates a multi-label attention mechanism to train a classifier that accurately predicts the business roles of companies associated with webpages. The model’s effectiveness is validated using real business datasets annotated by domain experts. Experimental results show that MDJL can effectively learn joint information from any two cross-correlated datasets. The resulting classifier exhibits high efficiency and robustness, especially when data from certain sources are partially missing or unknown. From a managerial standpoint, a trained MDJL model can further help SMEs digitize and consolidate the business knowledge of highly skilled employees, supporting more informed and efficient decision-making in partner search activities.

papers.title: Improvements to pharmaceutical manufacturing capacity; Ethiopia
papers.abstract: Abstract Problem Ethiopia's heavy dependence on imported pharmaceuticals created public health vulnerabilities, foreign exchange pressures and recurrent medicine stock-outs. Approach In 2015, Ethiopia launched a 10-year National Strategy and Plan of Action for Pharmaceutical Manufacturing Development to improve access to quality-assured medicines. The strategy, overseen by a Joint Steering Committee co-chaired by the Ministries of Health and Industry with technical assistance from the World Health Organization (WHO), combined industrial incentives, preferential centralized procurement and regulatory strengthening. Local setting Before strategy implementation, Ethiopia had limited manufacturing capacity. Local manufacturers supplied approximately 20% of national generic medicine demand, while supply chain fragmentation and foreign exchange constraints compromised access to imported medicines. Relevant changes By 2025, six facilities had achieved national good manufacturing practice compliance, 11 manufacturers were operational and the Ethiopian Food and Drug Authority reached WHO Maturity Level 3. Locally produced coverage of the National Essential Medicines List increased from 90 to 140 chemical entities, across 167 dosage forms, and a vaccine manufacturing initiative was launched. However, domestic supply only increased to 23% against a 60% public procurement target; active pharmaceutical ingredient production and WHO prequalification remained unachieved, and export and workforce targets were missed. Lessons learnt Combined, the strategy’s cross-sectoral governance, regulatory strengthening, preferential centralized procurement and industrial incentives advanced local production. However, foreign exchange constraints, dependence on imported raw materials and financing and capacity gaps limited progress. Future efforts should prioritize WHO prequalification, upstream manufacturing, skilled workforce development, export competitiveness and sustainable financing while maintaining patient-centred objectives.

papers.title: Accountability for large language models in health care
papers.abstract: Abstract Large language models are entering clinical workflows faster than health-care institutions can assign responsibility for their failures. This situation is creating governance gaps with consequences that extend beyond individual patients to public health systems. The result is an accountability vacuum in which responsibility for harm mediated by large language models can be spread across clinicians, institutions and vendors. This responsibility gap distributes harm inequitably, particularly in low- and middle-income countries where regulatory infrastructure for digital health is still developing. We propose earned delegation as a predeployment standard: authority should be delegated only when evidence is proportionate to clinical risk, substantive human oversight is integrated and resourced, and responsibility for foreseeable failure modes is assigned in advance. To operationalize this standard, health systems should adopt a predeployment accountability charter specifying intended use, excluded use, validation evidence, oversight design, escalation pathways, auditability, subgroup performance review and named accountable parties. The charter should be integrated into existing institutional review, accreditation and procurement structures. Earned delegation provides a governance framework that health ministries, regulators and institutional leaders can adopt to ensure that use of large language models serves public health goals without outpacing them.

papers.title: An oral health module for use in noncommunicable disease risk factor surveys
papers.abstract: Abstract The World Health Organization (WHO) Global strategy and action plan on oral health 2023–2030 emphasizes the need to strengthen oral health information systems, including surveillance, to support public health action. Objective 5 of the Global strategy and action plan on oral health 2023–2030 calls for reliable, timely and policy-relevant data to inform decision-making, promote accountability and monitor progress, in other words, surveillance of oral diseases. However, most countries face challenges in identifying and applying practical tools to generate such population-level data. Until recently, the WHO STEPwise approach to noncommunicable disease risk factor surveillance (STEPS) included an oral health module that relied on self-reported data on perceived oral health and oral health-seeking behaviour. However, this module is outdated. In response to growing global demand and policy needs, the new STEPS oral health module updated the self-reported questionnaire and added a clinical assessment component that can be done by oral or non-oral care workers after a short training. This paper presents the rationale, development process, structure and policy implications of the updated module. The paper provides an outline of the updated module and evidence to support this new approach as a practical, scalable and aligned solution to one of the most persistent gaps in noncommunicable disease surveillance. As countries move towards universal health coverage and integration of oral health into broader noncommunicable disease strategies, the updated WHO STEPS oral health module is a timely and necessary improvement in surveillance of noncommunicable diseases and their risk factors.

papers.title: Capacity for national health policy modelling; Bahrain; Kuwait; Oman; Qatar; Saudi Arabia; United Arab Emirates
papers.abstract: Abstract Gulf Cooperation Council countries (Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and United Arab Emirates) have similar governance structures, economic profiles and health system organization, creating an opportunity for collective action on health. Similarly, these countries have the same challenges including ageing populations, climate and heat risks, immigration, service delivery and disease profiles. We argue for the need to shift from opinion-driven policy discourse to computer-based, decision-focused policy analysis that is participatory, aware of inherent uncertainties surrounding decisions and context-specific. Despite areas of excellence, modelling capacity in these countries is fragmented and underresourced and models are rarely used to guide decision-making. The coronavirus disease 2019 pandemic saw very few decision-oriented models tied to local data from Gulf Cooperation Council countries. Gulf Cooperation Council models rely on outside modellers, which limits both the relevance and ownership of the findings. The coming decade will bring challenges that demand a change in how evidence is generated and applied. A structured, regionally anchored policy-modelling system can help governments test reforms, prioritize investments and engage in scenario planning before crises force reactive measures. Our paper outlines pragmatic steps towards effective health policy modelling based on four supporting pillars: (i) a regional co-produced modelling and knowledge translation strategy tied to priority decisions; (ii) embedded capacity-building across ministries, public health institutes and universities; (iii) a viable modelling stack that allows transparency, speed and reproducibility; and (iv) explicit communication and evaluation of the uncertainty of models to reduce risks within the choices made.

papers.title: How a 10-minute bout requirement for physical activity affects guideline adherence estimates; Germany
papers.abstract: Abstract Objective To examine how adherence to the World Health Organization’s (WHO) physical activity guidelines changes with and without the application of a 10-minute bout requirement. Methods We analysed accelerometry data from the baseline assessment of the German National Cohort, NAKO. Using predefined acceleration thresholds, we classified each participant’s volumes of moderate and vigorous intensity physical activity and compared these values with WHO guidelines. We analysed data with and without the 10-minute bout requirement. We used Welch’s analysis of variance and equal proportions tests to compare demographic and health characteristics between participants who met the activity guidelines and those who did not. Findings Of 63 134 participants, 22 226 (35.2%) met the guidelines with the bout requirement, while 62 532 (99.0%) met the guidelines without it. Participants who met the guidelines under each condition differed in demographic and health-related characteristics. For example, mean age was 48.6 years (SD: 13.0) among participants meeting the guidelines with the bout, 50.8 years (SD: 12.2) among those meeting only the guidelines without the bout and 60.8 years (SD: 10.4) among those meeting neither guidelines. Participants meeting the guidelines with the bout had a lower body mass index (25.2 kg/m2; SD: 4.0) than those meeting only the guidelines without the bout (27.0 kg/m2; SD: 5.1) and those meeting neither guidelines (30.6 kg/m2; SD: 7.1) Conclusion Removing the 10-minute bout requirement for accelerometry-measured activity volumes substantially increased estimated guideline adherence. The change has implications for interpreting time trends in guideline adherence and alters conclusions about which population subgroups meet the guidelines.

papers.title: Seasonal malaria chemoprevention effectiveness and drug resistance in Plasmodium falciparum: a matched parallel cohort study; Kenya
papers.abstract: Abstract Objective To evaluate seasonal malaria chemoprevention with sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine and amodiaquine in a semi-nomadic community in north-western Kenya, and to examine the relationship between parasite resistance and breakthrough infections. Methods A parallel cohort study conducted during the peak malaria season in 2024 involved 10 randomly selected villages in Turkana Central subcounty, where children younger than 5 years received seasonal malaria chemoprevention, and 10 matched villages in Turkana North subcounty (non-intervention cohort). We conducted surveillance of malaria symptoms weekly. The primary outcome was malaria-like symptoms plus a positive rapid diagnostic test result. We analysed Plasmodium falciparum genomic DNA in dried blood spot samples from children with symptomatic infections to identify pfdhfr and pfdhps gene substitutions associated with sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine resistance. Findings Children (198 in the intervention cohort and 200 in the non-intervention cohort) were followed until four weeks after the last chemoprevention cycle. In the intervention cohort, 72% (143/198) completed all five cycles. The incidence of malaria was significantly lower in the intervention than non-intervention cohort (adjusted incidence rate ratio 0.29; 95% confidence interval: 0.13–0.67). Plasmodium falciparum genomic DNA analysis of samples from 68 infected children showed that pfdhps gene mutations were more common in the intervention than non-intervention cohort and became more frequent as the number of treatment cycles increased. Conclusion Seasonal malaria chemoprevention with sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine and amodiaquine was associated with substantial protection against malaria in children in an area where sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine resistance was common. Treated children were more likely to harbour resistant parasites.

papers.title: Enhanced online detection of lithium plating via a dynamic threshold generation strategy with aging effect compensation
papers.abstract: Lithium plating (LP) is an abnormal side reaction during lithium-battery cycling that accelerates capacity loss and introduces safety risks. Existing online detection methods often suffer from LP-feature masking caused by gradual aging, baseline drift, and cell-to-cell inconsistency, which can delay warning and reduce adaptability. This study proposes a physically informed and experimentally validated cell-level online LP detection framework under controlled continuous charging conditions. The framework estimates a time-domain equivalent ohmic resistance using a second-order equivalent circuit model and an aging-aware OCV-SOC compensation strategy based on an iterative multi-objective Gaussian process. With the OCV-SOC tracking error controlled below 3.0% over the investigated aging stages, the compensated resistance sequence shows improved linear consistency with the EIS-based reference resistance. Based on this stabilized resistance sequence, sequential SOC-relative resistance (SRR) features are constructed to enhance localized high-SOC LP-associated mutations against macroscopic baseline offsets caused by condition variation, cell inconsistency, and residual polarization coupling. A semi-supervised dynamic K-means threshold strategy is further introduced to update battery-specific LP warning boundaries from historical and current high-SOC SRR features. Under the tested cell-level conditions, the proposed method advances the warning cycle by more than 15.0% relative to the selected baselines, while post-mortem SEM images show surface morphology consistent with the corresponding LP-associated warning states. The framework uses ordinary voltage-current cycling data and requires no specialized rest or pulse protocols under the tested continuous charging conditions. It therefore provides an experimentally validated cell-level algorithmic basis for future BMS-oriented validation.

Scalable and Interpretable Chemical Neurotoxicity Prediction via Multi-Modal Gated Fusion and ChemBERTa
papers.abstract: Abstract Chemical exposure causes adverse neurological outcomes, highlighting the need for high-throughput screening of chemical neurotoxicity. However, existing computational methods rely on single-modality inputs and lack complementary molecular information to sufficiently enhance the accuracy and efficiency of neurotoxicity risk assessment. Here, we present NeuroToxPredictor, a scalable and interpretable multimodal framework built on a curated chemical neurotoxicity dataset for accurate and efficient chemical neurotoxicity prediction. It integrates graph attention networks and molecular fingerprints with ChemBERTa, a pretrained chemical language model that provides contextual encoding of SMILES. A gated fusion module adaptively weights these complementary representations according to their predictive relevance to enhance modality-specific weight allocation through a gating fusion mechanism. NeuroToxPredictor achieved competitive performance across five independent training seeds (AUC = 0.919 ± 0.004; accuracy = 0.845 ± 0.014; F1-score = 0.861 ± 0.011; recall = 0.884 ± 0.013; precision = 0.839 ± 0.024; MCC = 0.688 ± 0.028), outperforming both single-modality and reduced-modality baselines. It demonstrates strong generalizability with an AUC of 0.861, as externally validated on an independent set of 279 compounds. NeuroToxPredictor is deployed on a publicly platform (https://www.ai4environ.cn/NeuroToxPredictor), enabling an end-to-end intelligent workflow from chemical retrieval, neurotoxicity prediction, applicability-domain assessment, and large language model-assisted result interpretation.

Does Digital Transformation Drive the Adjustment of Bank Loan Structure? Evidence From China
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This article examines the impact of digital transformation on bank loan structure. We employ text mining and the entropy weight method to measure the five‐dimensional digital transformation index of banks and conduct an empirical analysis based on the panel data of 132 commercial banks in China from 2013 to 2022. The results indicate that digital transformation significantly drives the adjustment of various types of bank loan structures, increasing the proportion of unsecured loans, personal loans, medium‐ and long‐term loans, manufacturing loans, and green loans. In terms of the impact mechanism, improving information screening capability and enhancing risk control capability are two key channels through which digital transformation exerts its impact. Furthermore, the heterogeneity analysis reveals that the impact of digital transformation on loan structures varies among banks with different asset size, profitability, and management efficiency. Finally, we propose targeted suggestions for commercial banks and regulatory authorities.

papers.title: How Brokers Enable Collective Identity Formation in Fragmented Industry Groups: The Case of Franciacorta Wineries
papers.abstract: Abstract This study illuminates the role of brokers, that is, actors spanning inter‐organizational boundaries, in the process of collective identity formation in fragmented industry groups. Through an in‐depth longitudinal analysis of the Franciacorta wineries from the 1960s to the 1990s, we uncover how technical consultants acting as brokers facilitated collective identity formation by interacting with wineries through three mechanisms: translation, cross‐pollination, and integration. Our grounded model of collective identity formation reveals a distributed and co‐creative pathway to cohesive identity understandings built from the interstices of fragmented industry groups, through the co‐creation of practices, the weaving of social connections, and the facilitation of an optimally distinctive collective identity via inward adaptation and outward alignment between broader industry domains and local contexts. Our study advances theory by foregrounding the more inconspicuous practice‐level and social work that precedes, and ultimately determines the success of, the more visible identity‐defining moments that happen via symbolic representation or institutional codification.

papers.title: Signaling uniqueness: The psycholinguistic effect of language precision on product perceptions
papers.abstract: Abstract This research reveals a psycholinguistic effect whereby more precise words in product communications increase consumer perceptions of product uniqueness. Drawing on Categorization Theory ( Cognitive Psychology , 7, 1975, 573; Foundations of cognitive psychology: Core readings , 2002, MIT Press, 251), the authors propose that more precise words in product descriptions are situated deeper within their semantic categories and denote narrower subsets of referents, thereby eliciting perceptions of product uniqueness. Four experiments provide robust evidence supporting the “precise‐unique effect” and its underlying psycholinguistic mechanism driven by categorical depth. The findings further suggest that consumers' need for product uniqueness moderates the downstream effects of language precision on perceived attractiveness and behavioral intention via perceived uniqueness. This research contributes to the growing literature on language effects in consumer psychology and provides practical implications for making strategic lexical choices that enhance product positioning and differentiation.

papers.title: Technology export controls and persistent firm innovation: evidence from cross-border technology transfer governance in China
A longitudinal and thematic analysis of entrepreneurial university research (1969–2024)
papers.abstract: Abstract This study presents the evolution of the ‘Entrepreneurial University’ concept with the literature dating back to sub-concepts published on in 1969, pre-dating the Bayh-Dole Act in 1980 or Etzkowitz’ (1983) coining of the term. Studying this evolutionary path offers suggestions for future directions of research, considering how universities navigate increasingly diverse, yet complementary, expectations from society, industry, government and their own disciplines. This study identifies 5857 articles via Web of Science, Scopus and Google Scholar and uses keyword co-occurrence analysis to identify 240 topics and their interrelationships relating to the entrepreneurial university literature. The dataset also reveals journals and topics beyond the realm of R&D management journals, including entrepreneurship education, regional development, public policy and public administration. Longitudinal analysis of the topics indicates how the literature has engaged in perspectives that are increasingly based on complex systems views, including technological, social and environmental systems, accompanied by measurement of associated variables (notably in entrepreneurial self-efficacy, orientation and intentions). Despite the exponential growth of the literature, the growth of topics is plateauing, indicating a maturation of the concept. The literature can be considered to span five approximate eras that organically layer onto each other: (i) technology transfer, (ii) clustering, (iii) innovation systems, (iv) social systems, and (v) human-centered systems. The methodology allows for the 240 topics to be categorized and visualized as a hierarchically topic map, with topics clustering around seven core themes, providing a highly nuanced overview of the core and peripheral concepts relating to the Entrepreneurial University. Overall, this study contributes to a more comprehensive and nuanced understanding of the Entrepreneurial University concept and the evolution of the underlying literature. These contributions open doors to discuss future directions and extensions, and more critical analysis of which topics are more or less peripheral. For instance, we argue that sustainability and wellbeing are beyond scope of the original definitions, and that there is room for more research to on university administration, leadership and strategy. In the appendices, this study identifies top journals and seminal articles that epitomize each of the seven core themes, thus providing a starting point for scholars or policy makers interested in each of the themes.

papers.title: Certified inside directors and tax planning: international evidence
Theorizing Cross‐Boundary Strategizing as Situated in Multilayered Supply Chains: A Strategy‐as‐Practice Approach to Supply Chain Management
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Supply chain strategy is increasingly recognized as a multilayered phenomenon, with firms strategizing not only within their own boundaries but across supply chain tiers, jurisdictions, and wider regulatory and ecological systems. Yet most existing supply chain management research tends to treat these tiers, jurisdictions, and systems as contexts for strategizing rather than as something strategizing helps to constitute, leaving the cross‐boundary character undertheorized. This article introduces the strategy‐as‐practice (SAP) lens as an epistemic tool for theorizing cross‐boundary strategizing in multilayered supply chains. Drawing on SAP's tripartite framework of practices, practitioners, and praxis (three Ps), we show that strategizing is inherently cross‐boundary, both implicitly through the knowledge practitioners draw on beyond their organization and explicitly through direct interaction with counterparts in other firms and institutions. We introduce three approaches SAP scholars use to conceptualize the complex systems within which strategizing is situated: a “tall” ontology separating intraorganizational from extraorganizational practice, a “flat” ontology treating strategizing as a web of practices stretching sideways, and a zoom‐in/zoom‐out approach tracing connectivity and identifying consequentiality across layers. Using a heuristic case of a European solar company and its Chinese supplier network, we show how each approach can shape the research orientation and theoretical payoff. We close with a research agenda for cross‐boundary strategizing in supply chains and argue that supply chains have the potential to extend SAP's own theoretical apparatus.

Accelerating construction decarbonization: biochar-Limestone Calcined Clay Cement (LC3) synergy for carbon mitigation and performance enhancement
papers.abstract: The integration of biochar into cementitious materials has emerged as a groundbreaking approach to carbon sequestration, yet its high-dosage utilization and synergistic effects with sustainable cement formulations remain largely unexplored. This study proposes a novel design for low-carbon cement composites by incorporating high levels of biochar up to 30 wt% into both ordinary Portland cement (OPC) and Limestone Calcined Clay Cement (LC 3 ) systems, fundamentally altering their hydration kinetics, microstructural evolution, and mechanical performance. The findings reveal that biochar enhances the flowability of OPC pastes but slightly reduces that of LC 3 due to its high surface area and interparticle friction. It promotes the hydration process of OPC through internal curing and intensifies the early-stage reaction of LC 3 via nucleation effects. Additionally, biochar's well-developed pore network may facilitate the redistribution of calcium species and the diffusion of CO 2 , dramatically promoting carbonation and inducing the crystallization of vaterite and calcite, while simultaneously increasing the polymerization degree of C-(A)-S-H and reducing unhydrated clinker content for both OPC and LC 3 pastes. Despite porosity-induced reductions in the compressive strength of biochar-modified cement, plain LC 3 and LC 3 with 15% biochar achieved an 18% and 4% enhancement in flexural strength over plain OPC pastes, attributed to the formation of nanostructured rod-like ettringite. Critically, the LC 3 mix with 30% biochar exhibited remarkable carbon reduction efficiency, achieving a mitigation potential of up to 88.2 kg CO 2 eq./m 3 /MPa for flexural strength and 1.1 kg CO 2 eq./m 3 /MPa for compressive strength, indicating its potential to contribute to the cement industry's decarbonization efforts. Overall, this work demonstrates the feasibility of incorporating high biochar contents into LC 3 composites, highlighting their carbon mitigation potential for sustainable construction.

papers.title: Effects of public space recreational service configurations on psychophysiological restoration: A virtual experiment
papers.abstract: Urban public spaces are increasingly recognized as important settings for psychophysiological restoration, which refers to recovery from stress as reflected in changes in psychological states and physiological responses. However, existing research has focused mainly on individual dimensions of recreational environment, recreational facilities, or management services, whereas multidimensional configurations of public space recreational service (PSRS) remain insufficiently examined. Using a typical community park recreational zone in Shanghai as the prototype, 28 PSRS configuration scenarios were constructed. A total of 210 participants were included, and physiological measures of cardiac activity, skin conductance, and brain activity were collected, together with self-reported positive and negative affect and ratings of how restorative each scenario was. Linear mixed models showed that psychophysiological restoration responses differed across PSRS configuration scenarios. Within the tested range, greater water coverage was consistently associated with brain activity indicative of greater relaxation, greater improvement in positive affect, and higher ratings of how restorative the scenarios were. The proportion of greenery visible at eye level and the proportion of activity space showed different directions of association across restoration outcomes. Correlation analysis identified weak but statistically significant correlations between greater improvements in positive affect and more favorable heart rate variability responses, and between greater reductions in negative affect and greater reductions in skin conductance. These findings indicate that PSRS configurations are associated with different psychophysiological restoration outcomes, providing preliminary empirical evidence to inform restoration-oriented design and management of community park recreational zones.

papers.title: Toward low-carbon management of Spartina alterniflora ecological restoration project in China: A multi-objective spatial optimization balancing carbon footprint and economic cost
Valorization of pumpkin-derived residues and waste: An analysis
papers.abstract: The global agricultural sector faces increasing pressure to manage the substantial volumes of waste generated throughout pumpkin production, processing, and utilization, which traditionally represents both an economic burden and an environmental liability. This paper explores the valorization of pumpkin waste within a circular bioeconomy framework, evaluating the conversion of heterogeneous pumpkin-derived biomass into value-added food, nutraceutical, environmental, material, and energy products. Through a comprehensive synthesis of contemporary research, this paper demonstrates that pumpkin residues contain diverse recoverable compounds and structural fractions that can serve as feedstock for multiple valorization pathways, including nutraceuticals, advanced environmental remediation media, and industrial composite materials. Quantitative evidence from recent studies reveals a range of reported performance metrics, including polysaccharide extraction yields, improvements in protein solubility, and recovery or enrichment of phenolic compounds. In the realm of environmental engineering, pumpkin-derived adsorbents have been reported to achieve substantial contaminant removal efficiencies and adsorption capacities, while the incorporation of pumpkin-based fillers has been shown to modify and, in some formulations, improve the mechanical properties of composite and construction materials. Furthermore, energy conversion pathways for biogas and biodiesel production have demonstrated variable reported conversion and yield values depending on feedstock characteristics and process conditions. Despite these reported technical advances, the transition from laboratory-scale demonstrations to technically, economically, and environmentally viable larger-scale implementation remains a primary hurdle. Key future research imperatives include the standardization of feedstock characterization, harmonization of performance metrics and experimental protocols, rigorous long-term ecological safety assessments, and the adoption of predictive digital frameworks to address the challenges posed by inherent biomass heterogeneity. The integration of hierarchical and cascaded biorefinery architectures could facilitate the sequential recovery and utilization of multiple pumpkin waste fractions, thereby providing opportunities to improve overall resource utilization relative to isolated valorization routes, where supported by integrated technical, economic, and environmental assessments. This systemic approach provides a basis for advancing pumpkin waste valorization from individual laboratory-scale applications toward integrated and scalable biorefinery systems, with potential contributions to resource efficiency, reduced reliance on fossil-derived materials, and the development of more sustainable agro-industrial value chains.

papers.title: Forest Conversion Reduces Soil Water Retention in Tropical Rainforest
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Extensive primary forests are being converted to secondary forests and plantations owing to human activities in recent decades, which have substantial effects on soil hydrological processes. However, the potential impact of forest conversion on soil water retention remains poorly understood. In this study, tropical primary forests (PF), secondary forests (SF), and rubber monocultures (RM) converted from tropical primary forests were selected on Hainan Island to examine the variation in soil water retention across three forest types and their controlling factors. We found that the primary forests exhibited significantly greater water retention capacity than secondary forests and rubber monocultures. However, secondary forests showed higher water retention than rubber monocultures in shallow soils but lower in deep soils. Similarly, primary forests demonstrated significantly greater soil water storage capacity than secondary forests and rubber monocultures, but secondary forests and rubber monocultures had obvious seasonal variations, which showed that secondary forests had a higher water storage capacity than rubber monocultures in the rainy season and displayed an opposite pattern in the dry season. The saturated hydraulic conductivity in primary forests was higher than that in secondary forests and rubber monocultures. Furthermore, forest types influenced soil properties, with secondary forests and rubber monocultures showing higher bulk density but lower soil capillary porosity compared with primary forests. Among all factors, soil porosity emerged as the dominant controller of water retention, where total porosity and capillary porosity accounted for 31.49% and 30.61% of variation respectively, while soil bulk density contributed relatively less (12.46%). These findings indicate that the conversion of tropical primary forests to secondary forests and rubber monocultures is detrimental to soil water retention and storage. Our results can provide scientific insights for forest development and management in the tropical rainforest.

papers.abstract: Using new consumer-panel data across multiple grocery retailers, I estimate that an additional SNAP dollar raises food-at-home spending by 48 cents (s.e. 6 cents). This multi-retailer estimate is broadly in line with the 59-cent estimate in Hastings and Shapiro (2018), reinforcing evidence that SNAP benefits are non-fungible. Linking food-at-home and food-away-from-home purchases to nutritional data, I find that SNAP substantially increases calorie purchases but has little effect on nutritional composition per calorie. A behavioral welfare calibration implies an efficiency cost of in-kind provision of 12–14 cents per SNAP dollar; because this calculation is highly sensitive to the MPC, pinning down the parameter is quantitatively important.

Information, goal setting and performance: Experimental evidence
papers.abstract: We investigate how information about relative performance shapes goal setting and subsequent performance. Combining a field experiment in a university course with a complementary laboratory experiment, we exogenously vary whether individuals receive baseline relative-performance feedback before or after setting non-binding goals. We document that uninformed individuals anchor goals primarily on subjective, often inaccurate beliefs. Providing information systematically corrects these distortions: individuals who underestimate their relative ability revise their goals upward, whereas overestimators adjust their targets downward. However, the effect of information on performance is limited – it only improves performance for underestimators in the field experiment. To explore the underlying mechanism, we leverage laboratory evidence to examine voluntary goal resetting. We find that delayed feedback affects final goals only when individuals reset them. Accordingly, treatment differences in final goals are substantially attenuated for underestimators but remain sizable for overestimators. Once this goal-adjustment process is accounted for, upward revisions among underestimators improve performance, whereas downward revisions among overestimators reduce challenge and impair ultimate performance.

Mobile internet connectivity and climate change literacy in Africa
papers.abstract: Addressing climate change requires individual behavioral shifts and a deep understanding of its impacts, yet the role of information and communication technologies (ICT), a powerful driver of social movements and cultural shifts, in shaping climate change literacy remains underexplored. This study addresses a critical gap by exploring how ICT, particularly mobile Internet connectivity, influences climate change literacy in Africa. I provide the first systematic evidence on the impact of mobile Internet connectivity on climate change literacy by exploiting variations in peer-based Internet connectivity in an instrumental variable strategy. Using newly georeferenced individual-level data on climate change literacy from over 42,000 respondents across 31 African countries, I show that mobile Internet connectivity has a modest yet robust effect on climate literacy, raising it by approximately 0.57 points for a typical adopter. Heterogeneity analysis shows that mobile Internet access primarily enhances the knowledge-based dimensions of climate literacy, particularly climate awareness and understanding, while also improving risk perceptions to a lesser extent. This suggests that mobile Internet contributes to climate literacy mainly by expanding access to factual information and knowledge about climate change. Suggestive evidence reveals that Internet connectivity can help close climate-related information gaps, among socio-economically disadvantaged groups, such as women, farmers, and those without formal education. Although Internet connectivity increases the frequency of using Internet and social media for news, there is no strong evidence that these platforms serve as channels linking Internet connectivity to climate literacy.

papers.title: Early-life adversity and long-term outcomes: evidence from the cocoa swollen shoot virus outbreak in the Gold Coast
papers.abstract: How do early-life economic shocks that do not directly affect human biology shape long-term development outcomes? While a large body of work documents persistent effects of early-life exposure to health crises, famines, and natural disasters, much less is known about shocks that operate through economic disruption. This study addresses this gap by examining the long-term effects of the Cocoa Swollen Shoot Virus Disease (CSSVD), an agricultural epidemic that devastated cocoa production in the Gold Coast (now Ghana) during the 1940s. Combining historical data on climatically suitable cocoa-growing areas with georeferenced household survey data, I exploit variation in exposure across birth timing and space to estimate the epidemic’s long-term effects. The results show that exposure during early childhood and school-going years led to substantial and persistent human capital deficits. Individuals exposed during early childhood lost about one year of schooling and were 8.5 percentage points (pp) less likely to obtain formal education, while those exposed during school-going years lost about 0.8 years of schooling and were 7.0 pp less likely to obtain formal education. Exposure is also associated with worse health outcomes, increasing morbidity by 6.2–8.5 pp and disability by 5–7.5 pp. In contrast, there is no systematic evidence of long-term effects on employment type or labor supply. Evidence on potential mechanisms points to both educational and occupational channels. Conditional on ever attending school, exposed individuals completed fewer years of schooling and were more likely to have incomplete primary education, indicating disruptions to both school progression and initial access to schooling. In addition, exposed individuals are more likely to work in the agricultural sector in adulthood, consistent with reduced educational attainment having narrowed their occupational options. These findings demonstrate that industry-specific economic shocks can generate long-term human capital deficits, even in the absence of direct biological exposure.

papers.title: Spatial perspective on perceived fairness of climate-related fuel tax increases
papers.abstract: We explore the perceived fairness of fuel tax increases from a spatial perspective. Actions in transport sector are needed to meet climate change mitigation targets, but such policies may disproportionately impact rural and urban residents, leading to spatially varying experiences of injustice. Perceived fairness is the most important determinant of public opinion towards mitigation policies, but perceived fairness of these policies itself has been understudied. We combine our inquiry of perceived fairness regarding fuel tax increases with considerations of spatial justice. We explore, whether residential area type, region, and variables such as climate concern, trust in climate policies, political orientation and use of fossil-fuelled car, are associated with perceived fairness of increasing fuel tax, and whether there are regional differences in these variables. Data were collected via a survey in June 2022 in three regions with different characteristics in Finland: Helsinki, Finland Proper, and Northern Ostrobothnia. Our results reveal that residents in rural areas and sparsely populated regions perceive fuel tax increases as less fair. Climate concern, trust and political orientation were found to influence fairness perceptions. Moreover, climate concern and trust were lower in sparsely populated regions. Considerations of fairness perceptions are important for successful climate mitigation policy.

The Evolution of Quantitative Equity Investing: Half a Century of Alpha Research and Institutional Adaptation
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This survey interprets the evolution of quantitative equity investing as a history of changing constraints rather than a succession of increasingly complicated forecasting models. Portfolio theory made diversification calculable; characteristic‐based investing converted value, momentum, profitability, and low‐risk effects into scalable processes; alternative data shifted competition toward information engineering; machine learning expanded the admissible class of return functions; and large language models and agentic systems are beginning to reorganize research itself. Yet each advance has exposed a new implementation boundary. A predictor must survive point‐in‐time reconstruction, model selection, portfolio translation, turnover, transaction costs, shorting frictions, capacity, latency, regime change, and institutional governance before it becomes alpha. The survey develops alpha decay as the mechanism linking these generations and gives particular attention to the limited transfer of machine‐learning research into production. It argues that artificial intelligence will accelerate both discovery and commoditization. Sustainable advantage is therefore unlikely to reside in a generic model class. It is more likely to arise from proprietary information transformation, economic structure, cost‐aware portfolio construction, execution, organizational memory, and tightly controlled human–machine systems.

papers.title: Policy-induced environmental technology and innovation: a retrospective
papers.abstract: The debate on the relationship between environmental protection and competitiveness has become one of the defining economic policy discussions in Europe and beyond. Critics argue that stricter environmental standards inevitably raise production costs and reduce profitability, with consequences for maintaining competitiveness. Supporters of ambitious climate goals and environmental policy, by contrast, argue that regulation and taxes can stimulate and redirect innovation, improve resource efficiency, and create new markets for clean technologies. In our 2015 study titled ‘Policy-induced environmental technology and inventive efforts: is there a crowding out?’, we aimed to contribute empirical evidence to this discussion by examining under what conditions potential trade-offs between compliance and innovation efforts arise, which types of firms they affect the most, and what policy can do to mitigate potential side-effects. A decade later, the topic is still high on the agenda of academics and policymakers. In this retrospective, we briefly present our initial findings, analyse how the literature has developed since then, and what newer data can tell us. Finally, we discuss implications and routes for future research.

Leadership and the shaping of a field: a study of presidents of the International Association for Feminist Economics
papers.abstract: This article studies the history of feminist economics by focusing on the work of the first 26 presidents of the International Association for Feminist Economists (IAFFE). We combine different types of materials and mix qualitative and bibliometric methods to capture how this group of women helped to shape the field and measure their intellectual links. This group of women does not represent the entire field of feminist economics. Nevertheless, their research and administrative responsibilities, their intellectual interactions and the way they embody a willingness to diversify the association’s leadership and membership are key pieces in the history of feminist economics.

Co-founder selection from a marriage market perspective: How the dark triad shapes judgments of interpersonal attraction, resources, and equity demand
papers.abstract: Co-founder selection is a pivotal decision in new venture formation, yet how lead founders evaluate potential partners remains underexplored. Drawing on insights from marriage market theory, we conceptualize co-founder selection as an act of individuated judgment guided by cooperative logic and associated joint utility projection, wherein lead founders assess co-founder candidates based on social-emotional, instrumental, and distributive considerations reflected in interpersonal attraction, resource contributions, and equity demand. We further propose that lead founders' dark triad shifts this judgmental process from joint utility logic to personal utility maximization. Using a conjoint experiment with 206 entrepreneurs making 3296 co-founder selection decisions, we find that interpersonal attraction and resource contributions positively influence willingness to select a co-founder candidate, whereas higher equity demand reduces candidate attractiveness. Critically, lead founders higher in the dark triad display distinct patterns: they discount interpersonal attraction and display heightened sensitivity to equity dilution—assessments that indicate their prioritization of personal over joint value creation. Taken together, these findings reveal how dispositional tendencies influence the judgments underlying co-founder selection, indicating a shift away from the cooperative logic assumed in marriage market theory and co-founder selection toward greater emphasis on personal utility considerations. We discuss theoretical implications of these findings and offer practical guidance for navigating the complexities of co-founder selection.

papers.title: Re‐thinking academic entrepreneurship: Micro, meso, and macro perspectives
papers.abstract: Abstract Research Summary We summarize and synthesize the papers contained in the special issue and use these studies to illustrate key micro, meso, and macro dimensions of academic entrepreneurship, where micro focuses on the scientist, meso is concerned with the university ecosystem, and macro refers to the broader entrepreneurial ecosystem. A key finding from our special issue is that routines, pivots, and intellectual property, which determine venture viability, emerge from granular individual action, including identity formation and evolution. We also find that macro instruments such as public funding/grants and institutional governance appear to steer resources toward viable science‐based ventures. Our essay concludes by presenting numerous additional micro, meso, and macro research questions to motivate future research on the managerial and public policy implications of academic entrepreneurship. Managerial Summary There are several key managerial implications of our essay and this special issue. “Managers” and those who supervise academic entrepreneurs need to develop and support their scientists entrepreneurial identity formation and evolution. Managers also need to enhance incentives for academic entrepreneurship and foster a culture within their academic departments, schools, and colleges that support these activities. Policymakers need to design entrepreneurial training for scientists with both “micro” and “macro” issues in mind.

papers.title: The Welfare Effects of Selling Leads in a Two-Sided Marketplace
papers.abstract: Digital platforms that connect customers with service providers often monetize by selling customer leads to interested providers. Examples include Bark, Google Local Services, HomeAdvisor, Modernize, Porch, and Thumbtack. This paper develops a game-theoretic model to analyze how lead pricing affects customer and provider welfare. When the platform raises the fee-per-lead for a customer-type, those customers—conditional on receiving the same number of provider quotes—are quoted lower prices. However, if the fee is sufficiently high, providers purchase fewer of these leads, which can reduce the number of quotes and diminish customer surplus. To maximize social welfare, a simple policy that sets a market-clearing fee-per-lead for each customer-type guarantees at least [Formula: see text] of the first-best welfare and at least [Formula: see text] of the welfare under the welfare-optimal fees. The first-best outcome can be achieved by subsidizing providers for each job well done, so that experienced providers with cheaper sources of leads do not exit the platform. Understanding these welfare trade-offs can help platforms design policies that support balanced marketplace growth and preserve a sustainable revenue stream. This paper was accepted by Srikanth Jagabathula, market design, platform, and demand analytics. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07399 .

papers.title: Early Environmental Shocks and Organizational Reconfiguration in High-Growth Ventures
papers.abstract: We study whether shocks from local natural disasters can leave durable organizational traces in young high-growth ventures. In principle, such firms may be relatively resilient to localized disruption because they are designed to scale beyond local markets and rely heavily on knowledge-based assets. We examine this possibility using a panel of 19,984 U.S. startups founded between 1985 and 2010 that subsequently received venture financing. We identify ventures whose founding counties experience natural disasters within 12 months of founding using FEMA Major Disaster Declarations. Ventures exposed to disasters at an early stage exhibit higher subsequent failure hazards and no general advantage in follow-on financing, yet show higher IPO hazards in favorable market windows, a pattern consistent with greater responsiveness to opportunities requiring substantial organizational reconfiguration. Descriptive employee-level evidence further documents differences in organizational structure and composition consistent with greater retained fluidity among exposed ventures. Drawing on organization design and imprinting theory, we interpret these patterns as consistent with the possibility that disasters function as forcing environments that entrench early-stage coordination features such as flatness, role fluidity, and broader expertise that would otherwise attenuate as ventures mature. These durable organizational traces may, in turn, shape ventures’ subsequent capacity for reconfiguration. We discuss implications for organizational adaptation, imprinting, entrepreneurial geography, and organizational responses to crises.

papers.title: Managerial delegation within firms and peer information environment
Digital ecosystems and supply chain resilience in manufacturing: the mediating role of supply chain complexity in technology-driven operations
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the association between digital ecosystems and supply chain resilience in manufacturing firms, with particular attention to the statistical mediating role of supply chain complexity. It addresses the limited understanding of how digital technologies, including AI, IoT, and cybersecurity, operate collectively rather than in isolation. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on the resource-based view (RBV) and dynamic capability view (DCV), the study employs a quantitative research design using survey data from 732 managerial and supervisory respondents working in manufacturing firms in Mississippi, West Virginia, and Arkansas. Structural equation modeling (SEM) using AMOS is applied to test the proposed relationships. Findings The results indicate that digital ecosystems are positively associated with supply chain resilience, with cybersecurity exhibiting the strongest association with the Digital Ecosystem construct. Supply chain complexity shows a positive but comparatively smaller association with resilience and the statistically significant indirect relationship is consistent with partial mediation. Research limitations/implications The study is limited to manufacturing firms in selected U.S. states, which may affect generalizability. Future research could explore cross-industry and cross-country contexts and examine additional mediating or moderating mechanisms. Practical implications The findings suggest that managers should consider investing in integrated digital infrastructure, prioritizing cybersecurity capabilities and using data-driven technologies while proactively managing the complexity of digital transformation. Originality/value This study advances a systems-level understanding of digital ecosystems in supply chains by showing that integrated digital capabilities, rather than isolated technologies, are positively associated with resilience in complex operational environments.

papers.title: Navigating Unknown Unknowns in Megaprojects: Insights from the Immersed Tunnel Section of the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge Project
How customer incivility reduces employees’ compassionate service behaviors: the exacerbating role of leader–member exchange
papers.abstract: Purpose Grounded in uncertainty reduction theory and conservation of resources theory, this study investigates the relationship between customer incivility and compassionate service behavior among frontline employees. In particular, it examines whether workplace uncertainty mediates this relationship and whether, and to what extent, leader–member exchange (LMX) amplifies the negative effect of workplace uncertainty on compassionate service behavior, thereby moderating the indirect effect of customer incivility on compassionate service behavior through workplace uncertainty. Design/methodology/approach This study employed a four-wave, time-lagged survey design using a sample of 316 customer-facing service employees in the United States, recruited through Prolific. The hypothesized moderated mediation model was tested using the PROCESS macro in IBM SPSS. Findings Results indicated a significant negative indirect effect of customer incivility on compassionate service behavior through workplace uncertainty. Furthermore, both the relationship between workplace uncertainty and compassionate service behavior as well as the indirect relationship between customer incivility and compassionate service behavior through workplace uncertainty were stronger for employees who reported higher LMX compared to those with weaker LMX. Originality/value This study contributes to the growing literature on the consequences of customer incivility by uncovering workplace uncertainty as a key mediating mechanism. It also challenges the conventional view of LMX as uniformly beneficial, showing that, under conditions of heightened uncertainty, employees in high-quality LMX relationships may experience stronger constraints on compassionate service behavior because uncertainty represents a greater disruption to their typical experience of relational clarity and predictability.

papers.title: A bibliometric assessment of hidden champions research: Mapping an evolving field
Promotion and prevention focus on playful work design: the role of inclusive leadership in the relationship between employee thriving and job burnout
papers.abstract: In the rapidly evolving workplace, employees need to adopt proactive strategies to thrive and avert job burnout. Playful work design (PWD) offers promising avenues for achieving these outcomes. Yet empirical evidence and its underlying psychological processes warrant further investigation. Building on regulatory focus theory (RFT), we hypothesize that PWD might impact employee thriving at work and job burnout through promotion and prevention focus under the boundary conditions of inclusive leadership. We collected three-wave data from full-time employees (N = 468) in Pakistan. Our results showed that promotion focus mediated the positive relationship between PWD and thriving at work, whereas prevention focus mediated the negative relationship between PWD and job burnout. Inclusive leadership moderated the positive indirect relationship between PWD and thriving at work via promotion focus. It also moderated the negative indirect relationship between PWD and job burnout via prevention focus. The findings of our study contribute to the applications of RFT by suggesting that PWD may function as a proactive self-regulatory process, while also offering actionable insights for managers and practitioners.

papers.title: Paradoxical effect of exploitative leadership on employee performance
papers.abstract: Based on paradox theory, this study aims to investigate the paradoxical consequences of exploitative leadership on employee work outcomes. From the perspective of the ‘performing–learning’ lens, we hypothesize that exploitative leaders boost employee task performance but inhibit employee creative performance. In a three-wave time-lagged field study with 106 leaders and 249 subordinates, the results confirm our hypotheses. We also find the mediating effects of performance pressure and intrinsic motivation, as well as the moderating effect of traditional values. Facing exploitative leaders, employees with high traditionality show high task performance out of performance pressure, whereas those low in traditionality display worse creative performance because of poor intrinsic motivation. The findings contribute to the exploitative leadership literature, emphasizing the distinct influences of exploitative leadership on different aspects of performance, and have implications for practice.
