papers.title: Closing the opportunity gap: Exploring micro-enterprises' behavioral intention to integrate with digital platforms for a broader agri-food system
papers.abstract: Digital agriculture platforms offer marginalized micro-enterprises a vital pathway to bridge the opportunity gap and overcome structural dependencies on focal companies. However, mainstream literature's focal-firm bias leaves the adoption logic of these grassroots operators underexplored. Addressing this gap, we operationalize an integrated Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) framework. Using PLS-SEM on data from 167 micro-enterprises, this study investigates their platform integration behaviors. Results reveal distinct adoption pathways: a platform's operational simplicity cannot trigger adoption without first cultivating a favorable organizational mindset (full mediation). Conversely, its tangible strategic benefits—unexpectedly anchored in macro-systemic food safety guarantees and ecological conservation rather than mere short-term profits—motivate integration both directly and indirectly (partial mediation). Socio-psychologically, although micro-enterprises clearly perceive external pressures like government mandates and peer emulation, these fail to translate into adoption intent—a recognition-action gap that leaves adoption strongly conditioned by financial affordability and technical readiness instead. Ultimately, these dynamics reframe the presumed myopic rationality of micro-enterprises: viewed through the lens of push-pull theory, the strategic draw of sustainable platform value is offset by baseline capability constraints, such that this value becomes actionable only when matched by sufficient capability. Theoretically, this demonstrates that cultivating truly inclusive digital ecosystems necessitates shifting the analytical focus from top-down focal designs to bottom-up grassroots decision-making. Practically, it advises policymakers and platform sponsors to move beyond normative persuasion toward tangible capability empowerment and value-driven platform architectures.

papers.title: When Does Mindfulness Translate Into Consumer Well‐Being? The Role of Mindful Consumption and Meditation Regularity
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Mindfulness correlates with higher life satisfaction, yet consumer wellbeing research rarely specifies the behavioral route through which this relationship emerges. Drawing on self‐regulation theory, the research proposes mindful consumption as that route and, drawing on self‐determination theory, evaluates meditation regularity as a boundary condition. Meditation regularity is selected over other candidate moderators given that meditation practice is the primary activity through which mindfulness is cultivated, so the regularity of that practice should govern how far mindful awareness has been internalized and, in turn, whether wellbeing gains run through consumption behavior or through a direct psychological pathway. Two studies test a moderated mediation model. Study 1, a controlled experiment with postgraduate students, provides the experimental benchmark, given that a 2‐month guided meditation intervention raised mindfulness and mindful consumption relative to a control condition, whereas the postintervention associations among mindfulness, mindful consumption, and life satisfaction supply explanatory evidence of mediation. Study 2, a survey of 503 consumers (74% nonstudents), supports the mediation and clarifies heterogeneity by meditation regularity, which strengthens both the mindfulness to mindful consumption association and the direct mindfulness to life satisfaction association, whereas the indirect effect through mindful consumption is significant among new meditators and non‐significant among regular meditators. The findings position self‐reported mindful consumption as a relevant behavioral mechanism that links mindfulness with consumer wellbeing and identify meditation regularity as a boundary condition that governs both the mindfulness to mindful consumption association and the direct pathway to life satisfaction. Implications emerge for interventions and marketing programs that promote consumer wellbeing through more intentional, consequence‐aware, value‐aligned consumption.

papers.title: From Conversational Agents Back to Human Agents? Drivers and Inhibitors of Customer Switching Intention and Behavior
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT In customer service, companies increasingly replace human agents (HAs) with AI‐powered conversational agents (CAs) because they provide efficiency gains, instant responses, and constant availability. Yet customer service still requires HAs, as customers continue to seek their assistance for different reasons. Against this background, we conducted a two‐wave longitudinal online study of European customers to examine which factors determine switching from CAs to HAs, capturing switching intention in study 1 ( N = 468) and self‐reported switching behavior 2 months later among recontacted participants in study 2 ( N = 237). The pull factor, driven by perceived usefulness of HAs, increases switching intention, whereas the mooring factor, driven by inertia and habit, inhibits both intention and behavior. The push factor reduces switching intention, suggesting that negative CA experiences may lead customers to disengage from customer service rather than switching to a HA. Task difficulty intensifies the push and pull factors while weakening the mooring factor. Switching intention positively influences subsequent behavior. Overall, the findings suggest that HAs are particularly valuable for difficult service tasks that CAs struggle to handle. Firms should therefore identify difficult or unresolved requests and provide customers with a visible and straightforward option to switch to a HA before they disengage from customer service.

papers.title: Paying for Pain: How Healthcare Costs Influence Physical Pain Predictions
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT As healthcare costs continue to rise in the United States, consumers increasingly encounter financial burdens that impact their economic well‐being along with their psychological experiences surrounding medical care. This research examines how the pain of paying, a well‐established concept in marketing, shapes consumers' predictions of physical pain associated with healthcare procedures. Across three experimental studies, we find that higher out‐of‐pocket costs increase anticipated physical pain through pain of paying and financial anxiety. Study 1 demonstrates that out‐of‐pocket costs heighten anticipated physical pain via a sequential pathway of pain of paying and financial anxiety. Study 2 shows that cost‐induced financial discomfort extends to behavioral intentions, reducing willingness to schedule a procedure. Study 3 identifies general financial stress as a moderator, such that effects on scheduling intentions are strongest among financially stressed consumers. These findings extend pain of paying theory into the healthcare domain by demonstrating how financial cues spillover into perceptual and affective judgments under medical uncertainty. The results offer implications for healthcare patients, marketers, providers, and policymakers by illustrating how payment structures and cost communication may inadvertently shape patients' expectations and intentions, particularly among financially vulnerable populations.

papers.title: The Algorithmic Well‐Being Paradox: When AI Decision Delegation Helps and Hurts Consumer Well‐Being
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT As generative AI increasingly shapes consumer decision‐making, its implications for consumer well‐being remain unclear. Existing research largely focuses on the trade‐off between algorithmic efficiency and autonomy loss. This research advances understanding by proposing the algorithmic well‐being paradox, whereby the same AI delegation can enhance or diminish well‐being depending on the consumption context. Integrating Savoring Theory and Self‐Determination Theory, we develop a framework that explains when and why these divergent outcomes occur. To test the proposed relationships, four studies were conducted with 2 × 2 between‐subjects experiments ( N = 1427) spanning multiple consumption domains, including cameras, guided tours, ergonomic chairs, glamping trips, smartphones, Arctic expeditions, and smart‐home systems. Study 1 demonstrates that the effects of algorithmic delegation differ between experiential and material consumption. Studies 2 and 3 identify anticipatory savoring and autonomy frustration as the underlying mechanisms, while Study 4 confirms the proposed dual‐mediation process in a high‐complexity context. Results show that consumption type shapes how consumers respond to AI delegation. In experiential consumption, AI delegation increases well‐being by enhancing anticipatory savoring, with these benefits outweighing autonomy concerns. In material consumption, AI delegation reduces well‐being by increasing autonomy frustration, which diminishes the benefits of convenience. These findings advance human‐AI interaction research by demonstrating that the impact of algorithmic delegation depends on consumers' underlying consumption goals and provide guidance for designing more human‐centered AI decision‐support systems.

papers.title: Mixed methods research: Critical review and guidelines for stronger design, integration, and contribution
papers.abstract: Mixed methods research has a prominent place in tourism and hospitality scholarship, yet adoption has advanced faster than methodological selectivity, which leaves many studies combining qualitative and quantitative strands without explaining why both strands were necessary, how the strands were related, or what integrated inference their combination alone made possible. Drawing on a critical review of 222 mixed methods studies published in leading tourism and hospitality journals, this article identifies dominant patterns, strengths and weaknesses, and underused possibilities. In response, the article offers a stage-based guide that links problem formulation, purpose selection, design fit, sampling bridges, strand roles, integration, divergence handling, reporting architecture, and contribution development. In doing so, the article advances a more demanding standard for mixed methods scholarship and argues that the next phase of tourism and hospitality research should shift from routine method combination toward integrated inferences that are conceptually sharper, methodologically clearer, and practically more useful.

papers.title: Digital Search Disruption and Corporate Governance: Evidence From Google's Withdrawal and Executive Gender Diversity in China
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Research Question/Issue This study examines whether disruptions to digital information infrastructure influence corporate governance outcomes. Specifically, it investigates how Google's 2010 withdrawal from mainland China affected executive gender diversity by altering firms' external visibility within global information networks. Research Findings/Insights Using a difference‐in‐differences framework, the study finds that firms with greater prewithdrawal exposure to Google experienced a significant decline in executive gender diversity after the withdrawal. The results remain robust across alternative specifications and identification tests. Mechanism analyses suggest that reductions in foreign media visibility and weakened foreign investor monitoring are important channels, which reduce external governance pressures. Further analyses reveal that the effect is stronger in regions with less supportive gender‐norm environments and greater information‐accessibility constraints, with gender norms showing a more robust moderating role. Theoretical/Academic Implications This study extends corporate governance research by identifying digital information infrastructure as an important governance‐relevant information intermediary. The findings broaden existing perspectives beyond traditional disclosure and monitoring mechanisms by showing that governance outcomes are also shaped by the infrastructures that determine firms' visibility and accessibility to external stakeholders. The study further demonstrates that executive gender diversity responds not only to internal organizational choices but also to changes in firms' external informational environments. Practitioner/Policy Implications The findings highlight the importance of maintaining reliable and accessible digital information infrastructures that support external accountability mechanisms. Firms should treat digital visibility as a strategic governance resource and develop diversified channels to maintain stakeholder connections when key information infrastructures are disrupted.

papers.title: Ethical Foundations of Social Entrepreneurship Competencies: A Systematic Review and Integrative Framework
papers.abstract: Social entrepreneurship education is flourishing. However, research on social entrepreneurship competencies remains highly fragmented. Without a coherent understanding of these competencies and their ethical underpinnings, researchers cannot explore how they affect the social impact and financial viability of social entrepreneurship, nor can educators determine learning outcomes. We conduct a systematic review of 147 social entrepreneurship articles and identify 12 distinct social entrepreneurship competencies. Guided by deontological, utilitarian, and care ethics, we group these into normative , pragmatic , and relational competencies. We furthermore identify and discuss their relationships, antecedents, and outcomes, resulting in propositions. Our paper enables research on how competencies help social entrepreneurs navigate ethical dilemmas, whether education effectively cultivates them, and whether their acquisition leads to desired outcomes and social impact. We hope this review stimulates more systematic empirical research on the effects of social entrepreneurial competencies and longitudinal studies on how to develop them. In particular, we argue that new outcome variables (beyond mere intention) must be investigated, especially individual behaviour, team dynamics, organisational performance, and social impact.

papers.title: The Relevance and Materiality of Illegal Acts: Examining Auditor and Investor Judgments
papers.abstract: Abstract The audit expectation gap exists and persists due to changing “…social, economic, and political developments of the time.” (Sikka, et al., 1998) Like stakeholders’ demands for and the profession’s response to fraud detection in the 2000s, investors are increasingly interested in C-suite employees’ and entity’s illegal acts, finding them both relevant and material (Cline, Walkling & Yore, 2018). This study identifies a gap between auditors’ and investors’ relevance and materiality judgments of a CEO’s illegal act. Varying role (auditor vs. investor) and using experience as a control (audit vs no audit), results show that non-auditor investors rate a CEO’s illegal act as significantly more relevant and material than do auditors placed in either role, while auditors in an investor role find a CEO’s illegal act significantly more material than auditors in an auditor role. Qualitative comments indicate that investors see managers’ personal misconduct as indicative of their lack of personal integrity and lose trust in them across personal to work situations. Auditors do not make the same connection. Our findings highlight challenges for the audit profession in meeting investors’ expectations in the context of managers’ illegal acts.

papers.title: Distressed firms and loan guarantee programmes during the COVID-19 crisis
Towards mission theory: A systematic literature review of its critiques and avenues for progress (2010–2025)
papers.abstract: During the last 15 years, researchers and practitioners alike showed a newfound interest in the potential of ‘mission-oriented’ innovation policy to tackle current societal challenges. In this period, the approach prompted multiple reflections and critiques from orthodox and heterodox scholars alike. However, a structured appraisal of this debate has been missing. Untangling its analytical complexity, this paper presents a systematic literature review of 224 articles and book chapters published between 2010 and 2025 to appraise the state-of-the-art debate within ‘mission theory’. Using the PRISMA Protocol and abductive thematic analysis, the paper identifies 18 themes mapped across two analytical dimensions: positioning (identifying either ‘external’ challenges or ‘internal’ gaps within mission theory); and layering (identifying challenges and gaps based on a ‘foundational’, ‘theoretical’, or ‘empirical’ ground). Building on the findings, the paper reflects on the sociological conditions preventing the progress of mission theory in contemporary research efforts – ultimately calling for greater epistemological reflexivity in the strategies adopted by researchers and practitioners to develop avenues for its further progress.

papers.title: From impact to legitimacy: Communicative responsibility and the governance of research impact
papers.abstract: Universities face growing pressure to make clearer the public value of research, yet documented impact does not automatically translate into public recognition or legitimacy. This paper develops the concept of Communicative Responsibility, the institutional and ethical obligation to communicate research outcomes in ways that are legible, accessible, and resonant beyond specialist assessment contexts. Drawing on responsible research literatures, including Responsible Research and Innovation (RRI) and Responsible Research in Business and Management (RRBM), we argue that communication should be treated as a core component of research governance and legitimacy. Empirically, we use the UK Research Excellence Framework (REF) 2021 Impact Database to examine the communicative strengths and limitations of existing impact evidence. REF impact case studies are not the only way to understand research impact, nor are they primarily written for public audiences. However, they offer a useful proxy for examining how impact might be perceived and how it could be shared more effectively. Using mixed methods, we combine qualitative content analysis of 119 purposively sampled Business and Management cases with quantitative text analysis of all 504 non-redacted cases in the field. Findings show diverse impacts generated through collaboration, interdisciplinarity, and international partnerships, but also substantial variation in communicability. Cases that identify beneficiaries, pathways to change, and accessible dissemination routes are better positioned to reduce the impact-recognition gap. We contribute to theorizing Communicative Responsibility as a governance-relevant extension of responsible research. Our findings have wider implications for how universities communicate impact beyond assessment systems.

papers.title: The Means of Prediction: How AI Really Works (and Who Benefits)
When women lead: local political representation and pro-women institutions
papers.abstract: Whether women in office govern differently from men is well documented; whether they govern differently for women is not. The latter is the crux of active representation theory, which expects representatives to act for those they mirror: does electing women change what governments do for women? We investigate the relationship between electing female mayors and councilors and the existence of Pro-Women Institutions across all 5,565 cities of Brazil during four election cycles (2008, 2012, 2016 and 2020). Our results partially support the active representation relationship. While female mayors’ presence increases the likelihood of pro-women institutions, local councilors either do not or are negatively linked to them. Robustness checks through a regression discontinuity design corroborate these findings, and heterogeneous treatment effects on race paint a wider picture about intersectionality. Our findings highlight how female elected representatives might achieve substantial change for their female constituents in local government.

papers.title: Claiming sociodigital futures? Knowledge practices and their consequences
papers.abstract: There is currently intense and widespread speculation about the implications of digital technologies for future societies, despite a wealth of evidence that past claims to predict how technology will shape the future have usually failed. Nonetheless, it is now well established that claims to knowledge about how emerging technologies will shape future worlds are performative, exercising powerful effects on the futures they claim to describe. Building on the Sociology of Expectations and work on Sociotechnical Imaginaries, this paper turns attention to the ontological and epistemological ‘nuts’ and ‘bolts’ of claims about digital technologies, social life and the future. We ask: how are these entities and the relations between them constituted and given traction as knowledge practices? Specifically, we explore the practices used by major future-claiming institutional actors in a selection of published documents. We find a strikingly coherent ontological performance of the relations between ‘the digital’, ‘the social’ and ‘the future’ and the circulation of (what comes to count as) knowledge across these institutions. Indeed, what is striking is the re-purposability of these knowledge practices despite the distinctive institutional interests in play. These knowledge practices offer a limited grasp on the futures that are currently in the making. Moreover, they enable the persistence of a latent set of assumptions which are powerful in limiting consideration of critical questions about the future.

papers.title: Whose voices and which effects? A scoping review of migration and social media effects
papers.abstract: Social media plays a central role in shaping migration experiences and public perceptions of migration. However, despite growing research activity, no systematic overview exists on how social media effects are examined across host and migrant populations. This scoping review synthesizes 65 empirical studies on social media effects in the context of migration published between 2020 and 2025. Guided by the differential susceptibility to media effects model, the analysis focuses on content types, sample characteristics, the conceptualization of social media, effect types, and mediating and moderating factors. The findings reveal two largely disconnected strands of research: quantitative, host-focused studies that emphasize negative attitudinal effects, and qualitative, migrant-centered studies that focus on empowerment. Framing effects, platform affordances, producer perspectives, and individual, structural, and social factors remain largely neglected. Overall, the review highlights the need for integrative research that bridges the perspectives of both hosts and migrants and pays greater attention to how migrants themselves perceive, interpret, and respond to social media portrayals and migration-related content.

papers.title: A response to Francis and Wesselink’s “measuring structural racism in neighborhoods”
Estimation of the relative effectiveness and waning of the monovalent third dose of COVID-19 vaccine against hospital admission in France: a novel self-controlled case series analysis
Correction: Effects of two community violence interruption programs on firearm violence in Washington, DC
Structure–behavior integrated risk prediction of vehicle groups using Graph Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Accurate identification of vehicle-group-level traffic risk is important for intelligent transportation safety management. Existing risk-prediction studies have mainly focused on individual vehicles, pairwise interactions, or aggregated surrogate safety indicators, while the role of group-level structure–behavior coupling remains insufficiently examined. To address this issue, this paper proposes a leakage-aware structure–behavior graph learning framework for Vehicle Group (VG) risk modeling. First, time-resolved VG graphs are constructed from high-frequency MAGIC trajectory data using an impact-induced grouping strategy with controlled supplementary spatial adjacency. Second, node-level surrogate risk states are defined using inverse Time-to-Collision (iTTC) and activated Post-Encroachment Time (PET), and then aggregated into VG-level surrogate risk labels through a group-risk ratio. Third, structural descriptors and behavioral features are integrated within a Graph Attention Network (GAT) for VG-level risk classification. To improve methodological transparency, the revised framework explicitly justifies the surrogate-labeling thresholds using empirical distributions, threshold tradeoff curves, and sensitivity analyses. It also includes leakage-audit experiments to examine whether model performance is driven by label-proximal surrogate quantities. Experiments on the MAGIC dataset show that the proposed model achieves strong and stable performance under repeated random seeds, with F1-score = 0.960 ± 0.002, ROC-AUC = 0.949 ± 0.008, PR-AUC = 0.991 ± 0.001, and Brier score = 0.058 ± 0.002. Compared with linear, neural, tree-based, and graph-based baselines, the proposed model provides competitive risk-identification performance, particularly in recall, false-negative control, and positive-class ranking. Additional robustness, prospective-prediction, and interpretability analyses indicate that the learned structure–behavior representation remains informative under temporal and sampling-frequency shifts and can highlight risk-relevant vehicles within VGs. The findings should be interpreted as evidence of structure-aware predictive association under a surrogate-labeling framework, rather than as proof that VG risk is inherently structural or that the model is deployment-ready. Overall, this study provides a more transparent and auditable graph-learning approach for VG-level surrogate risk modeling, offering decision-support insights for future CAV-oriented traffic safety management subject to external validation and deployment-oriented computational testing.

papers.title: Measuring Automatic Cognitive Responses to Erotic Stimuli Using Implicit Association Tests: Reliability and Validity Aspects
papers.abstract: Recently, implicit associations have been forwarded as relevant cognitive determinants of sexual desire and arousal. In the present study, using a cross-sectional design, implicit association tests (IAT) were used to measure the strength of automatic associations of erotic stimuli with positive versus negative valence (liking IAT) and with wanting versus not wanting (wanting IAT). The internal consistency and temporal stability, and the construct and criterion validity of the IATs were investigated. Additionally, the effects of stimulus mode on the psychometric properties of these IATs were examined. For this purpose, picture-and-word and full-picture IAT versions of the liking and wanting IATs were compared. Sexual function was measured using the Female Sexual Function Index for women and the International Index of Erectile Function for men. To examine the construct and criterion validity of the IATs, the Sexual Opinion Survey (SOS) and the Sexual Thoughts Questionnaire (STQ) were administered. A community sample was examined (N = 335 total; 234 women). The internal consistency and temporal stability of all IATs were found satisfactory to excellent. The criterion validity of the IATs demonstrated only a few small-size correlations with explicit sexual attitudes. Contrary to similar previous research, the IATs did not predict sexual function level. Speculative explanations for these unexpected findings are presented.

papers.title: Use of Post-Coital Strategies to Prevent Pregnancy: Findings from a National Sample of Adolescents and Young Adults in the United States
papers.abstract: In the context of increasing restrictions on sexual and reproductive health care, inadequate sex education, and increasing antihormonal contraceptive sentiment, we examined post-coital pregnancy prevention behavior among a nationally representative sample of U.S. adolescents and young adults (AYA). We developed a novel measure of post-coital contraceptive strategies (i.e., actions taken after sexual intercourse with the intent of reducing the likelihood of pregnancy) and fielded this measure for the first time as part of a 2025 online, population-based survey of English-speaking 15–29-year-olds assigned female at birth (n = 1,259). Of the 633 AYA who reported having ever had penile-vaginal sex and were not currently pregnant, 25.0% used at least one post-coital strategy to prevent pregnancy the last time they had sex. While methods with established effectiveness (i.e., emergency contraception and copper intrauterine device) were used by 8.9% respondents, 16.1% reported using a non-medically evidenced post-coital strategy, the most common being praying (9.4%). Post-coital strategy use varied by age, race and ethnicity, and number of contraceptive methods used. In multivariable analyses, contraceptive knowledge was negatively associated with post-coital strategy use. Regardless of effectiveness, post-coital strategies are common enough to warrant inclusion in behavioral surveillance and attention in health education and clinical practice.

papers.title: The Relationship Between Cognitive Processes, Self-Stigma, and Internalizing Psychopathology in Individuals with Sexual Interests in Minors
Being a Partner or a Mother: Breastfeeding Mothers’ Perceptions and Experiences of Breast Milk and Sexuality in the Postpartum Period
papers.abstract: Abstract This study aimed to explore breastfeeding mothers’ perceptions and experiences related to breast milk and sexuality between the third and sixth months postpartum. A descriptive qualitative design was employed. The sample consisted of 10 mothers, including primiparous ( n = 4) and multiparous ( n = 6) women, with a mean age of 29 years. Data were collected through individual semi-structured interviews. Thematic analysis was used to analyze the data. Three main themes emerged from the analysis: avoidance of sexuality, maintaining sexuality as a responsibility, and coping with the effects of breastfeeding on sexuality. Six subthemes were identified within these main themes: physical changes in sexual dynamics; psychological changes in sexual dynamics; religious, social, and cultural influences on sexuality; fulfillment of the female role; changing perceptions of breasts; and various coping strategies. The findings suggest that breastfeeding and postpartum physiological and sociocultural factors shape mothers’ sexual experiences, with sexuality often being perceived as inappropriate during this period due to cultural and religious norms, while participants’ perceptions related to breast milk also contribute to these experiences. Mothers attempt to balance breastfeeding with maintaining their sexual relationships, which frequently leads to emotional distress. It is recommended that healthcare professionals address breastfeeding, breast milk, and sexuality within breastfeeding education programs and provide individualized, culturally sensitive guidance for couples.

papers.title: Burnout Market Feminism: Urban Chinese Businesswomen in the Internet Age Ling Tang. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 2026. 208 pp. $50.00 (pbk). ISBN 9780262051880
Multi-electrolyzer system energy management strategy incorporating cold-hot start for improving green hydrogen production and electrolyzer lifespan
Decarbonization dispatch for AI computing center parks considering task-level carbon traceability
papers.abstract: The decarbonization dispatch of AI computing centers should not stop at controlling total park-level carbon emissions; it should also trace the energy sources, carbon-emission responsibility, and low-carbon labels of individual AI tasks. To address the limitation that existing studies mainly adopt park-average accounting and therefore cannot support task-level accounting, this paper proposes a decarbonization dispatch optimization method for AI computing center parks considering task-level carbon traceability. Taking the task execution trajectory as the main line, the proposed method links resource-pool startup and shutdown, IT power consumption, thermally inertial cooling, network storage, and energy-storage operation, thereby forming a closed relationship among the task ledger, energy-consumption ledger, and low-carbon ledger. Meanwhile, a unique low-carbon electricity claim and a label-violation CVaR constraint are introduced to control the risk of label failure under uncertain scenarios. Rolling-dispatch results on the Chenggong, Yunnan, China and the modified IEEE 118-bus system show that the proposed method can significantly improve task-level low-carbon performance with only a small increase in low-carbon attribute procurement and energy-storage throughput. In the Chenggong park case, the operating cost is reduced by 6.6%, and market-based park carbon emissions are reduced by 11.3%. The method provides a dispatch modeling basis for shifting low-carbon computing services from park-average accounting to task-level verification.

papers.title: Exploiting dynamics of electricity–hydrogen–carbon markets using adaptive operating rules for hybrid energy systems
papers.abstract: Electricity markets have traditionally shaped the operating strategies of hybrid energy systems (HESs) integrating hydropower, wind, and photovoltaic resources. Meanwhile, the rapid emergence of hydrogen and carbon markets is transforming system operation by linking electricity supply, hydrogen production, and carbon-related revenues. However, existing electricity–hydrogen operating rules do not account for how pathway-dependent carbon values alter the allocation of renewable electricity between grid delivery and hydrogen production. This study embeds pathway-dependent carbon valuation into the shared energy-allocation decision, allowing the carbon signal to reshape the relative benefits of grid delivery and hydrogen production and propagate into hybrid system operation and operating-rule parameters. An operation-mediated price-feedback framework is incorporated into the long-term operation model to maximize operating benefit and supply assurance. The optimized results are then synthesized into adaptive operating rules through a parameterization–simulation–optimization framework. A case study of the Ertan hydro–hydrogen–wind–photovoltaic system shows that the reservoir release is the key decision variable in rule formulation. The derived optimal operating rules achieve 616.03 million USD in operating benefit and a 98.96% assurance rate, improving conventional rules by 14.94% and 10.79%. These results demonstrate that adaptive operating rules can effectively exploit electricity–hydrogen–carbon market dynamics, thereby enhancing the energy use efficiency of HESs.

papers.title: A two-stage restoration model for power distribution systems with integrated satellite-terrestrial communication networks
papers.abstract: With the development of the satellite internet, the low Earth orbit (LEO)-based satellite communication network (SCN) is gradually applied to power grids to meet the emergency communication requirements. By the advantages of SCN, this paper proposes a two-stage restoration framework for power distribution systems (PDSs) with an integrated satellite-terrestrial communication network (STCN). In Stage 1, a multi-time period operation simulation model for LEO satellite constellation is established to derive the available satellite communication links during restoration. Then, a MILP restoration model is developed that considers the operation constraints of PDSs and STCNs in Stage 2 to obtain the optimal PDS restoration strategy under cyber-physical interaction. The STCN includes an SCN and a terrestrial communication network (TCN), which are coordinated to transmit the operation information of PDSs. Finally, the effectiveness of the optimal restoration strategy is verified by constructing a constellation with 1000 LEO satellites for the PDSs in a practical area. Also, the influences of LEO satellite operation parameters are analyzed in the case studies.

papers.title: Evaluating the global economy-wide impact of energy efficiency policies in buildings

Household infrastructure expansion without spatial convergence during urbanization: Evidence from Chinese cities
papers.abstract: Infrastructure provision underpins basic needs and socioeconomic development, yet systematic city-level evidence on how household infrastructure service provision and its spatial inequalities evolve during the rapid urbanization remains limited. Using official statistics for 295 prefecture-level cities in China from 2006 to 2022, we assess household access to water and energy services. To account for fuel substitution, natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas are treated as substitutable energy carriers, with the higher of their supply rates representing household energy provision. We construct a two-dimensional infrastructure provision index ( IP ), quantify population-weighted inequality across cities and provinces, decompose inequality changes into mean-provision and spatial-dispersion effects, and classify provincial trajectories of within-province inequality. The population-weighted mean IP increased from 0.21 to 0.51, and provision improved in 289 of the 295 cities. Despite this broad expansion, between-city inequality increased from 0.29 to 0.42, while between-province inequality increased from 0.23 to 0.28. Decomposition shows that rising average provision exerted an inequality-reducing effect, but this was more than offset by increasing spatial dispersion. Within-province trajectories were heterogeneous, ranging from decline or reversal to strong increase, with differences primarily associated with the magnitude and timing of dispersion growth. Socioeconomic development and urbanization were positively associated with provision in descriptive comparisons, but these relationships were not stable across panel specifications. These results show that broad improvements in household infrastructure provision do not necessarily lead to spatial convergence, underscoring the need to evaluate both the overall expansion and spatial distribution of infrastructure services.

papers.title: Needs for more integrated, inclusive, and policy-Relevant modeling of food system transitions: Insights from a systematic review
Insufficient Environmental Protection by the European Regulatory Framework for Pesticides
papers.abstract: Abstract Schriever et al. (2025) argue that environmental risk assessment of pesticides in the European Union is sufficiently protective and that regulatory thresholds are rarely exceeded. Here, we reexamine these claims based on existing evidence from monitoring, systematic reviews, and different types of field studies. The available evidence indicates that measured pesticide concentrations frequently exceed predicted concentrations and regulatory thresholds and are associated with adverse ecological impacts. The mechanisms driving this result include the joint action of pesticides applied in temporal and spatial proximity, varied environmental conditions, interactive effects of pesticides with additional stressors, and indirect ecological effects that propagate within biological communities. These neglected intricacies explain why current single-substance prospective assessments tend to underpredict real-world pesticide exposure and impact in field settings. The corollary is that the current regulatory framework in Europe proves to be insufficient to protect biodiversity and ecosystems. Priority regulatory reforms include strengthening postregistration monitoring, refining predictive exposure models, and explicitly considering landscape context, indirect and mixture effects, and interactions with nonchemical stressors.

papers.title: Ebullition-Enhanced Release of Microplastics from Aquatic Sediment to Overlying Water: An Overlooked Transport Pathway
papers.abstract: Abstract Microplastics (MPs) in aquatic systems are typically attributed to wastewater, runoff and atmospheric inputs, whereas the remobilization of sediment-associated MPs by benthic gas ebullition remains poorly understood. Here, we show that air-purged ebullition mobilized four common MPs, polyethylene (PE), polyethylene terephthalate (PET), polyvinyl chloride (PVC), and polylactic acid (PLA), from sediments into the overlying water, with release ratios of 8.9%–12.1% over 9 d. Suspended MP concentrations in the overlying water increased rapidly during the first 48 h, followed by slower release and eventual plateauing, with the decelerating release behavior empirically described by a power-law model. Theoretical calculations suggest that aggregation with suspended sediment can reduce the flotation velocities of MPs from 9.38–9.99 cm·s–1 to 8.64–9.95 cm·s–1. Combined experimental observations and theoretical analyses support a coupled flotation mechanism involving MPs attachment to rising bubbles, bubble-driven flow that counteracts gravitational settling, and transient pressure gradients. These processes could convert sediments from a long-term sink into a secondary source of MPs during ebullition. Overall, this study identifies benthic gas ebullition as an underappreciated pathway for MP remobilization and provides a mechanistic framework for understanding the fate and transport of sediment-associated MPs in aquatic environments.

papers.title: High Sewage Sludge Loading Drives N2O-Dominated Warming Potential and Destabilizes Soil Microbial Networks during Ryegrass Cultivation
papers.abstract: Abstract The application of sludge as a fertilizer contributes to greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, but the associated microbial and geochemical mechanisms across sludge application rates remain unclear. A field experiment evaluated three sludge application rates (0, 3, and 30 kg/m2) under seedling transplanting (T0, T3, and T30), with an additional direct-seeding treatment (S30) at 30 kg/m2 (wet-weight basis). The results indicated that higher sludge rates elevated cumulative CO2 and N2O emissions, with N2O contributing 69.26–97.74% to the total global warming potential. In contrast, sludge application shifted cumulative CH4 fluxes from net emission in T0 to net uptake in all sludge-amended treatments. S30 produced 1.14 and 2.94 times more CO2 and N2O, respectively, than did T30. The K-edge XANES of calcium revealed dynamic shifts in soil calcium speciation associated with GHG variations, with CaC2O4 (14–23%) peaking at maximum GHG emissions and Cax(C6H8O6)y increasing to 32.8% at later stages, consistent with a calcium pump effect. High sludge application altered microbial diversity, co-occurrence patterns, and network stability. Functional gene analysis indicated an enhanced incomplete denitrification potential through increased norC abundance and reduced N2O reduction capacity. Overall, the sludge application rate was the primary driver of N2O-dominated warming potential, while the planting method exerted additional effects under high sludge loading.

papers.title: Inhalation of Environmentally Simulated PET Nanoplastics Induces Demyelinating Disorders via the CXCL12/CXCR4 Axis
papers.abstract: Abstract The health threat from airborne nanoplastics (NPs) remains unclear, as despite inhalation being a more direct brain entry route than ingestion, current understanding relies on oral exposure and commercial particle models that obscure realistic risks. Here, by integrating environmentally simulated polyethylene terephthalate (PET)-NPs with an aerosol inhalation model that mirrors real-world human exposure (0.1, 1, and 10 mg/m3), we demonstrate that chronic NP inhalation translocated to the brain and induced demyelination, neuroinflammation, and cognitive deficits. The most pronounced effects were observed at the highest exposure dose (10 mg/m3), which is relevant to the occupational settings. Mechanistically, NP exposure triggered astrocytic CXCL12 release, leading to CXCR4-dependent microglial activation and cytokine network dysregulation. In vitro, blockade of CXCR4 with AMD3100 attenuated NP-induced microglial migration and oligodendrocytic myelin basic protein reduction. Our study thus definitively links realistic airborne NP exposure to the key neuropathological features of demyelinating disorders and pinpoints a modifiable molecular pathway that could inform exposure-based preventive strategies. These findings underscore the need for further assessment of airborne NP risks, particularly in occupational settings.

papers.title: Rising food production and persistent inequality over global border areas: A conflict between growth and distribution

A scenario-based evaluation framework for renewable capacity scale and photovoltaic capacity ratio in a hydro–wind–photovoltaic–pumped-storage hybrid energy system
papers.abstract: Renewable-capacity planning in hydro–wind–photovoltaic–pumped-storage hybrid energy systems is jointly affected by wind–photovoltaic output, inflow, renewable capacity, and photovoltaic capacity ratio, yet their coupled effects on operation and capacity preference remain unclear. This study develops a scenario-based resource–operation–capacity evaluation framework for a cascade hydropower–wind–photovoltaic–pumped-storage system. Five cumulative-probability levels of wind–photovoltaic joint output and five hydrological exceedance-frequency levels form 25 combined scenarios. Normalized historical recurrence weights are derived through similar-year intersections from 26 assigned historical years. In each scenario, 210 fixed combinations of renewable capacity and photovoltaic capacity ratio are evaluated using a medium- and short-term operational model solved by the non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (NSGA-II). A two-level decision method identifies the highest-scoring configuration in each scenario and then aggregates configuration scores across all scenarios using recurrence weights. Application to the clean-energy base in the middle reaches of the Yalong River Basin shows that inflow dominates operational-performance variation by affecting hydropower availability and the generation-plan level. Wind–photovoltaic resource conditions alter the balance between renewable output and flexible regulation, whereas the photovoltaic capacity ratio changes joint-output stability and the regulation required from cascade hydropower and pumped storage. Increasing renewable capacity raises transmitted energy, but excessive expansion increases curtailment and load-loss risks. The scenario-dependent highest-scoring configurations span 9000–12000 MW and photovoltaic capacity ratios of 35 %–55 %. Cross-scenario weighting identifies 9000 MW and a 40 % photovoltaic capacity ratio as the probability-weighted optimal configuration under the adopted settings. The framework links representative resource conditions, system operation, and capacity decisions for hydro-dominated renewable-energy planning.

papers.title: Time-interleaved multistage heat pipe-assisted adsorptive dehumidification for stable and high-efficiency supply air control
papers.abstract: This study proposes a multistage heat pipe-assisted adsorptive dehumidifier (HP-AD) designed to address the inherent limitations of conventional desiccant systems, such as excessive supply air temperature rise and high regeneration energy requirements. A fundamental deficiency in single-module HP-ADs is the occurrence of high-amplitude, sawtooth wave-like fluctuations in the supply air’s hydrothermal states. These instabilities are intrinsically tied to the adsorption/desorption kinetics of the adsorbent coupled with the discrete 180° rotation cycles of the module, which collectively compromise the consistency of indoor air quality. To mitigate these fluctuations, a multistage architecture comprising five adsorbent-coated fin-heat pipe modules was developed and experimentally validated. Central to this system is a time-interleaved operational sequence, where each module rotates 180° based on a predefined phase-shift interval to achieve quasi-steady-state dehumidification. To maximize thermal effectiveness via the thermosyphon effect, the heat pipes were oriented parallel to the gravitational vector, enabling the latent heat of the working fluid to passively recover adsorption heat and facilitate water vapor desorption in the regeneration section. Experimental results demonstrate that the five-stage configuration significantly stabilizes the outlet conditions, achieving a 59.5% reduction in temperature variation and a 91.5% decrease in humidity fluctuation compared to a single-module baseline. Furthermore, the moisture removal rate and coefficient of performance improved by 2.9 and 2.5 times, respectively, due to superior thermal utilization. These findings validate the proposed system as a high-performance, high-efficiency, and robust prototype for advanced ventilation applications requiring high-precision indoor air quality control.

Projected changes in global soil organic carbon stocks and their vulnerability to drought
papers.abstract: Projected changes in global soil organic carbon (SOC) stocks under intensifying drought remain incompletely characterized, limiting assessments of terrestrial carbon vulnerability under climate change. We combined bias-corrected climate drivers with a skill- and independence-weighted ensemble of seven CMIP6 Earth system models. We then used standardized drought indices, multiscale partial-Spearman analyses, and land-cover comparisons to examine historical and projected changes in SOC stocks and heterotrophic respiration (R h ) fluxes, which represent complementary stock and respiratory-flux indicators. Under SSP5-8.5, the multi-model weighted mean projected a small decrease in late-century SOC relative to the 1985–2014 baseline (−0.26%), whereas changes among the seven individual models ranged from −4.68% to +3.32%, with five models projecting increases. In contrast, R h increased in all seven models, and the weighted-ensemble mean for 2070–2099 was 43.54% higher than the historical baseline. Projected SOC decreases in the weighted ensemble were concentrated in parts of the Northern Hemisphere mid- and high latitudes, whereas changes across lower-latitude and subtropical regions were spatially heterogeneous. At the global scale, SSMI showed the largest selected association magnitude with SOC, whereas the selected association magnitudes for Rh were generally similar for SPEI and SSMI. Across the 1–120-month candidate range, the selected accumulation scales varied across grid cells and drought indices. We interpret these values as descriptive summaries of the accumulation windows associated with the largest retained partial-Spearman coefficients. These association results are based on MMEM-derived drought indices paired with MMWM SOC and R h products, and their model dependence remains unquantified. The analysis maps scenario- and region-dependent patterns of drought-associated SOC vulnerability. Differences in CMIP6 soil‑carbon structure and among benchmark products limit quantitative interpretation.

papers.title: Mapping European land-use driven carbon losses and gains: How scenarios, indicators, and methods shape outcomes
Monitoring and evaluating the just transition: Reflections on a of for Scotland, with lessons for beyond
Balancing Productivity, Ecology, and Social Well‐Being: Insights From Three Decades of Farmland Transformation in China
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Balancing food security, social equity, and ecological sustainability remains a persistent challenge in global agricultural systems. While economic and ecological aspects of land‐use transitions have been extensively studied, the long‐term dynamics of social functions and their interactions with other functions are less understood. This study investigates the decadal spatiotemporal patterns, functional relationships, and spatial association factors of farmland multifunctionality in China's major grain‐producing regions in 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2020. A multidimensional indicator system was developed to capture economic, social, and ecological functions across 185 prefecture‐level cities, and a CRITIC‐entropy hybrid weighting method was applied to construct multifunctionality indices. Correlation analysis with false discovery rate correction was used to examine trade‐offs and synergies, and the GeoDetector model was employed to identify the explanatory power of factor stratification and factor interactions. The results reveal a paradoxical trajectory across the four benchmark years: while economic and ecological functions improved substantially, the social function declined. Functional relationships were reconfigured, with economic‐ecological interactions changing from conflict to synergy, whereas social‐ecological interactions changed from synergy to trade‐off. Natural conditions were weakly associated with spatial heterogeneity, market and demographic variables exhibited stronger associations before 2010, and policy‐related variables, especially farmland protection policy indicators, showed the strongest statistical associations thereafter. These findings provide one of the most comprehensive large‐scale and long‐term assessments of farmland multifunctionality transitions in China's grain regions. They highlight the importance of institutional arrangements in explaining spatial variation in trade‐offs and synergies, and underscore the need for integrated governance strategies that simultaneously promote productivity, ecological integrity, and rural social well‐being.

papers.title: Economies of Scale to Consumption in Collective Households
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Browning et al. (2013) model collective‐household economies of scale in goods consumption by having each good be partly shared, instead of each good being public or private. We modify their model to achieve simple point identification and estimation of the economies of scale of consumption of each good, and we provide a new index of household level economies of scale. Our model has a linear form, permits households of varying composition, including children, and accommodates unobserved heterogeneity in both preferences and in the economies of scale of each good. We provide estimates using Canadian Surveys of Household Spending data.

papers.title: Financing Risk in Infrastructure FDI : A Property Rights Perspective
papers.abstract: Abstract Property rights theory (PRT) focuses on how allocation of residual control rights of ownership resolves incentive problems from incomplete contracts. However, when asset ownership is efficient for a transacting party, PRT ignores financial resource constraints preventing the party from purchasing it. We include creditors, who provide financial resources but are exposed to agency conflicts with equity‐owners, in property rights analysis. Multinational enterprises (MNEs) reduce agency conflict with creditors through contractual covenants and collateral. Yet contracts are incomplete. Under incomplete contracts, how do MNEs mitigate financing risk, the risk that supply of capital from creditors is delayed or entirely unavailable? We distinguish between incomplete contracts arising from weak property rights institutions and weak contracting institutions. We theorize that allocation of specified control rights through operating and maintenance (O&M) contracts to MNE‐owners mitigates financing risk in countries with weak property rights institutions because MNE‐owners possess high‐powered incentives to exert requisite effort to adapt operations to unexpected contingencies. In contrast, such allocation of O&M contracts to MNE‐owners increases financing risk in countries with weak contracting institutions because such allocation increases agency conflict between MNE‐owners and creditors. Empirical analyses of 363 project‐financed investments in 52 countries worth US$1.53 trillion over 1990–2018 support our theory.

papers.title: Guiding Attention for Sustainability‐Oriented Innovation: How Strategic Leaders Translate Ethical Values
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Research on sustainable leadership recognizes the importance of leaders' values but says less about how these values gain organizational awareness. Drawing on the attention‐based view of the firm, this study examines how strategic leaders translate ethical values into organizational attention and under what conditions this process supports sustainability‐oriented innovation. We conduct a comparative multiple‐case study of six organizations in France, based on 92 interviews across hierarchical levels, site visits, and documentary evidence. The analysis identifies three configurations. Where formal attentional structures are weak, innovation projects temporarily bridge leaders and employees around shared values. Where leaders provide “air coverage,” ethical commitments guide strategic boundaries but remain partly decoupled from operational routines. Where attention is structurally distributed, ethical and business priorities are tightly coupled across organizational levels. These findings show that values do not automatically translate into action: Their organizational effects depend on perceived authenticity, communication channels, and attentional structures. The study extends sustainable leadership research by specifying the conditions of value enactment and extends the attention‐based view by revealing the normative foundations of attention distribution.

papers.title: Can Beauty Save the World? A Multimethod Analysis of Regulatory Focus Appeals in Climate Change Advertising
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigates how organizations can strategically design climate change advertising to foster greater consumer involvement by comparing the effectiveness of promotion‐ and prevention‐focused advertising appeals. Using a sequential explanatory mixed‐methods design, a facial coding experiment revealed that promotion appeals reduced sadness, which in turn positively influenced attitudes toward the ad and increased climate change involvement. A follow‐up qualitative study with communication managers provides practical insights into how these findings can inform the design of climate change advertising campaigns. By identifying the affective mechanism through which promotion‐focused appeals enhance climate change involvement, this study advances research on green advertising and climate change advertising and offers evidence‐based guidance for organizations seeking to design advertising campaigns that more effectively involve consumers with climate change. As organizations increasingly rely on green advertising to support sustainability initiatives, understanding how to design communications that motivate meaningful climate action remains a critical challenge for both researchers and practitioners.

papers.title: From ESG to Biodiversity: Decoupling and Its Asymmetries as a Source of Biodiversity Risk
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT While environmental, social and governance (ESG) research has extensively documented the risks stemming from disclosure and performance gaps, the growing demand for biodiversity reporting raises concerns that analogous inconsistencies may amplify corporations' exposure to biodiversity risk. Using a sample of 917 firm‐year observations from 2015 to 2023, this study examines whether biodiversity decoupling, the divergence between biodiversity disclosure and performance, is associated with corporations' exposure to biodiversity risk. Drawing on the legitimacy theory, we find that higher levels of biodiversity decoupling are associated with increased biodiversity risk. However, when distinguishing between the types of decoupling, we observe no significant association for positive decoupling, whereas negative decoupling is associated with lower biodiversity risk, suggesting that disclosure‐performance gaps operate differently in the context of biodiversity. We further show that environmental audit moderates the relationship between biodiversity decoupling and biodiversity risk by attenuating the association of positive biodiversity decoupling and the risk‐reduction association of negative biodiversity decoupling. Overall, our findings offer timely insights for corporations seeking to manage legitimacy pressures, for investors aiming to understand the drivers of biodiversity risk and for policymakers wishing to develop more robust biodiversity reporting standards.

papers.title: Balancing risk and opportunity: Digital transformation, cybersecurity investments, and export performance in low-tech firms
Navigating the paradox: Empowerment and power dynamics in international social entrepreneurship
Business Model Bundles: Implications for Innovation in the Circular Economy
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Business model (BM) innovation is essential to the transition towards a circular economy, yet customers often resist circular BMs. This study investigates how manufacturers can innovate BMs for circularity in ways that increase customer acceptance. Drawing on a multiple‐case study of four manufacturers offering 21 product‐service system BMs, we introduce a new concept, the business model bundle: a strategic offering that packages multiple BMs within one contract and gives customers flexibility to move between them over time. We identify three defining characteristics: the combination of different BMs, contractual flexibility, and temporal transition. We theorize the BM bundle as a new form of BM innovation that creates, delivers, and captures value through the configuration of existing BMs rather than the invention of new ones. Our evidence indicates that the flexibility offered by BM bundles can reduce customers' initial commitment and make previously resisted circular BMs more acceptable. However, bundles may lead towards either greater or lesser circularity and therefore require deliberate design. The study extends innovation management and BM research by introducing the BM bundle that could open a new avenue in the field of BM innovation, and by identifying flexibility as a mechanism linking BM bundles to firm‐perceived customer acceptance.

Central Bank Economic Transparency and Managerial Learning
papers.abstract: Abstract Central banks increasingly disclose their private information regarding the economy’s current and future state (CBET). Consistent with CBET shifting investors’ collection and pricing of aggregate-level (where managers do not have an information advantage) toward firm-level (where managers do have an information advantage) information, we find that CBET reduces managers’ learning from stock price. The results are (1) pronounced when firms do not provide guidance and when noise trading in firms’ stock is low, and (2) robust to using the 2013–2014 amendments to the Bank of England’s Inflation Report as an exogenous shock. Additional evidence suggests that CBET lowers investment efficiency. (JEL E22, E52, M41)

papers.title: Directing the Labor Market: Shared Directors and Employee Flows
papers.abstract: Abstract Using résumé data on over 20 million U.S. workers, we find that the flow of employees between a pair of firms sharply drops by about 20% during periods in which the firms share a board director. This relationship is stronger in settings where firms have greater potential gains from limiting worker mobility and is most pronounced for higher-skilled employees. Moreover, we find more connected firms have lower rates of internal promotion and no improvements in employee satisfaction. The evidence is consistent with shared directors serving as a mechanism for labor market coordination. (JEL G34, G38, J42, J62, J08, K21, K31, M50)

Macroeconomic Implications of Executive Pay Caps,
papers.abstract: I study the introduction of statutory caps on executive pay ratios (pay caps) in a span-of-control economy with heterogeneous managerial talent. Managers hire fewer workers than they would in the absence of pay caps, and the marginal product of labour is not equalized among firms. The ability of the marginal manager declines. Inequality between managers and workers, and among managers, declines, but inequality among workers increases. Quantitatively, overall inequality decreases substantially, especially via a reduction in top income shares, but the GDP losses are also significant. In addition, the redistribution favours the “middle” deciles between 50 and 90, rather than the bottom 50% of the income distribution. Future work will build on this “first pass” to analyse the effect of pay caps in economies distorted by monopsony power, non-pecuniary benefits of control, and managerial rent extraction.

The carbon reduction effects of new infrastructure construction: Evidence from local government special bonds in China
The fast and the studious? Ramadan observance and student performance
papers.abstract: Abstract We examine how religious observance affects educational performance by studying the years in which Ramadan overlapped with the national end-of-secondary-school exams in the Netherlands. Using administrative microdata and a difference-in-differences design, we find that students who are most likely to fast obtain lower exam scores and are more likely to fail to graduate. As expected given the structure of the Dutch exam system, the increase in failure risk is concentrated among students near the pass threshold. Effects are larger in more religiously segregated schools. For longer-term outcomes, we document a substantially higher likelihood of dropping out among students aged 18 and older, who are legally permitted to leave school and therefore at risk of doing so. Finally, analyses of exam timing suggest that modest adjustments—such as avoiding scheduling two exams on the same day during Ramadan—may help reduce the disadvantages experienced by observant students.

papers.title: How confirmation bias makes persuaders more honest
papers.abstract: We study a Bayesian persuasion game in which a decision maker (DM) incurs psychological costs from belief-disconfirming information and chooses whether to engage with the sender’s experiment. We model preference-based confirmation bias as psychological discomfort from exposure to signals that conflict with the DM’s prior beliefs. Whenever persuasion is feasible, the sender must commit to a strictly more informative experiment than in the Kamenica–Gentzkow (2011) benchmark. This increases the DM’s “actual” welfare, defined as material welfare excluding the psychological cost term, when confirmation bias is moderate, while persuasion fails when the bias exceeds a threshold and the DM disengages. We then introduce processing-based confirmation bias, modeled as systematic misperception of signals. In isolation, it does not change equilibrium behavior or the DM’s “actual” welfare, but when combined with preference-based bias it strengthens the disciplining effect for the DM. A dynamic extension shows that future engagement concerns further increase the sender’s incentive to provide informative signals.

papers.title: Selection and screening in cyber insurance markets
papers.abstract: Abstract This paper studies how information frictions shape demand, screening, and contract design in the U.S. cyber insurance market. I develop a framework in which firms sort into coverage based on latent cyber risk while insurers screen using coarse signals and manage residual exposure more through coverage quantities than through price. Using proprietary broker data, I document three findings consistent with this mechanism. First, higher‐risk firms are more likely to enter the brokered market and apply for coverage. Second, conditional on application, insurer acceptance is more closely related to a survey‐based score than to external risk measures that better capture realized incidents. Third, among issued policies, differences in assessed risk are reflected more in limits and adjusted coverage than in price. The results show that cyber insurance capacity is constrained not only by aggregate supply, but by how coarse risk classification generates residual adverse selection that insurers manage through contract design.

papers.title: What can we gain from pooling VAR and local projection impulse response functions?
N-LAS-IAM: Climate change in a balance-of-payments framework
papers.abstract: Climate change is becoming a macro-financial development problem for peripheral economies, yet integrated assessment models remain poorly equipped to analyse climate vulnerability in externally constrained developing countries. Existing heterodox models are mostly closed or global, while balance-of-payments-constrained growth models treat climate in reduced form and incompletely formalise the financial channel. This paper introduces the N-LAS-IAM, a recursive framework coupling a Thirlwall–Hussain growth core with endogenous green structural change, capital flows under financial fragility, sovereign risk, and a climate module mapping global emissions into damages that feed back into profitability and sovereign fragility. Green structural change is endogenised through logistic diffusion equations governing trade income elasticities as functions of green R&D and the real exchange rate. The model is explored via Monte Carlo experiments in which damage intensity and climate-to-risk transmission vary while emissions, policy, and structural-change parameters remain fixed. Three results emerge. First, higher damage produces a more fragile debt regime with elevated spreads, tighter financing, and prolonged deleveraging. Second, damages widen the elasticity gap between exports and imports, slowing green upgrading and locking the economy into lower-sophistication trade patterns. Third, the damage-to-fragility relationship is nonlinear: below a threshold the economy absorbs shocks, but above it a self-reinforcing regime emerges where lower productivity, higher spreads, weaker inflows, and structural regression feed on one another. These findings suggest that physical damages erode policy capabilities by raising external finance costs when green investment is most needed, and that early mitigation may yield convex macroeconomic returns for peripheral economies under balance-of-payments constraints.

papers.title: Know its worth? Factors affecting the social acceptability of water reuse: A mixed methods planned behavior model
papers.abstract: Due to strong demographic pressure, rapid urban development, and climate change, water demand is increasing while usable freshwater supplies are being depleted. The reuse of treated wastewater (RTWW) is one of the avenues currently being explored to ensure the quantitative and qualitative security of the water supply. The interests for social acceptability emerged with risk management approaches and the subsequent debates on the role of technical progress, the implementation of major development projects, and their consequences for the environment between the late 1970s and early 1980s. The purpose of this article is to identify the factors that influence the building of RTWW acceptability. This study was carried out in southern France. It combines a quantitative survey on behavior related to engaging in RTWW, based on Ajzen's theory of planned behavior, with a qualitative socioeconomic study aimed at understanding representations and beliefs regarding RTWW. The findings show that a lack of knowledge about RTWW and the implementation of only a few RTWW projects result in a normative gap and a perceived lack of control. In addition, trust in managers and public authorities, the quality of treatments, as well as risks perceptions – particularly those relating to health – significantly influence intentions to engage in RTWW. Lastly, several factors such as emotions, types of uses, and environmental awareness play an underlying role by helping build perceptions of water reuse, trust in relevant stakeholders, and more accurate perceptions of risks.

papers.title: Assessing the conditional calibration of interval forecasts using decompositions of the interval score
High-dimensional portfolio optimization with weight constraints: Forecasting models utilizing GARCH-EVT, R-vine copula, and SCAD penalty
Random satisficing model: Characterization and (generic) identification
papers.abstract: Satisficing choice is a well-known decision-making rule. However, as the literature shows, its predictive power is limited because identifying the underlying primitives is difficult. We consider a random satisficing model (RSM) where the decision maker is endowed with a preference, a random threshold, and a random search order. We characterize RSM with two axioms that use the concept of “virtual satisficing sets” introduced in the paper. We also show that the underlying preference can be generically identified when the distribution of search orders has full support and is known to the analyst. Further, we consider a possible generalization of the result when the analyst does not have full knowledge of the distribution of search orders, and when the stochastic search orders do not necessarily have full support.

papers.title: Valuing local water quality in Ontario using revealed preference data
papers.abstract: Abstract Improving water quality is an important goal for policymakers, yet understanding the economic benefits people receive from changes in water quality is challenging because many of the benefits are non‐market in nature. We use spatially explicit lake Secchi disk depth measures and information on over 320,000 property sales to provide the most extensive revealed preference value estimates of water clarity improvements in Canada. We find that a 10% increase in water clarity (as measured by Secchi disk depth) appreciates nearby property values by 0.56%. We do not find evidence for higher price premiums for properties located within 0–250 m of a lake compared to 250–500 m. The findings remain consistent when employing property fixed‐effect models and a series of alternative model specifications. A 10% improvement in lake water clarity in southern Ontario is estimated to yield a total benefit of $2 billion across properties with an aggregate property value of $359 billion, translating to an average benefit of $151 per household. The increase in property values could provide $31 million in additional annual municipal tax revenue to fund water quality improvement initiatives.

papers.title: What Are the Impacts of Certificate‐of‐Need Laws? A Review of the Evidence
papers.abstract: This study reviews the literature on the impacts of Certificate-of-Need (CON) laws on outcomes related to hospitals. CON laws require the approval of states' health planning agencies for health care providers to engage in regulated actions such as opening or expanding facilities or purchasing equipment. Economic theory suggests that barriers to entry should reduce competition, leading to higher prices, greater per-firm quantity but lower market quantity, and larger net revenues for incumbent providers. However, defenders of CON laws argue that they ensure high quality standards for new entrants, while also offsetting distortions that disadvantage hospitals and put some at risk of closure. The preponderance of available evidence points toward CON laws restricting entry of new competitors, which in turn increases the number of procedures per hospital. At the same time, CON laws also appear to inhibit hospital expansion, and there is little evidence of increased prices or higher hospital profitability. Studies on hospital efficiency and quality of care for procedures performed exclusively at hospitals mostly point to null or negative effects, but evidence on quality is more mixed for services that can be provided outside of hospitals. With that said, there is a need for new research that utilizes the latest tools for identifying causal effects and better accounts for the wide variation in CON laws across states.

papers.title: Symbolic Incentives Can Affect the Frequency of Blood and Plasma Donations: Evidence From 12 Years of Donors' Behavior
papers.abstract: We investigate how donors respond to symbolic incentives, specifically medals, tied to donation intensity and duration. To this aim, we employ panel data encompassing the entire population of blood and plasma donors affiliated with the primary donor association (AVIS) in Tuscany, Italy, covering the period from 2008 to 2019. The structure of the award scheme adopted by AVIS enables us to examine the impact of two distinct characteristics of the symbolic incentives: the assignment as either private or public and the criterion of assignment based exclusively on the number of donations (donation-only) or, under less demanding donation requirements, also on the years of membership (donation-and-membership). After controlling for time-constant unobservable individual traits that may influence the level and the evolution of performance over a donor's career, we find that (i) these symbolic awards do not affect behavior before their obtainment, (ii) receiving an award through the donation-and-membership criterion leads to a subsequent increase in donation frequency, and (iii) receiving an award through the donation-only criterion, regardless of whether it is announced publicly or privately, does not boost donors' performance. These findings suggest that symbolic awards are effective when bestowed upon less accomplished donors by making their attainment not solely contingent on performance but also on membership, and are related to community identification and self-image concerns rather than status-seeking behavior.

papers.title: Convergence to collusion in algorithmic pricing
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence algorithms are increasingly used by firms to set prices. Previous research shows that they can learn to collude, but how quickly and reliably they can do so has remained an open question. I study average-reward soft actor-critic algorithms that set continuous prices in the workhorse environment of this literature: a repeated Bertrand duopoly with symmetric firms, deterministic logit demand, and constant marginal costs, where agents observe only market prices and their own profits. The algorithms can converge to a collusive outcome within 50,000 periods, and in 36% of simulations learned punishments make one-period deviations unprofitable, so that high prices are mutual best responses. Successful simulations show cooperative behaviour supported by reward-punishment schemes that discourage deviations. When high prices are not supported by punishments, profitable deviations are typically on the order of hundredths of a percent.
